internet-of-things.tagline: Sensors, ESP32, MQTT, cloud, edge and IoT security.

lessons.title: What is the Internet of Things? Definition and architecture
yt: internet of things introduction architecture layers
IoT applications smart home smart agriculture industry 4.0

blocks.x: The **Internet of Things (IoT)** is a network of physical objects ("things") with sensors, processing ability and connectivity that collect and exchange data over the internet, often acting on it with little human input.
Why now?
Cheap sensors and microcontrollers (an ESP32 costs a few hundred rupees), ubiquitous Wi-Fi/4G/5G, cloud computing, and better analytics and AI.
Basic building blocks

x: **Things / devices:** sensors (measure), actuators (act), a microcontroller or small computer.
**Connectivity:** Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Zigbee, LoRaWAN, NB-IoT, cellular.
**Data processing:** at the device (edge), a gateway (fog) or the cloud.
**User interface / application:** mobile app, dashboard, alerts.

blocks.x: Layered architectures

**Three-layer:** Perception (sensors, actuators) → Network (transport) → Application (services). **Five-layer:** Perception → Transport → Processing (middleware, storage, analytics) → Application → Business (policies, revenue, privacy). **Cloud-edge view:** Device → Gateway → Cloud, with decisions made at the most suitable level.
Characteristics
Connectivity, sensing, intelligence, scalability (billions of devices), low power, heterogeneity (many vendors and protocols), and security/privacy needs.
Examples

x: **Smart home:** lights, thermostat, door locks.
**Smart agriculture:** soil-moisture sensors control irrigation pumps.
**Healthcare:** wearables monitor heart rate and SpO2.
**Industry 4.0 / IIoT:** predictive maintenance of machines.
**Smart city:** street lights, waste bins, traffic and air-quality monitoring.
**Logistics:** GPS and temperature tracking of cold-chain goods.

blocks.x: India: Smart Cities Mission, smart electricity meters, FASTag, agriculture sensors.
IoT versus M2M
M2M is direct machine-to-machine communication, often over closed cellular networks. IoT adds internet-scale connectivity, cloud services and analytics.
IoT data flow example
Temperature sensor → ESP32 reads and averages → sends JSON over MQTT → broker → cloud database → dashboard graph → rule triggers a fan relay.
Challenges
Security, privacy, interoperability, power consumption, scalability, reliability in harsh environments, and data volume.
Sense → connect → process → act.

qa.q: Define the Internet of Things.
qa.a: A network of physical objects embedded with sensors, software and connectivity that collect and exchange data over the internet and can act on it.

qa.q: Describe the three-layer IoT architecture.
qa.a: The perception layer senses and acts on the physical world, the network layer carries the data, and the application layer delivers services to users.

qa.q: Difference between a sensor and an actuator?
qa.a: A sensor converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal; an actuator converts an electrical signal into physical action such as motion or light.

qa.q: Give three IoT application areas.
qa.a: Smart agriculture, healthcare wearables, smart cities, smart homes and industrial predictive maintenance.

qa.q: Name key challenges in IoT.
qa.a: Security and privacy, interoperability, limited power, scalability and handling large volumes of data.

problems.q: Define the Internet of Things and name the four layers of a typical IoT architecture from bottom to top.
problems.a: The Internet of Things is a network of physical objects fitted with sensors, software and connectivity so they can collect and exchange data and act on it. Layers from bottom to top: perception (sensors and actuators), network (connectivity), processing (edge, cloud, storage, analytics) and application (apps and dashboards).

problems.q: Explain the data flow of a smart home temperature system from the sensor to the user's phone and back to a fan.
problems.a: A temperature sensor in the room (perception) reads the value, a microcontroller sends it over Wi-Fi using MQTT (network) to the cloud (processing) where it is stored and checked against a rule. The mobile app (application) shows the value. If the temperature is above the limit, a command goes back through the cloud to the device and the actuator (relay) switches the fan on.

problems.q: Differentiate IoT and M2M. Give three challenges of IoT with one example each.
problems.a:
M2M is direct device-to-device communication over a point-to-point link, often with cellular or wired networks and proprietary solutions. IoT connects devices to the internet and cloud platforms with open protocols, analytics and applications, so it scales to many services.
Challenges: security (default passwords on cameras), interoperability (devices from different vendors with different protocols), power and battery life (a sensor must run for months), scalability and privacy of collected data.

lessons.title: Sensors, actuators, ADC and signal conditioning
yt: iot sensors types DHT11 LDR PIR ultrasonic soil moisture
ADC analog to digital conversion voltage divider

blocks.x: Sensors
A sensor turns a physical quantity into an electrical signal.
Specifications: range, **resolution**, accuracy, precision, sensitivity, response time, power use.
Analog and digital signals

A microcontroller pin reads either a digital level (0 or 1) or, through an **ADC (Analog-to-Digital Converter)**, a number proportional to the voltage. **ADC resolution:** an n-bit ADC has 2^n levels. ESP32 has 12-bit ADCs (0–4095) for 0–3.3 V, so one step is 3.3/4095 ≈ **0.806 mV**. Arduino Uno: 10-bit, 0–1023 over 5 V ≈ 4.88 mV per step. Voltage from reading: V = reading × Vref / (2^n − 1). LM35 gives 10 mV per °C, so 0.25 V means **25 °C**.
Voltage divider

Vout = Vin × R2/(R1 + R2). With Vin = 5 V, R1 = 10 kΩ, R2 = 20 kΩ: Vout = 5 × 20/30 = **3.33 V**. It is used to read an LDR or to **level-shift 5 V signals to 3.3 V** for the ESP32 (whose pins are not 5 V tolerant).
Sensor reading in code (simulated)
Output:
Noise and filtering

Real readings jump. Common fixes: take the **average** of N samples, **moving average**, **median filter** (removes spikes), and add a capacitor across the sensor supply. Calibrate against a reference.
Actuators

x: **LED/buzzer:** digital output with a current-limiting resistor. For a 5 V supply, 2 V LED and 20 mA: R = (5 − 2)/0.02 = **150 Ω**.
**Relay module:** lets a low-voltage pin switch mains loads safely (fans, pumps). Mains voltage is dangerous; use isolation and proper enclosures.
**DC motor:** driven through a transistor or motor driver (L298N, L293D).
**Servo:** angle control by a PWM signal.
**Stepper:** precise steps.
**Display:** OLED (I2C), LCD.

blocks.x: **PWM (Pulse Width Modulation)** simulates analog output by switching quickly; duty cycle 25% on an 8-bit scale is 64/255.
Pull-ups and debouncing
Buttons use pull-up/pull-down resistors so the pin never floats; mechanical contacts bounce and need a small delay or capacitor.
A microcontroller only understands voltages; the ADC and a little maths turn them into meaning.

qa.q: What is the resolution of a 12-bit ADC with 3.3 V reference?
qa.a: 3.3 V / 4095 ≈ 0.806 mV per step.

qa.q: Why use a voltage divider with an ESP32?
qa.a: To scale 5 V signals down to 3.3 V, since ESP32 GPIO pins are not 5 V tolerant, or to convert a resistive sensor such as an LDR into a voltage.

qa.q: How do you compute the series resistor for an LED?
qa.a: R = (supply voltage − LED forward voltage)/desired current, for example (5 − 2)/0.02 = 150 Ω.

qa.q: What is PWM used for?
qa.a: Controlling average power by varying duty cycle, such as LED brightness, motor speed and servo angle.

qa.q: How can sensor noise be reduced?
qa.a: By averaging multiple samples, using moving-average or median filters, adding decoupling capacitors and calibrating.

problems.q: Differentiate between a sensor and an actuator with two examples of each.
problems.a: A sensor converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal (temperature sensor LM35, soil moisture sensor, PIR motion sensor). An actuator converts an electrical signal into physical action (relay, servo motor, buzzer, water pump).

problems.q: A 10-bit ADC has a 5 V reference. Find the voltage step (resolution) and the voltage for a reading of 512. An LM35 gives 10 mV per degree Celsius: what temperature is a voltage of 0.25 V?
problems.a: A 10-bit ADC has 2^10 = 1024 levels. Step = 5 / 1024 = 4.88 mV. A reading of 512 corresponds to 512 x 5 / 1024 = 2.5 V. LM35: 0.25 V / 0.01 V per degree = 25 degrees Celsius.

problems.q: A voltage divider uses R1 = 10 kilo-ohm and R2 = 10 kilo-ohm on 5 V. Find the output. Find the series resistor for a red LED (2 V, 20 mA) on a 5 V supply. Why is signal conditioning (filtering) needed?
problems.a:
Vout = Vin x R2 / (R1 + R2) = 5 x 10 / 20 = 2.5 V. Resistor = (5 - 2) / 0.02 = 150 ohm.
Sensor signals are small and noisy; amplification brings them to the ADC range and filtering removes noise, so readings are stable and accurate.

lessons.title: Microcontrollers and boards: Arduino, ESP32, Raspberry Pi
yt: arduino vs esp32 vs raspberry pi difference
ESP32 pinout GPIO deep sleep

blocks.x: Microcontroller vs microprocessor

A **microcontroller (MCU)** puts CPU, RAM, flash memory and peripherals (GPIO, ADC, timers, UART, I2C, SPI) on one chip: cheap, low power, runs one program with no OS. A **microprocessor** (as in a PC or Raspberry Pi) needs external memory and runs an OS.
Popular boards
ESP32 features

GPIO pins (3.3 V logic), 12-bit ADC, 2 DAC, touch sensors, PWM, UART/I2C/SPI, Wi-Fi 802.11 b/g/n, Bluetooth, **deep-sleep** mode (microamp current), RTC memory, and OTA (over-the-air) updates. Some GPIOs are input-only (34–39) and ADC2 pins cannot be used while Wi-Fi is on.
Communication buses

x: **UART:** two wires TX/RX, asynchronous (GPS, serial monitor).
**I2C:** two wires SDA/SCL, many devices by address (OLED, BMP280).
**SPI:** four wires (MOSI, MISO, SCK, CS), fast (SD cards, displays).
**1-Wire:** one data line (DS18B20).

blocks.x: Programming

x: **Arduino IDE / PlatformIO** (C/C++): `setup()` runs once, `loop()` runs forever.
**MicroPython** on ESP32: Python on the board.
**ESP-IDF** (professional C framework with FreeRTOS).

blocks.x: Blink and sensor sketch (ESP32 Arduino, shown for reference)
Avoid long `delay()` in real products; use timers or non-blocking code with `millis()`.
Power management

Battery life = capacity / average current. A 2000 mAh battery with a constant 20 mA lasts **100 hours**. Wake for 5 s at 80 mA once a minute and deep sleep at 10 µA the rest of the time: average ≈ 6.7 mA, so about **300 hours (12.5 days)**. Sleeping is the key to battery IoT.
Choosing a board
Need Wi-Fi/BLE and low cost → ESP32. Heavy processing, camera AI, Linux → Raspberry Pi. Ultra-low power for years → special low-power MCUs with LoRa.
MCU = tiny computer for one job; Raspberry Pi = small Linux computer.

qa.q: Difference between a microcontroller and a microprocessor?
qa.a: A microcontroller integrates CPU, memory and peripherals on one chip for dedicated control tasks; a microprocessor is a CPU needing external memory and peripherals, typically running a full OS.

qa.q: Why is ESP32 popular for IoT?
qa.a: It combines a fast dual-core CPU, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, many peripherals, deep sleep and low cost.

qa.q: Compare I2C and SPI.
qa.a: I2C uses two wires and addresses many devices on one bus but is slower; SPI uses four wires (plus chip selects), is faster and full duplex but needs more pins.

qa.q: What do setup() and loop() do in Arduino code?
qa.a: setup() runs once at start for initialisation; loop() runs repeatedly forever.

qa.q: How does deep sleep extend battery life?
qa.a: The device turns off most circuitry and draws microamps, waking only briefly to measure and transmit, which cuts the average current.

lessons.title: IoT connectivity: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Zigbee, LoRaWAN, NB-IoT and cellular
yt: iot communication technologies lora zigbee ble wifi comparison
LoRaWAN architecture gateway network server

blocks.x: Choosing a link means trading **range, data rate, power, cost and infrastructure**.
Short range

x: **Wi-Fi (802.11):** high data rate (tens–hundreds of Mbps), ~50 m indoors, high power. Good for mains-powered devices and cameras.
**Bluetooth / BLE:** ~10–100 m, low power, phones and wearables, beacons. BLE uses the GATT profile (services and characteristics).
**Zigbee (802.15.4):** ~10–100 m, 250 kbps, **mesh** network, low power, used in smart homes; a hub/coordinator is needed.
**Thread/Matter:** IP-based smart home standards.
**RFID / NFC:** very short range identification (NFC ≈ 4 cm): payments, access cards, inventory.

blocks.x: Low-Power Wide-Area Networks (LPWAN)

x: **LoRa / LoRaWAN:** long range (2–5 km urban, 10+ km rural), very low power, low data rate (0.3–50 kbps), unlicensed ISM band (865–867 MHz in India). Star-of-stars architecture: **end devices → gateways → network server → application server**. Great for agriculture, metering, tracking. Small payloads, limited messages per day.
**NB-IoT / LTE-M:** cellular LPWAN using licensed spectrum; good indoor penetration; needs a SIM and operator support.
**Sigfox:** ultra-narrowband (very small messages).

blocks.x: Cellular
2G/3G/4G/5G for mobile assets (vehicle tracking) and high bandwidth (video). 5G adds low latency (URLLC) and massive IoT (mMTC).
Comparison
Data volume example
One reading of 20 bytes every 10 seconds is 8,640 readings a day = 172,800 bytes ≈ **169 KB per day** — tiny, so LoRa or NB-IoT is enough. A video camera needs Wi-Fi or 4G/5G.
Network topologies
Star (BLE, Wi-Fi, LoRaWAN), mesh (Zigbee, Thread: devices relay for each other, extending range and resilience), tree, and point-to-point.
Addressing: IPv6
IPv4 (4.3 billion addresses) cannot name billions of devices; **IPv6** (128-bit) can. **6LoWPAN** compresses IPv6 headers for tiny 802.15.4 devices. NAT is used behind routers.
Choosing
Mains power + high rate → Wi-Fi; battery + phone → BLE; mesh in a building → Zigbee/Thread; battery + kilometres → LoRaWAN/NB-IoT.
Range, rate and power form a triangle: you can optimise only two.

qa.q: Why is LoRaWAN suited to agriculture?
qa.a: It has long range (kilometres), very low power use so sensors run on batteries for years, and uses unlicensed spectrum, though only for small, infrequent messages.

qa.q: What is a mesh network?
qa.a: A network in which nodes relay data for one another, extending range and providing alternative paths if a node fails; Zigbee and Thread use it.

qa.q: Compare BLE and Wi-Fi.
qa.a: BLE has low data rate, very low power and works with phones; Wi-Fi has high data rate but much higher power consumption.

qa.q: What is the role of a LoRaWAN gateway?
qa.a: It receives LoRa radio messages from end devices and forwards them over IP to the network server.

qa.q: Why is IPv6 important for IoT?
qa.a: Its 128-bit addresses provide enough unique addresses for billions of devices, which IPv4 cannot.

problems.q: Name four wireless technologies used in IoT and say what each is best suited for.
problems.a: Bluetooth Low Energy: short range, low power wearables and beacons. Zigbee: low-power mesh networks for home automation. Wi-Fi: high data rate for cameras and hubs. LoRaWAN: long range, low data rate sensors in fields or cities. NB-IoT (cellular): metering and tracking using the mobile network.

problems.q: Compare LoRaWAN and Wi-Fi for a soil sensor in a farm 3 km from the house. Which is better and why?
problems.a: LoRaWAN is better: it reaches kilometres, needs very little power so a battery lasts for years, and the small soil data packets fit its low data rate. Wi-Fi reaches only tens of metres, uses more power and needs a router coverage over the whole farm.

problems.q: A sensor sends 100 bytes every 10 seconds. How many bytes per day? A node uses 20 mA for 2 s every minute and 0.01 mA while sleeping for the other 58 s. Find the average current and the life of a 2000 mAh battery.
problems.a: Messages per day = 86400 / 10 = 8640, so 8640 x 100 = 864,000 bytes (864 KB). Average current = (20 x 2 + 0.01 x 58) / 60 = (40 + 0.58) / 60 = 0.676 mA. Battery life = 2000 / 0.676 = about 2957 hours, about 123 days.

lessons.title: IoT application protocols: MQTT, HTTP/REST, CoAP
yt: mqtt protocol explained publish subscribe qos topics broker
coap vs mqtt vs http iot protocols

blocks.x: HTTP / REST
Request–response over TCP. Simple and universal (`GET /sensors/12`, `POST /readings` with JSON), but heavy headers and no server push, so poor for tiny battery devices. Use HTTPS.
MQTT (Message Queuing Telemetry Transport)
The most popular IoT protocol: lightweight **publish/subscribe** over TCP (port 1883, 8883 with TLS).

x: **Broker:** central server (Mosquitto, EMQX, HiveMQ) that routes messages.
**Clients** publish messages to **topics** and subscribe to topics. Publishers and subscribers never talk directly (decoupled).
**Topic:** a hierarchy like `home/kitchen/temperature`.
**Wildcards:** `+` matches one level (`home/+/temperature`), `#` matches all remaining levels (`home/#`) (subscribe only).

blocks.x: Quality of Service
Other features

x: **Retained message:** broker stores the last message for new subscribers.
**Last Will and Testament (LWT):** message the broker publishes if a client disconnects unexpectedly (device offline alert).
**Keep-alive** ping, **persistent sessions**, small 2-byte minimum header.

Publishing from Python (needs a broker and the paho-mqtt library)

import json, paho.mqtt.client as mqtt
c = mqtt.Client()
c.connect("broker.example.com", 1883)
c.publish("farm/field1/soil", json.dumps({"moisture": 41, "unit": "%"}), qos=1)
CoAP (Constrained Application Protocol)

REST-like (GET/POST/PUT/DELETE) but over **UDP** with tiny binary headers, designed for constrained devices; supports **observe** (subscribe to changes), multicast and optional reliability (confirmable messages). Secured with DTLS.
Comparison
Others
AMQP (enterprise queues), XMPP, WebSocket, DDS (robotics/industrial), OPC UA (industrial), LwM2M (device management).
Data format
Payloads are usually **JSON** (human readable) or CBOR/Protobuf (compact). Example: `{"id":"node1","t":28.4,"h":61}`.
MQTT: devices talk to a broker, not to each other.

qa.q: What is MQTT and why is it popular in IoT?
qa.a: A lightweight publish/subscribe protocol over TCP with a central broker. Its small overhead, simple API and QoS levels suit constrained devices and unreliable networks.

qa.q: Explain the three MQTT QoS levels.
qa.a: QoS 0 delivers at most once with no acknowledgement; QoS 1 delivers at least once, possibly duplicated; QoS 2 delivers exactly once using a four-step handshake.

qa.q: What are the wildcards in MQTT?
qa.a: + matches exactly one topic level and # matches any number of remaining levels.

qa.q: What is the Last Will and Testament?
qa.a: A message registered by a client at connect time which the broker publishes if the client disconnects unexpectedly, often used for offline status.

qa.q: Why is CoAP preferred over HTTP for very small devices?
qa.a: It runs over UDP with a compact binary header, so it needs less memory, energy and bandwidth, while still giving REST-style operations.

problems.q: Explain the publish-subscribe model of MQTT with the roles of publisher, subscriber, broker and topic.
problems.a: Publishers send messages to a topic on a broker; subscribers register interest in topics with the broker; the broker delivers each message to every matching subscriber. Publishers and subscribers do not know each other, which decouples them. A topic is a hierarchical name such as home/room1/temp.

rubric.t: Roles of publisher, subscriber and broker

problems.q: Explain MQTT QoS 0, 1 and 2, and the wildcards + and # with an example.
problems.a: QoS 0: at most once (no acknowledgement, may be lost). QoS 1: at least once (acknowledged, may be duplicated). QoS 2: exactly once (four-step handshake, slowest). Wildcards: + matches one level (home/+/temp matches home/room1/temp), # matches all remaining levels (home/room1/# matches every topic below room1).

problems.q: Compare MQTT, HTTP and CoAP on transport, pattern and best use. What are retained messages and the last will message?
problems.a:
MQTT: TCP, publish-subscribe, small overhead, good for many devices pushing telemetry. HTTP: TCP, request-response, heavy headers, good for web APIs. CoAP: UDP, request-response similar to HTTP but lightweight, good for constrained devices.
A retained message is stored by the broker so a new subscriber gets the last value immediately. A last will message is sent by the broker if a client disconnects unexpectedly, so others know it is offline.

lessons.title: IoT cloud platforms, dashboards and the data pipeline

iot data pipeline time series database grafana

blocks.x: Why a cloud?
Devices have limited storage and compute. The cloud provides **storage, analytics, dashboards, device management, scalability and remote access**.
Platform examples

x: **ThingSpeak:** simple, free tier, HTTP/MQTT, MATLAB charts. Good for learning.
**Blynk, Adafruit IO:** easy mobile dashboards.
**AWS IoT Core, Azure IoT Hub, Google Cloud IoT alternatives:** device registry, authentication with certificates, rules engine, integration with storage and ML.
**Open source:** Mosquitto + Node-RED + InfluxDB + Grafana; ThingsBoard; Home Assistant.

blocks.x: Typical pipeline

x: **Device** reads sensor and publishes JSON.
**Broker/Ingestion** (MQTT broker or cloud endpoint).
**Stream processing / rules**: validate, filter, convert units, trigger alerts.
**Storage:** time-series database (InfluxDB, TimescaleDB) or object storage for raw logs.
**Analytics/ML:** trends, anomaly detection, prediction.
**Visualisation and alerts:** Grafana dashboard, SMS/email/push.
**Control path back:** commands/shadow updates to devices.

blocks.x: Device shadow / digital twin
A cloud copy of a device's state (reported and desired). The app writes the *desired* state ("fan = ON"); when the device reconnects it syncs, which handles intermittent connections.
Data handling in code (simulated)

import json, statistics
messages = ['{"id":"n1","t":28.1}', '{"id":"n1","t":28.4}', '{"id":"n1","t":35.9}', '{"id":"n1","t":28.2}']
temps = [json.loads(m)["t"] for m in messages]
mean = statistics.mean(temps)
alerts = [t for t in temps if t > 33]
print(round(mean, 2), alerts)
Output:
Rules like this (`temperature > 33 → send alert`) run in the cloud's rules engine or in Node-RED.
Over-the-air (OTA) updates
Update firmware remotely, with signed images and rollback if the new version fails.
Interoperability and APIs
REST APIs, webhooks, and standards (oneM2M, Matter) connect platforms.
Cost and scale
Pay per message/device; sending data every second from 1,000 devices is 86.4 million messages a day, so batch, compress and send only changes (report by exception).
Time-series data tips
Timestamp in UTC, include device ID and units, keep raw data for a short time and aggregate for long-term storage (hourly averages).
Edge collects, broker routes, database stores, dashboard shows, rules act.

qa.q: List the stages of an IoT data pipeline.
qa.a: Device sensing, ingestion through a broker or endpoint, processing and rules, storage in a database, analytics, visualisation and alerts, and control commands back to devices.

qa.q: What is a device shadow?
qa.a: A cloud-held representation of a device's reported and desired state, allowing applications to interact even when the device is offline.

qa.q: Why use a time-series database for sensor data?
qa.a: It is optimised for timestamped data, fast writes, range queries and downsampling over time.

qa.q: What is an OTA update?
qa.a: Remotely sending new firmware to a deployed device over the network, ideally signed and with rollback capability.

qa.q: How can message cost be reduced?

problems.q: List the stages of an IoT data pipeline and name one tool or service for each.
problems.a: Ingestion (MQTT broker, AWS IoT Core, Azure IoT Hub), storage (time-series database such as InfluxDB, or a cloud database), processing (rules engine, stream processing, Python), visualisation (Grafana, ThingsBoard) and alerting (email, SMS, push notifications).

problems.q: What is a time-series database and why is it better than a plain table for sensor data? Design the fields for temperature readings.
problems.a: A time-series database stores values with timestamps and is optimised for fast writes, time-range queries, downsampling and automatic retention of old data. Fields: timestamp, device_id, location, temperature, battery (optionally humidity). A plain table can store this but becomes slow and large without these optimisations.

problems.q: A cloud rule says: if temperature is above 40 for 3 consecutive readings send an alert. Explain why 3 readings are required and describe the storage cost of 1000 sensors sending 100 bytes every 10 seconds for one day.
problems.a: Requiring 3 readings filters out a single noisy spike or glitch and reduces false alarms. Storage per day = 1000 sensors x 8640 messages x 100 bytes = 864,000,000 bytes = about 864 MB (before indexing and compression).

blocks.x: Why not send everything to the cloud?

x: **Latency:** a brake or safety system cannot wait 200 ms for a cloud reply.
**Bandwidth and cost:** raw video from a thousand cameras is huge.
**Reliability:** the network may fail.
**Privacy:** keep sensitive data local.

blocks.x: Edge, fog and cloud

x: **Edge computing:** processing on the device or right next to it (microcontroller, gateway).
**Fog computing:** an intermediate layer of gateways/local servers between devices and cloud.
**Cloud computing:** large-scale storage and heavy analytics.

blocks.x: Typical split: filter and react at the edge (milliseconds), aggregate in fog (seconds), long-term learning in cloud (hours or days).
Gateways
A gateway connects devices using local protocols (BLE, Zigbee, LoRa) to IP networks and the cloud. It can translate protocols, buffer data during outages, run rules and apply security.
Edge analytics example

A vibration sensor samples at 1 kHz. Sending 1,000 readings/second is wasteful. The edge device computes a feature (RMS value) each second and sends only that, or an alert when it exceeds a threshold. Data volume drops by about 1000 times.
TinyML
Running machine-learning models on microcontrollers with kilobytes of memory.

x: Train on a PC (TensorFlow/Keras, Edge Impulse), **quantise** weights to 8 bits, convert to **TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers**, and deploy as a C array.
Use cases: wake-word detection, gesture recognition (accelerometer), anomaly detection in motors, people counting.
Benefits: low latency, low power, works offline, privacy.
Limits: tiny models and memory, reduced accuracy.

Real-time operating systems
FreeRTOS and Zephyr schedule tasks with deadlines on MCUs (see Operating Systems: scheduling).
Fog use cases
Smart factory (local control loops), connected vehicles, smart grid, video analytics at the camera.
Do the urgent work near the data; send the summary to the cloud.

qa.q: Why is edge computing used in IoT?
qa.a: It reduces latency, bandwidth use and cost, keeps working during network failure, and improves privacy by processing data locally.

qa.q: Difference between edge and fog computing?
qa.a: Edge computing processes data on or very near the device; fog computing uses an intermediate layer of gateways or local servers between the edge and cloud.

qa.q: What is TinyML?
qa.a: Machine learning models optimised to run on very small, low-power microcontrollers.

qa.q: What is quantisation?
qa.a: Reducing the precision of model weights (for example from 32-bit floats to 8-bit integers) to shrink size and speed up inference with small accuracy loss.

qa.q: What functions can an IoT gateway perform?
qa.a: Protocol translation, local processing and rules, buffering when offline, security enforcement and forwarding to the cloud.

problems.q: Differentiate edge, fog and cloud computing in IoT.
problems.a: Edge computing processes data on the device or very close to it. Fog computing uses nearby gateways or local servers between the devices and the cloud. Cloud computing uses remote data centres with large storage and computing power. Moving from edge to cloud increases power and delay.

problems.q: 1000 sensors each send 1 KB per second to the cloud. If an edge gateway sends only a 1 KB summary per sensor every minute, find the data sent per second in both cases and the reduction.
problems.a: Raw: 1000 x 1 KB = 1000 KB per second. With edge summaries: 1000 KB every 60 s = 16.7 KB per second. Reduction = 1 - 16.7 / 1000 = about 98.3%. Edge processing also reduces latency and cost.

problems.q: What is TinyML? A model is 250 KB in 32-bit floating point. What is its size after 8-bit quantisation? Give one use case and one limitation.
problems.a: TinyML runs machine learning models on very small, low-power microcontrollers. 8-bit quantisation stores each weight in 1 byte instead of 4, so the model becomes 250 / 4 = 62.5 KB. Use case: keyword spotting or detecting vibration anomalies in a motor without sending data to the cloud. Limitation: small memory and compute, so models are small and may lose some accuracy.

lessons.title: IoT security and privacy
yt: iot security threats mirai botnet best practices
TLS certificates secure boot IoT devices

blocks.x: IoT devices are attractive targets: they are numerous, often cheap, rarely updated and sit inside homes and factories.
Security goals (CIA + more)
**Confidentiality**, **Integrity**, **Availability**, plus authentication, authorisation, non-repudiation and privacy.
Threats by layer

x: **Device:** physical tampering, stolen flash dumps with secrets, debug ports (UART/JTAG) left open, default passwords.
**Network:** eavesdropping, man-in-the-middle, replay, spoofing, jamming, **DoS/DDoS**.
**Cloud/app:** weak APIs, injection, broken authentication, misconfigured storage.
**Supply chain:** malicious firmware or components.

blocks.x: **Mirai botnet (2016)** infected cameras and routers using default credentials and launched record DDoS attacks.
Defences

x: **Strong unique credentials**; no hard-coded or default passwords.
**Encryption in transit:** TLS for MQTT (port 8883) and HTTPS; DTLS for CoAP; WPA2/WPA3 on Wi-Fi.
**Authentication:** per-device **X.509 certificates** or keys; mutual TLS.
**Secure boot** and **signed firmware** with secure OTA updates.
**Least privilege:** device may publish only to its own topics (broker ACLs).
**Hardware security:** secure element/TPM, encrypted flash, disable debug ports.
**Network segmentation:** place IoT devices on a separate VLAN/guest network.
**Monitoring and logging**, anomaly detection, regular patching.
**Privacy by design:** collect minimum data, anonymise, give users control.

blocks.x: Cryptography on small devices

Symmetric AES (fast, hardware-accelerated on ESP32), hashing SHA-256, public-key ECC (smaller keys than RSA for the same strength: 256-bit ECC ≈ 3072-bit RSA). Lightweight ciphers exist for the tiniest nodes. Random numbers must come from a proper hardware RNG.
Example: authenticating a message with HMAC

import hmac, hashlib
key = b"device-secret-key"
msg = b'{"id":"n1","t":28.4}'
tag = hmac.new(key, msg, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
ok = hmac.compare_digest(tag, hmac.new(key, msg, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest())
tampered = hmac.compare_digest(tag, hmac.new(key, b'{"id":"n1","t":99}', hashlib.sha256).hexdigest())
print(len(tag), ok, tampered)
Output:
64 True False
Any change to the message changes the tag, so tampering is detected (integrity and authenticity).
Privacy and law

Smart devices collect sensitive data (location, voice, health). India's **Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023** requires consent and purpose limitation. Regulations and standards: IEC 62443 (industrial), ETSI EN 303 645 (consumer IoT), OWASP IoT Top 10.
Practical checklist for student projects
Change default passwords, never commit secrets to GitHub, use TLS, keep firmware updated, limit open ports.
Security is a process: secure the device, the network, the cloud and the people.

qa.q: What made the Mirai botnet possible?
qa.a: Many IoT devices such as cameras and routers used default or hard-coded passwords and were exposed to the internet, allowing mass infection and DDoS attacks.

qa.q: Why use TLS with MQTT?
qa.a: It encrypts traffic and authenticates the broker (and optionally the client), preventing eavesdropping and man-in-the-middle attacks.

qa.q: What is secure boot?
qa.a: A mechanism where the device verifies the digital signature of the firmware at start-up and refuses to run unsigned or modified code.

qa.q: What is the purpose of broker ACLs?
qa.a: They restrict which topics each client may publish or subscribe to, applying least privilege.

qa.q: What does an HMAC provide?
qa.a: Integrity and authenticity of a message: a tag computed with a shared secret key that changes if the message is altered.

quiz.why: Weak default logins allowed mass takeover.

quiz.q: MQTT over TLS typically uses port
quiz.why: 8883 is the secure port.

quiz.q: Signed firmware helps ensure
quiz.why: The device checks the signature.

quiz.q: Which gives similar strength with smaller keys?
quiz.why: A 256-bit ECC key ≈ 3072-bit RSA.

quiz.q: Network segmentation means
o: keeping IoT devices on a separate network
quiz.why: It limits the damage if a device is compromised.

visuals.title: Basic steps to secure an IoT device
visuals.data: Change default passwords and use unique credentials; Encrypt data with TLS; Sign and update firmware regularly; Give each device the least privilege it needs; Monitor devices and turn off unused services

problems.q: List four common security threats to IoT devices and one defence for each.
problems.a: Default or weak passwords (use unique strong credentials). Unencrypted communication (use TLS). Outdated firmware with known bugs (regular signed updates). Physical tampering (secure boot and tamper detection). Also valid: botnets such as Mirai (network segmentation) and denial of service.

problems.q: What was the Mirai botnet and what does it show about IoT security?
problems.a: Mirai (2016) was malware that scanned the internet for IoT devices such as cameras and routers using default passwords, took them over and used them for large denial-of-service attacks. It shows that unmanaged devices with default credentials can be abused at scale, so every device needs unique passwords, updates and network protection.

rubric.t: Lesson on default passwords and updates

problems.q: Explain secure boot, over-the-air (OTA) updates and device authentication using certificates. Name two privacy principles for IoT data.
problems.a:
Secure boot checks a digital signature of the firmware at start-up so only trusted code runs. OTA updates deliver fixes remotely and should be signed and verified. Certificates give each device a unique identity (mutual TLS) so the cloud and device authenticate each other.
Privacy: data minimisation (collect only what you need) and consent with transparency (tell users what is collected and why); also encryption and retention limits.

rubric.t: Secure boot, signed OTA and certificates

blocks.x: Build a complete system and apply everything from this module.
Problem
Farmers waste water and time. We want a node that measures soil moisture, temperature and humidity, switches a water pump automatically, and reports to a phone dashboard.
Hardware (approximate)

ESP32 board, capacitive soil-moisture sensor, DHT22 (temperature and humidity), 5 V relay module, small submersible pump with separate power supply, jumper wires, breadboard, optional OLED. Power the pump from its own supply and share only ground.
Block diagram
Sensors → ESP32 (decision + Wi-Fi) → MQTT broker → Node-RED / cloud database → dashboard. Dashboard commands (manual ON/OFF) return to ESP32 through an MQTT topic.
Topics

x: `farm/field1/soil` (published JSON: moisture %, temperature, humidity)
`farm/field1/pump/set` (subscribed: "ON"/"OFF")
`farm/field1/status` (retained; LWT "offline")

blocks.x: Control logic with hysteresis
Switching exactly at one threshold makes the pump chatter. Use two thresholds:

x: Turn the pump **ON** when moisture < 30 %.
Turn it **OFF** when moisture > 45 %.

blocks.x: Also add a maximum run time (for example 5 minutes) as a safety cut-off in case the sensor fails.
Output:
Between 30 and 45 the pump keeps its previous state, so it does not chatter.
Calibrating the soil sensor
Record the raw ADC value in dry air (e.g. 3000) and in water (e.g. 1300); then moisture % = (dry − raw)/(dry − wet) × 100. The numbers differ for each sensor, so calibrate yours.
Firmware outline (ESP32)

x: Connect to Wi-Fi; connect to the MQTT broker with TLS and a unique client ID; set Last Will.
Every 60 s: read sensors, average 10 ADC samples, build JSON, publish with QoS 1.
In the MQTT callback, handle manual pump commands.
Apply hysteresis control and safety timer.
Use deep sleep between cycles if on battery or solar.

blocks.x: Dashboard
Node-RED gauge for moisture, line chart of temperature, switch for the pump, and an alert (message to phone) when the tank is empty or the node goes offline.
Extensions
Weather API to skip watering if rain is forecast; solar panel and battery; LoRa link for a remote field; TinyML to predict irrigation needs.
Testing and report

Test with dry/wet soil, simulated network loss, sensor unplugged (should fail safe: pump OFF), and measure power. Report sections: objective, block diagram, circuit, code, results, cost, limitations, future work.
Safety
Keep mains voltage away from the breadboard, use a fuse, waterproof the enclosure, and never power a pump from the ESP32 pin.
Sense, decide with hysteresis, act, report, and always fail safe.

qa.q: Why use hysteresis in the pump controller?
qa.a: Two thresholds prevent rapid on-off switching around a single threshold, protecting the pump and relay.

qa.q: How is a soil moisture sensor calibrated?
qa.a: Record the raw reading in dry air and in water and convert readings to a percentage: (dry − raw)/(dry − wet) × 100.

qa.q: Why add a maximum pump run time?
qa.a: As a safety measure if the sensor fails or the soil never reads wet, preventing flooding and pump damage.

qa.q: How does the dashboard control the pump?
qa.a: It publishes ON/OFF to an MQTT command topic to which the ESP32 is subscribed, and the ESP32 acts on it.

qa.q: What should happen if the sensor is disconnected?
qa.a: The system should fail safe: switch the pump off, raise an alert and publish an error status.

problems.q: List the components of a smart irrigation system and what each does.
problems.a: Soil moisture sensor (measures wetness), microcontroller such as ESP32 (reads sensor and decides), relay (switches the pump), water pump or valve (waters the plants), power supply, and Wi-Fi or LoRa link to a cloud dashboard or phone app.

rubric.t: Sensor, controller and relay or pump

problems.q: Write the control rule (pseudo-code) for the irrigation system: water for 5 minutes if soil moisture is below 30% and rain is not expected. Why add a minimum gap between waterings?
problems.a:
if moisture < 30 and not rain_expected and minutes_since_last_watering > 60: relay on; wait 5 minutes; relay off; log the event.
A minimum gap prevents over-watering because water takes time to soak in and the reading may still be low right after watering, and it avoids repeated rapid switching of the pump.

problems.q: The pump delivers 2 litres per minute and runs 5 minutes per watering, 4 times a day. Find the daily water use. Suggest two ways to test the project and one way to make it more reliable.
problems.a:
One watering uses 2 x 5 = 10 litres, so 4 waterings use 40 litres per day.
Testing: calibrate the sensor in dry soil and in a glass of water to map readings to percentages; run the pump with a flow-measuring jug; test Wi-Fi failure to check the device still waters using its local rule.
Reliability: add a maximum run time (fail-safe) and a watchdog timer, so a stuck relay or crashed program cannot flood the plants.

blocks.x: Advanced Java builds on core Java. This lesson refreshes the parts used everywhere later.
Four pillars of OOP

x: **Encapsulation:** private fields with public getters/setters.
**Inheritance:** `class Dog extends Animal` reuses code. Java allows single inheritance of classes, but many interfaces.
**Polymorphism:** one call, many forms. *Overloading* (same name, different parameters, compile time) and *overriding* (subclass redefines a method, run time).
**Abstraction:** `abstract` classes and `interface`s hide details and define contracts.

Exceptions
An **exception** is an event that disrupts normal flow. Hierarchy: `Throwable` → `Error` (not meant to be caught, e.g. `OutOfMemoryError`) and `Exception`.

x: **Checked** exceptions (`IOException`, `SQLException`) must be handled or declared with `throws`.
**Unchecked** (`RuntimeException`: `NullPointerException`, `ArithmeticException`, `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`) need not be.

Strings

`String` is **immutable**; use `StringBuilder` for repeated edits (not thread-safe, fast) or `StringBuffer` (synchronised). Compare with `equals()`, not `==` (which compares references). Common methods: `length`, `charAt`, `substring`, `indexOf`, `split`, `trim`, `toUpperCase`, `replace`, `String.join`.

qa.q: Difference between overloading and overriding?
qa.a: Overloading uses the same method name with different parameters in one class and is resolved at compile time. Overriding redefines a superclass method in a subclass with the same signature and is resolved at run time.

qa.q: Checked versus unchecked exceptions?
qa.a: Checked exceptions are verified by the compiler and must be caught or declared; unchecked exceptions (subclasses of RuntimeException) need not be.

qa.q: What does finally do?
qa.a: It contains code that runs whether or not an exception occurs, usually releasing resources.

qa.q: Why is String immutable?
qa.a: Immutability makes strings safe to share, cache (string pool), use as hash keys and in security-sensitive code.

qa.q: Difference between == and equals() on Strings?
qa.a: == compares object references; equals() compares the character contents.

Polymorphism: a method overridden in a subclass and called through an Animal reference. Abstraction: an abstract class or interface that hides the details, such as interface Shape with area().

problems.q: What is printed by this code, and in what order? try { int x = 10 / 0; } catch (ArithmeticException e) { System.out.println("A"); } finally { System.out.println("F"); } System.out.println("E");
problems.a: Output: A, then F, then E (each on its own line). The division throws an ArithmeticException, the catch block prints A, the finally block always runs and prints F, and since the exception was handled the program continues and prints E.

problems.q: For String s1 = "hi", s2 = "hi", s3 = new String("hi"); give the values of s1 == s2, s1 == s3, s1.equals(s3) and s1 == s3.intern(). Why are strings immutable and when should StringBuilder be used?
problems.a:
s1 == s2 is true (same pooled literal). s1 == s3 is false (new creates a separate object on the heap). s1.equals(s3) is true (same characters). s1 == s3.intern() is true (intern returns the pooled string).
Strings are immutable for security, thread safety, caching of hash codes and the string pool. Use StringBuilder when building strings in loops, because each concatenation of a String creates a new object.

Iterating
Enhanced for, `Iterator` (supports `remove()`), `forEach` with lambda. Modifying a list while looping with enhanced for throws `ConcurrentModificationException` — use the iterator's `remove`.
equals() and hashCode()
`HashMap`/`HashSet` use `hashCode()` to choose a bucket and `equals()` to compare. If two objects are equal they **must** have the same hash code. Override both together.
Comparable and Comparator

x: `Comparable<T>`: natural order via `compareTo` inside the class.

blocks.x: Generics
Generics give **compile-time type safety** and remove casts.
Output:

false

Wildcards: `List<?>` (unknown), `List<? extends Number>` (read-only producer), `List<? super Integer>` (consumer). Generics use **type erasure**: type information is removed at run time. Primitives are not allowed (`List<int>` is illegal; use `Integer` with autoboxing).

qa.q: Difference between ArrayList and LinkedList?
qa.a: ArrayList is backed by an array with fast random access but slow insertion in the middle. LinkedList is a doubly linked list with fast insertion and deletion at known positions but slow indexed access.

qa.q: How does HashMap work?
qa.a: It computes the key's hashCode to find a bucket, then uses equals() to find the exact key within the bucket. Collisions are chained in a list or tree.

qa.q: Why override hashCode when overriding equals?
qa.a: Equal objects must produce the same hash code, otherwise hash-based collections cannot find them.

qa.q: Difference between Comparable and Comparator?
qa.a: Comparable defines one natural ordering inside the class via compareTo; a Comparator defines a separate ordering and lets you have many.

qa.q: What is type erasure?
qa.a: The compiler removes generic type information after checking, so at run time List<String> and List<Integer> are the same class.

blocks.x: Java 8 added **functional programming** features.
Functional interface and lambda

A **functional interface** has exactly one abstract method (`Runnable`, `Comparator`, `Function<T,R>`, `Predicate<T>`, `Consumer<T>`, `Supplier<T>`). A **lambda** `(params) -> expression` implements it concisely. A **method reference** `String::length` is shorthand.
Stream API
A stream is a pipeline over a data source (it does not store data or modify the source):

x: **Source:** `list.stream()`, `Arrays.stream`, `Stream.of`, `IntStream.range`.
**Intermediate** (lazy) operations: `filter`, `map`, `sorted`, `distinct`, `limit`.
**Terminal** operation (starts the work): `collect`, `forEach`, `count`, `sum`, `reduce`, `anyMatch`.

blocks.x: Output:

true
Optional
`Optional<T>` represents a value that may be absent, avoiding null checks: `opt.orElse("none")`, `opt.ifPresent(...)`.
Parallel streams
`list.parallelStream()` splits work across cores; useful only for large, CPU-heavy, independent tasks.
Why use streams?
Short, readable code; operations are declarative ("what" rather than "how").
Common functional interfaces
Collectors

`Collectors.toList()`, `toSet()`, `joining(", ")`, `counting()`, `groupingBy(classifier)`, `partitioningBy(predicate)`, `toMap(keyFn, valueFn)`. Example: `list.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(s -> s.marks() >= 80))` splits students into two groups.
Lambda rules

x: A lambda can use local variables only if they are **effectively final** (never reassigned).
`this` inside a lambda refers to the enclosing class, unlike an anonymous class.
Lambdas replace anonymous classes for single-method interfaces: `new Thread(() -> work())`.

blocks.x: Default and static methods in interfaces
Java 8 let interfaces carry `default` methods (with a body) so that new methods like `forEach` could be added to old interfaces without breaking existing classes.

qa.q: Difference between intermediate and terminal operations?
qa.a: Intermediate operations such as filter and map return a new stream and are lazy. Terminal operations such as collect or count trigger execution and end the stream.

qa.q: Can a stream be reused after a terminal operation?
qa.a: No. A stream can be consumed only once; a second use throws IllegalStateException.

problems.a: A functional interface has exactly one abstract method (Runnable, Comparator, Function). A lambda gives its implementation: Comparator<String> byLen = (a, b) -> a.length() - b.length(); or list.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length));

problems.q: Use streams to find the sum of the squares of the even numbers from 1 to 10. What is the result?
problems.a: IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 10).filter(i -> i % 2 == 0).map(i -> i * i).sum(); The even numbers are 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 with squares 4, 16, 36, 64, 100. Sum = 220.

problems.q: Group the words apple, fig, kiwi, plum, pear by length using streams and give the result. What is the difference between intermediate and terminal operations, and why is a stream lazy?

Intermediate operations (filter, map, sorted) return a new stream and do nothing yet; terminal operations (collect, forEach, sum) start the processing. blocks.x: A **thread** is a lightweight unit of execution inside a process. Java lets one program run several tasks at the same time (for example downloading a file while the screen stays responsive). This lesson covers only creating threads and their life cycle.
Creating a thread

x: **Extend `Thread`** and override `run()`.
**Implement `Runnable`** and pass it to a `Thread` (preferred: the class can extend something else).
A lambda: `new Thread(() -> ...)`.

blocks.x: Call **`start()`** (not `run()`) to create a new thread of execution. Calling `run()` directly just runs the method in the current thread.
Output:

Hello from worker-1
Hello from lambda thread
main finished after joins
`join()` makes the caller wait until that thread dies; here it also keeps the output order fixed.
Life cycle states (`Thread.State`)

x: **NEW:** created, `start()` not yet called.
**RUNNABLE:** ready or running (the scheduler decides).
**BLOCKED / WAITING / TIMED_WAITING:** temporarily not running (for example `sleep(ms)` gives TIMED_WAITING).
**TERMINATED:** `run()` finished.

blocks.x: A terminated thread cannot be restarted.
Useful methods
`sleep(ms)`, `join()`, `isAlive()`, `getName()`, `setPriority(1–10)`, `Thread.currentThread()`, `interrupt()`. Daemon threads (`setDaemon(true)`) do not keep the JVM alive.
Thread priority
Hints to the scheduler (`MIN_PRIORITY` 1, `NORM_PRIORITY` 5, `MAX_PRIORITY` 10). The actual order is not guaranteed.

Thread एक हल्की execution unit है। `start()` नया thread बनाता है, `run()` सिर्फ़ method call है। Life cycle: New → Runnable → (Waiting) → Terminated।
start() creates a new thread; run() alone does not.

qa.q: Why use Runnable instead of extending Thread?
qa.a: A class can extend only one class, so implementing Runnable keeps inheritance free, and it separates the task from the thread that runs it.

qa.q: What happens if you call run() instead of start()?
qa.a: The code runs in the calling thread like an ordinary method, so no new thread is created.

qa.q: Name the states in the life cycle of a thread.
qa.a: New, Runnable, Blocked, Waiting, Timed Waiting and Terminated.

qa.q: What does join() do?
qa.a: It makes the calling thread wait until the target thread has finished.

qa.q: Can a terminated thread be started again?
qa.a: No. Calling start() again throws IllegalThreadStateException.

problems.q: Show two ways to create a thread in Java. What is the difference between start() and run()?
problems.a:
1) class Worker extends Thread { public void run() { ... } } then new Worker().start(); 2) class Task implements Runnable { public void run() { ... } } then new Thread(new Task()).start(). Implementing Runnable is preferred because the class can still extend another class.
start() creates a new thread of execution and calls run() in it; calling run() directly just executes the method in the current thread like an ordinary method.

problems.q: A thread t prints "T". The main thread starts t, calls t.join() and then prints "M". What is the output and why? What changes without join()?
problems.a: Output: T then M. join() makes the main thread wait until t finishes, so M is always printed after T. Without join() the order is not guaranteed because both threads run independently, so M may appear before T.

problems.q: Give the state of a thread t after: new Thread(r); t.start(); during Thread.sleep(1000) inside run; after run ends. What happens if you call t.start() twice?
problems.a: After new Thread(r): NEW. After start(): RUNNABLE. While sleeping inside run: TIMED_WAITING. After run ends: TERMINATED. Calling start() a second time throws IllegalThreadStateException, because a thread can be started only once.

blocks.x: Java's `java.net` package supports network programming.
Network basics

x: **IP address** identifies a host (IPv4 such as 192.168.1.5, IPv6). **Port** (0–65535) identifies an application on that host; 80 is HTTP, 443 HTTPS, 22 SSH. Ports below 1024 are well-known.
**TCP:** connection-oriented, reliable, ordered (web, email). **UDP:** connectionless, faster, may lose packets (video calls, DNS, games).
**Socket** = IP address + port: an endpoint of two-way communication.

blocks.x: TCP client-server steps
Server: create `ServerSocket(port)` → `accept()` (blocks until a client connects) → get streams → read/write → close. Client: `new Socket(host, port)` → get streams → read/write → close.
Working example (server and client in one program)
Output:
ECHO: HELLO FUTURESELF
A real server handles each client in its own thread so one slow client does not block others.

The sender builds a `DatagramPacket(data, length, address, port)` and calls `send`; the receiver calls `receive` on a `DatagramSocket(port)`. There is no connection and no delivery guarantee.

blocks.x: **JDBC (Java Database Connectivity)** is the standard API (`java.sql`) for Java programs to talk to relational databases.
Architecture
Application → **JDBC API** → **DriverManager** → **JDBC driver** (vendor-specific JAR) → Database. The database can be changed by switching the driver and URL, with little code change.
Driver types

x: Type 1: JDBC-ODBC bridge (removed).
Type 2: native API driver.
Type 3: network protocol (middleware).
**Type 4: pure Java thin driver** (used today: MySQL Connector/J, PostgreSQL, SQLite).

blocks.x: Steps to connect

x: Add the driver JAR to the class path (modern drivers auto-register).
Open `Connection con = DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, pass);`

blocks.x: URL examples: `jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/college`, `jdbc:postgresql://localhost/college`, `jdbc:sqlite:college.db`.

x: Create `Statement`/`PreparedStatement`.
Execute: `executeQuery` (SELECT, returns `ResultSet`), `executeUpdate` (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, returns row count), `execute`.
Process the `ResultSet`: `while (rs.next()) rs.getString("name")`.
Close resources (try-with-resources).

x: `Statement`: plain SQL, vulnerable to **SQL injection**.

`CallableStatement`: calls stored procedures.

With string concatenation `"... WHERE name='" + input + "'"` the input `' OR '1'='1` returns every row. With `PreparedStatement`, the input is treated only as data.
Transactions
`con.setAutoCommit(false); ... con.commit();` and `con.rollback()` on error, giving the ACID behaviour of the DBMS course. **Batch updates** (`addBatch`, `executeBatch`) speed up many inserts.
ResultSet types
Default is forward-only and read-only; scrollable and updatable result sets can be requested. `ResultSetMetaData` gives column names and types.
Connection pooling
Opening a connection is expensive; production systems use a pool (HikariCP, DBCP) that reuses connections.

blocks.x: How the web works
A browser sends an **HTTP request** (method, URL, headers, body); the server returns an **HTTP response** (status code, headers, body).

x: Methods: **GET** (read; parameters in the URL), **POST** (send data in the body), PUT, DELETE, HEAD.
Status codes: 200 OK, 201 Created, 301/302 redirect, 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 500 Server Error.
HTTP is **stateless**, so sessions and cookies are added for memory.

blocks.x: Servlet

A **servlet** is a Java class that runs inside a **web container** (Apache Tomcat, Jetty) and handles requests. It extends `HttpServlet` (package `javax.servlet` in older versions, `jakarta.servlet` from Jakarta EE 9 / Tomcat 10+).
Life cycle

x: **Loading and instantiation** by the container.
**`init()`**: called once.
**`service()`** → `doGet()` / `doPost()`: called for each request (each in its own thread of one servlet instance).
**`destroy()`**: called once at unloading.

blocks.x: Example servlet (runs in Tomcat; shown for reference)
Visiting `/hello?name=Anil` shows "Hello, Anil!". Output must be escaped when it contains user input, to prevent cross-site scripting (XSS).
Request and response objects
`getParameter`, `getParameterValues`, `getHeader`, `getSession`, `getRequestDispatcher`; response: `setContentType`, `getWriter`, `sendRedirect`, `setStatus`, `addCookie`.
Deployment descriptor and annotations
Servlets can be mapped using `web.xml` (`<servlet>` and `<servlet-mapping>`) or the `@WebServlet` annotation.
forward versus redirect

x: `RequestDispatcher.forward()`: server-side, same request, URL does not change.
`response.sendRedirect()`: tells the browser to make a **new** request, URL changes.

blocks.x: Session management

x: **Cookies:** small data stored in the browser.
**HttpSession:** server-side object per user, identified by the `JSESSIONID` cookie: `session.setAttribute("user", name)`.
**URL rewriting** and **hidden form fields**.

blocks.x: Filters and listeners
Filters intercept requests (logging, authentication); listeners react to events such as application start or session creation.
Hindi saransh
Servlet एक Java class है जो Tomcat जैसे container में चलती है। Life cycle: init → service (doGet/doPost) → destroy। HTTP stateless है, इसलिए session और cookie इस्तेमाल होते हैं।
init once, service many times, destroy once.

qa.q: Explain the servlet life cycle.
qa.a: The container loads the servlet and calls init() once, then calls service() (doGet or doPost) for every request, and finally calls destroy() once before unloading it.

qa.q: Difference between doGet and doPost?
qa.a: doGet handles GET requests with parameters in the URL (visible, size-limited, idempotent); doPost handles POST requests with data in the body, used for forms and sensitive data.

qa.q: Difference between forward and sendRedirect?
qa.a: forward is handled inside the server with the same request and no URL change; sendRedirect sends a response asking the browser to make a new request to another URL.

qa.q: Why is HTTP called stateless and how is state kept?
qa.a: Each request is independent and the server does not remember earlier ones. Cookies, HttpSession and URL rewriting maintain state across requests.

qa.q: What is a web container?
qa.a: Server software such as Tomcat that manages servlets: it receives HTTP requests, creates request/response objects, calls servlets and manages their life cycle.

blocks.x: **JavaServer Pages (JSP)** let you write HTML with embedded Java. The container **translates a JSP into a servlet** on first request, compiles it and runs it.
JSP elements

x: **Directives:** `<%@ page import="java.util.*" %>`, `<%@ include file="header.jsp" %>`, `<%@ taglib ... %>`.
**Declaration:** `<%! int count = 0; %>`.
**Scriptlet:** `<% ... %>` Java code.
**Expression:** `<%= name %>` prints a value.
**Comments:** `<%-- hidden --%>`.
**Actions:** `<jsp:include>`, `<jsp:forward>`, `<jsp:useBean>`.

blocks.x: Implicit objects

Example (reference)

Welcome, <%= name == null ? "guest" : name %>

Page, request, session and application: where an attribute lives. `request.setAttribute("students", list)` shares data with a JSP after a forward.

**View:** presentation (JSP).

JavaBean
A reusable class with a no-argument constructor, private fields and getters/setters, usable by JSP via `jsp:useBean` or EL.

Validate input, use PreparedStatement, escape output (`<c:out>`), store passwords hashed, use HTTPS, and set session timeout.

lessons.title: What is a DBMS and why do we need one?
yt: what is DBMS database management system introduction
DBMS vs file system advantages

blocks.x: A **database** is an organised collection of related data. A **Database Management System (DBMS)** is the software that lets many users and programs create, store, query and protect that data. Examples: MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server, SQLite, MongoDB. A **database system** is the whole package: the data, the DBMS software, and the applications that use them.
File system versus DBMS
Before DBMSs, every application kept its own files. This caused well-known problems:

x: **Data redundancy and inconsistency:** the same student address is copied into the library file, the hostel file and the exam file, and the copies drift apart.
**Difficulty in accessing data:** a new question ("students with CGPA above 8 who live in hostel B") needs a new program to be written.
**Data isolation:** data is scattered across files in different formats.
**Integrity problems:** rules such as "balance must never be negative" are buried in application code and are easy to break.
**Atomicity problems:** if the system crashes halfway through a bank transfer, one account is debited and the other is not credited.
**Concurrent-access anomalies:** two users updating the same record at the same time can overwrite each other.
**Security problems:** it is hard to say "this clerk may read but not change salaries".

blocks.x: What a DBMS provides

x: **Data independence** (the application is shielded from how data is physically stored).
**Efficient access** through indexes and query optimisation.
**Integrity constraints** enforced centrally.
**Transactions** with ACID guarantees, giving atomicity and crash recovery.
**Concurrency control** so many users can work safely together.
**Security and authorisation** by user, role and object.
**Backup and recovery.**

blocks.x: Components of a DBMS

x: **DDL (Data Definition Language)** defines schemas: `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`.
**DML (Data Manipulation Language)** queries and modifies data: `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`.
**Query processor:** parser, optimiser and executor that turn SQL into an efficient plan.
**Storage manager:** buffer manager, file manager, transaction manager.
**Data dictionary (catalogue):** data about data, called **metadata**.

blocks.x: People who work with a DBMS
Database administrator (DBA), database designers, application programmers, and end users (naive users, sophisticated users such as analysts).
Disadvantages

A DBMS costs money, needs trained staff, adds overhead for very simple jobs, and a failure can affect many applications at once. For a tiny single-user task, plain files may still be the better choice.
A DBMS is not the data itself. The DBMS is the software; the database is the data it manages.

qa.q: What is the difference between a database and a DBMS?
qa.a: A database is the organised collection of data. A DBMS is the software that creates, stores, queries and protects that data. MySQL is a DBMS; the tables you create inside it are the database.

qa.q: Why is data redundancy a problem in file systems?
qa.a: The same fact is stored in many places, so it wastes space and, worse, the copies can become inconsistent when only some of them are updated.

qa.q: What is metadata?
qa.a: Data about data: table names, column types, constraints, indexes and users. It is kept in the data dictionary (system catalogue).

qa.q: Name two jobs a DBMS does that a file system does not.
qa.a: Enforcing integrity constraints centrally and guaranteeing atomic, isolated transactions with crash recovery. Concurrency control and fine-grained security are other correct answers.

qa.q: Is a DBMS always better than files?
qa.a: No. For a very small, single-user, short-lived task the cost and overhead of a DBMS is not justified.

quiz.q: Which problem is a direct result of storing the same data in many separate files?
quiz.why: Copies of the same data in different files can disagree after updates, which is inconsistency.

quiz.q: Data about data (table names, column types, constraints) is called
quiz.why: Metadata is stored in the data dictionary or system catalogue.

quiz.q: Which one is a DDL command?
quiz.why: DDL defines structure: CREATE, ALTER, DROP. SELECT, UPDATE and INSERT are DML.

quiz.q: A bank transfer crashes after debiting one account but before crediting the other. Which DBMS feature prevents a half-finished transfer?
quiz.why: Atomicity means the transfer happens completely or not at all, and recovery undoes the partial work.

quiz.q: The software that manages the database is called
quiz.why: The DBMS is the software. The schema is the structure and a relation is a table.

visuals.title: File system and DBMS
visuals.data: File system=Same data repeated in many files~Hard to search and combine~Weak security and sharing~No safe handling of two users at once; DBMS=One controlled copy of data~Query language (SQL)~Access control by user~Transactions, backup and recovery

problems.q: List four disadvantages of a file-processing system that a DBMS removes.
problems.a: 1) Data redundancy and inconsistency (the same data stored in many files). 2) Difficulty in accessing data (a new query needs a new program). 3) Data isolation (data in different formats and files). 4) Integrity problems (rules are buried in program code). 5) Atomicity problems on failure. 6) Concurrent access anomalies. 7) Security problems. Any four are acceptable.

rubric.t: Each disadvantage is stated clearly, not just named

problems.q: Who are the main types of database users? Describe the role of the Database Administrator (DBA).
problems.a: Users: naive (end) users who use ready-made applications, application programmers who write programs, sophisticated users who write queries directly, and database designers. The DBA has central control: defines the schema, decides the storage structure, grants access authorisation, monitors performance, takes backups and handles recovery.

problems.q: A college keeps student data in separate Excel files for the office, library and hostel. Describe five problems this creates and how a DBMS solves each.
problems.a: 1) Redundancy: a student's address appears in three files; a DBMS stores it once. 2) Inconsistency: the address is updated in one file only; central storage updates it once. 3) Integrity: a roll number can be typed wrongly; constraints such as primary and foreign keys reject bad data. 4) Security: everyone can open every file; a DBMS gives role-based access. 5) Concurrent access: two staff editing the same file lose changes; transactions and locking keep updates safe. Backup and recovery is another valid benefit.

lessons.title: Three-schema architecture and data independence
yt: three schema architecture DBMS data independence
physical and logical data independence explained

blocks.x: A database has an overall design (the **schema**) and the actual data stored at a moment in time (the **instance**, also called the database state). Schemas change rarely; instances change constantly. The **three-schema architecture** separates the database into three levels so that changes at one level do not disturb the others.
The three levels

x: **External (view) level:** many schemas, one per user group. Each shows only the part of the data that group needs. A student sees marks and fees; a librarian sees borrowed books.
**Conceptual (logical) level:** one schema describing the whole database for the community of users: entities, attributes, relationships, constraints. It hides physical details.
**Internal (physical) level:** how data is actually stored: file structures, indexes, record layout, compression, access paths.

blocks.x: Between the levels sit **mappings**: external/conceptual mapping and conceptual/internal mapping. The DBMS uses them to translate a request on a view into operations on stored data.
Data independence
Data independence is the ability to change a schema at one level without rewriting the schema at the next higher level.

x: **Logical data independence:** change the conceptual schema (add a column, split a table) without changing external schemas or application programs. This is harder to achieve because applications depend on logical structure.

**Physical data independence:** change the internal schema (add an index, change the file organisation, move to a faster disk) without changing the conceptual schema. This is easier and widely achieved.

blocks.x: Example

Suppose the `Student` table gets a new column `email`. With logical independence, a view that exposes only `roll_no` and `name` keeps working untouched. If the DBA adds an index on `name`, queries run faster but no SQL needs changing: that is physical independence.
Database languages in this picture
The DBA uses DDL to define conceptual and internal schemas, and **VDL** (view definition language) for external ones. Users use DML to read and update data.
Remember: the higher the level, the more abstract. External is closest to the user, internal is closest to the disk.

qa.q: What are the three levels of the three-schema architecture?
qa.a: External (view) level, conceptual (logical) level and internal (physical) level.

qa.q: What is the difference between a schema and an instance?
qa.a: The schema is the design or structure and changes rarely. The instance is the data actually stored at a particular moment and changes with every insert, update or delete.

qa.q: Which kind of data independence is harder to achieve, and why?
qa.a: Logical data independence, because application programs and views depend on the logical structure, so changing tables can force changes above them.

qa.q: Give an example of physical data independence.
qa.a: Adding an index or moving the table to another disk makes queries faster, but no SQL statement and no conceptual schema has to change.

qa.q: What do mappings do between the levels?
qa.a: They let the DBMS translate a request written against one level into operations at the next level down, for example from a view to stored tables.

quiz.q: Which level describes how data is physically stored on disk?
quiz.why: The internal (physical) level covers file structures, indexes and storage details.

quiz.q: Changing the internal schema without changing the conceptual schema is called
quiz.why: Physical data independence protects the conceptual level from storage changes.

quiz.q: A view for the library staff showing only issued books belongs to which level?
quiz.why: Views are external schemas tailored to a group of users.

quiz.q: Which statement is true?
o: The instance changes often while the schema changes rarely
Schema and instance mean the same thing
quiz.why: The schema is the design; the instance is the current content.

quiz.q: Adding a new column to a table without breaking existing user views demonstrates
quiz.why: Logical data independence lets the conceptual schema grow while external schemas stay valid.

visuals.title: Three-schema architecture
visuals.data: View level (external): what each user group sees; Conceptual level: logical design of the whole database; Physical level (internal): how data is stored on disk

problems.q: Name the three levels of the three-schema architecture and say what each describes.
problems.a: External (view) level: the part of the database each user or application sees. Conceptual (logical) level: the structure of the whole database for the community, with entities, attributes and constraints. Internal (physical) level: how data is actually stored, with files, indexes and record layout.

problems.q: Explain physical and logical data independence with one example of each.
problems.a: Physical data independence: changing the internal schema (for example adding an index or moving a file to a new disk) without changing the conceptual schema or application programs. Logical data independence: changing the conceptual schema (for example adding a new column) without changing external views or applications. Logical independence is harder to achieve.

problems.q: For each change, state which independence is involved: (a) creating an index on the Name column, (b) adding an Email column to the Student table so existing reports still work, (c) changing from heap file storage to a sorted file. What role do the mappings between levels play?
problems.a:
(a) physical data independence. (b) logical data independence. (c) physical data independence.
Mappings translate a request on an external view to the conceptual schema, and then to the internal schema. When a lower level changes, only the mapping is updated, so higher levels and programs stay unchanged.

lessons.title: ER model: entities, attributes and relationships
yt: ER model DBMS entities attributes relationships
ER diagram cardinality participation constraints

blocks.x: The **Entity-Relationship (ER) model** is a high-level way to design a database before any tables exist. It is drawn as an **ER diagram (ERD)**.
Entities

x: An **entity** is a real-world thing that can be told apart from others: a student, a course, a book.
An **entity set** is a collection of similar entities (all students). It is drawn as a rectangle.

A **strong entity** has its own key. A **weak entity** has no complete key of its own and depends on an **owner (identifying) entity**; it is drawn as a double rectangle and identified by the owner's key plus a **partial key** (discriminator). Example: `Dependent` of an `Employee`.

blocks.x: Attributes

x: **Simple** (atomic) versus **composite** (Name made of First, Last).
**Single-valued** versus **multivalued** (phone numbers); multivalued is drawn with a double ellipse.
**Derived** attributes can be calculated from others (Age from DateOfBirth); drawn with a dashed ellipse.
**Key attribute** uniquely identifies an entity; it is underlined.
**NULL** means unknown, not applicable or missing.

blocks.x: Relationships
A **relationship** associates entities; a diamond in the diagram. The **degree** is the number of entity sets involved: unary (recursive), binary, ternary.
Cardinality ratio (for a binary relationship)

x: **One-to-one (1:1):** a department has one head and a person heads at most one department.
**One-to-many (1:N):** one department has many employees; each employee works in one department.
**Many-to-many (M:N):** a student takes many courses; a course has many students.

blocks.x: Participation constraint

x: **Total participation** (double line): every entity must take part. Every employee must belong to a department.
**Partial participation** (single line): some entities may not take part.

blocks.x: A relationship can have its own attributes. In `Student takes Course`, the attribute `grade` belongs to the relationship, not to either entity.
Role names and recursion
When the same entity set plays more than one role, label the roles. In `Employee supervises Employee` the roles are supervisor and subordinate.
Design tips

x: Find the nouns: they become entities or attributes.
Find the verbs: they become relationships.
Pick keys early.
Do not store derivable facts twice.

blocks.x: A weak entity cannot exist without its owner. If the employee row is deleted, the dependent rows go with it.

qa.q: What is the difference between a strong and a weak entity?
qa.a: A strong entity has a primary key of its own. A weak entity has no full key; it is identified by the key of its owner entity combined with its own partial key, and it depends on the owner for existence.

qa.q: What is a multivalued attribute? Give an example.
qa.a: An attribute that can hold more than one value for a single entity, such as the phone numbers of a student. It is drawn with a double ellipse.

qa.q: What is total participation?
qa.a: Every entity in the set must take part in the relationship at least once, for example every employee must belong to some department. It is drawn with a double line.

qa.q: Where does the attribute "grade" belong in Student-takes-Course?
qa.a: On the relationship, because the grade depends on the pair (student, course), not on the student alone or the course alone.

qa.q: What does the degree of a relationship mean?
qa.a: The number of entity sets that take part in it. Two is binary, three is ternary, one is unary or recursive.

quiz.why: A weak entity borrows its identity from an owner entity.

lessons.title: Extended ER: specialization, generalization and aggregation
yt: EER model specialization generalization aggregation DBMS
superclass subclass inheritance ER diagram

blocks.x: The **Extended ER (EER) model** adds object-oriented ideas to basic ER so that real designs with "kinds of" entities can be modelled cleanly.
Superclass and subclass

A **subclass** is a special kind of a **superclass**. `Student` and `Teacher` are subclasses of `Person`. A subclass **inherits** all attributes and relationships of its superclass and may add its own. A subclass entity is the same real-world entity as the superclass entity, seen in a specific role.
Specialization (top-down)
Start from a general entity set and define subgroups that have extra attributes or relationships. From `Employee` we define `Engineer` (with `specialty`) and `Secretary` (with `typing_speed`).
Generalization (bottom-up)

Start from several entity sets with common features and combine them into a general one. `Car` and `Truck` share `reg_no` and `owner`, so we generalise them to `Vehicle`. Specialization and generalization are the same idea from opposite directions.
Constraints on specialization

x: **Disjoint (d)** versus **overlapping (o):** can one entity belong to more than one subclass? A person who is only a Student or only a Teacher is disjoint; a person who is both is overlapping.
**Total** versus **partial completeness:** must every superclass entity belong to at least one subclass? In total specialization (double line) yes; in partial (single line) no.

blocks.x: So there are four combinations: disjoint-total, disjoint-partial, overlapping-total, overlapping-partial.
Aggregation

A plain ER relationship cannot relate to another relationship. **Aggregation** treats a relationship set (with its participating entities) as a higher-level entity so that it can take part in another relationship. Example: `Employee works_on Project` is aggregated and then related to `Machine` through `uses`, to record which machine is used for which assignment.
Union types (categories)
A **category** is a subclass whose members come from the union of several different superclasses, for example `Owner` may be a Person, a Company or a Bank.
Inheritance in EER is not the same as inheritance in Java: here it is a data-modelling idea that is later mapped to tables.

qa.q: What is the difference between specialization and generalization?
qa.a: Specialization is top-down: split a general entity set into more specific subsets. Generalization is bottom-up: merge similar entity sets into one general set. They describe the same hierarchy from opposite directions.

qa.q: What do disjoint and overlapping mean?
qa.a: In a disjoint specialization an entity can belong to at most one subclass. In an overlapping one it can belong to several at once.

qa.q: What is total specialization?
qa.a: Every entity in the superclass must belong to at least one subclass, shown by a double line to the specialization circle.

qa.q: Why do we need aggregation?
qa.a: ER relationships connect entity sets only. Aggregation turns a relationship into an abstract entity so it can participate in another relationship.

qa.q: What does a subclass inherit?
qa.a: All attributes and relationship types of its superclass, plus it can have its own local attributes and relationships.
