problems.q: Differentiate between specialization and generalization with an example.
problems.a: Specialization is top-down: start with a general entity and split it into more specific sub-entities, for example Employee into Engineer and Manager. Generalization is bottom-up: combine entities with common features into one super entity, for example Car and Truck into Vehicle. Sub-entities inherit attributes of the super entity.

problems.q: Explain the constraints disjoint versus overlapping, and total versus partial participation, in a specialization. Give an example for each.
problems.a: Disjoint: an entity belongs to at most one subclass (a Vehicle is a Car or a Truck, not both). Overlapping: it can belong to several (a Person can be both Student and Employee). Total: every super-entity must belong to some subclass (every Account is either Savings or Current). Partial: some may belong to no subclass (an Employee need not be a Manager).

A relationship cannot normally participate in another relationship. Aggregation treats the relationship Works_On (Employee, Project) as a single higher-level entity, so Monitors can link Sponsor with that assignment.
Tables: Works_On(EmpID, ProjID) with primary key (EmpID, ProjID); Monitors(SponsorID, EmpID, ProjID) where (EmpID, ProjID) is a foreign key to Works_On.

lessons.title: Mapping an ER diagram to relational tables
yt: ER to relational mapping DBMS
convert ER diagram to tables weak entity many to many

blocks.x: After designing with ER, we convert the diagram to **relations** (tables). The rules below are standard and give a correct, loss-free schema.
Step 1: strong entities
Create a table for each strong entity with its simple attributes. For a composite attribute keep only its simple parts. The key attribute becomes the **primary key**.
`Student(roll_no PK, first_name, last_name, dob)`
Step 2: weak entities
Create a table with the weak entity's attributes plus the **owner's primary key as a foreign key**. The primary key is (owner key + partial key).
`Dependent(emp_id FK, dep_name, relation)` with primary key `(emp_id, dep_name)`.
Step 3: binary 1:1 relationships
Add the primary key of one side as a foreign key on the other, preferably on the side with total participation. Alternatives are merging the two tables or a separate relationship table.
Step 4: binary 1:N relationships
Put the primary key of the **"one" side** into the **"many" side** table as a foreign key, together with any relationship attributes.
`Employee(emp_id PK, name, dept_id FK)` for `Department 1:N Employee`.
Step 5: binary M:N relationships
Create a **new table** whose primary key is the combination of both participating keys. Relationship attributes go here.
`Enrolls(roll_no FK, course_id FK, grade)` with primary key `(roll_no, course_id)`.
Step 6: multivalued attributes
Create a new table holding the attribute value and the owner's key. Primary key is the pair.
`StudentPhone(roll_no FK, phone)` with primary key `(roll_no, phone)`.
Step 7: n-ary relationships
Create a table with the keys of all participating entities as foreign keys; the primary key is usually the combination of them (adjusted by cardinality).
Step 8: specialization (four options)

x: One table per class, subclasses carry the superclass key.
One table per subclass only (works for total, disjoint).
One single table with a type attribute (many NULLs possible).
One table with several boolean type flags (for overlapping).

blocks.x: Derived attributes
Not stored; compute them in queries or views.
Quick rule: 1:N puts a foreign key on the N side. M:N always needs its own table.

qa.q: How is a many-to-many relationship converted to tables?
qa.a: Create a separate table whose primary key is the combination of the primary keys of the two entities, which are also foreign keys. Relationship attributes become columns of this table.

qa.q: Where does the foreign key go for a 1:N relationship?
qa.a: On the "N" (many) side, referencing the primary key of the "1" side.

qa.q: How is a multivalued attribute stored in the relational model?
qa.a: In a separate table with the owner's key and the attribute value, with both columns together as the primary key.

qa.q: What is the primary key of a weak entity's table?
qa.a: The primary key of the owner entity combined with the weak entity's partial key.

qa.q: Are derived attributes stored?
qa.a: Normally not. They are calculated when needed, for instance with an expression in a query or a view.

lessons.title: Relational model and keys
yt: relational model DBMS keys super key candidate key primary key foreign key
types of keys in DBMS with examples

blocks.x: Proposed by E. F. Codd (1970), the **relational model** represents all data as **relations**: tables of rows and columns.
Terminology

x: **Relation** = table. **Tuple** = row. **Attribute** = column. **Domain** = set of allowed values of an attribute.
**Degree** = number of attributes. **Cardinality** = number of tuples.
A **relation schema** `R(A1, A2, ..., An)` is the structure; a **relation instance** is the current set of tuples.
A relation is a **set** of tuples, so there is no order and no duplicate rows. Each value is **atomic**.

blocks.x: Keys

x: **Super key:** any set of attributes that uniquely identifies a tuple. `{roll_no}`, `{roll_no, name}` are super keys.
**Candidate key:** a **minimal** super key (no attribute can be removed). A table can have several.
**Primary key:** the candidate key chosen to identify tuples. It cannot be NULL and is unique.
**Alternate key:** candidate keys not chosen as primary.
**Composite key:** a key made of more than one attribute.
**Foreign key:** attribute(s) in one relation that refer to the primary key of another (or the same) relation. It creates the link between tables.
**Unique key:** enforces uniqueness; allows NULL in most systems.

blocks.x: Example
Here `roll_no` and `email` are candidate keys of `Student`; `roll_no` is chosen as primary, `email` is an alternate key. In `Enroll`, `roll_no` is a foreign key.
Counting super keys

If a relation has n attributes and a single candidate key of one attribute, the number of super keys is 2^(n-1), because the key attribute must be present and each of the other n-1 attributes may be present or absent.
Properties of the relational model
Each table has a unique name, each column a unique name within the table, values come from a single domain, and the order of rows and columns is not significant.
Primary key = unique + not null. Candidate key = minimal super key.

qa.q: What is the difference between a super key and a candidate key?
qa.a: A super key is any attribute set that uniquely identifies rows. A candidate key is a super key with no redundant attribute, that is, a minimal one.

qa.q: Can a primary key contain NULL?
qa.a: No. A primary key must be unique and not null (entity integrity).

qa.q: What is a foreign key and why is it used?
qa.a: It is an attribute (or set) in one table that refers to the primary key of another table. It links tables and enforces referential integrity.

qa.q: Can a table have more than one candidate key? More than one primary key?
qa.a: A table can have many candidate keys but only one primary key.

qa.q: A relation has 4 attributes and only one single-attribute candidate key. How many super keys does it have?
qa.a: 2^(4-1) = 8, because the key attribute is always present and each of the other three attributes can be included or not.

quiz.q: Which key may refer to the primary key of another table?
quiz.why: A foreign key stores values from the referenced primary key.

quiz.q: The number of tuples in a relation is its
quiz.why: Cardinality counts rows; degree counts columns.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a property of a relation?
quiz.why: The order of tuples in a relation is not significant.

quiz.q: Relation R(A,B,C,D) has the single candidate key A. How many super keys does it have?
quiz.why: Any subset that contains A is a super key: 2^3 = 8.

problems.a: Candidate keys: RollNo and Email. Primary key: RollNo (chosen). Alternate key: Email. A super key that is not minimal: (RollNo, Name), because RollNo alone already identifies the row.

problems.a: A foreign key is an attribute (or set) in one table that refers to the primary key of another table. Employee.DeptID references Department.DeptID. It guarantees that every employee's DeptID is either NULL or equals an existing department, so no employee points to a department that does not exist.

problems.q: R(A, B, C, D) has candidate keys A and B only. How many super keys does R have? Show the counting method.
problems.a: Every subset of the 4 attributes is 2^4 = 16 subsets. A subset is a super key if it contains A or contains B. Subsets that contain neither A nor B are the subsets of {C, D}: 2^2 = 4. So super keys = 16 - 4 = 12.

rubric.t: Subtracts the 4 subsets without A or B

lessons.title: Integrity constraints
yt: integrity constraints DBMS domain entity referential
referential integrity cascade on delete SQL

blocks.x: **Integrity constraints** are rules that the DBMS enforces so that stored data stays correct and consistent.
Domain constraints
Each attribute value must come from its declared domain: correct data type, length, range or allowed list.
Key constraints
Every relation has at least one candidate key; values of a key must be **unique** across tuples.
Entity integrity
No primary-key attribute may be NULL, because NULL means unknown and a row with an unknown identity cannot be told apart from others.
Referential integrity

If a tuple in table R1 has a foreign key referring to R2, the referenced primary key value **must exist** in R2 (or the foreign key must be NULL). So an enrolment cannot refer to a student who does not exist.
Actions on delete/update of the referenced row

x: **RESTRICT / NO ACTION:** reject the operation.
**CASCADE:** delete or update the referencing rows too.
**SET NULL:** set the foreign key to NULL.
**SET DEFAULT:** set the foreign key to its default value.

blocks.x: Other constraints

x: **NOT NULL:** column must have a value.
**UNIQUE:** no two rows may repeat the value.
**CHECK:** a condition on a row.
**DEFAULT:** value used when none is supplied.
**Assertions and triggers:** general business rules across tables (for example, "a department cannot have more than 100 employees").

blocks.x: When are constraints checked?
After each INSERT, DELETE or UPDATE statement, or at COMMIT if declared as deferrable. A violating operation is rejected and the database stays valid.
Entity integrity is about primary keys (no NULL). Referential integrity is about foreign keys (must match something).

qa.q: What is referential integrity?
qa.a: A foreign key value must either be NULL or match an existing primary key value in the referenced table, so no row points to something that does not exist.

qa.q: What does ON DELETE CASCADE do?
qa.a: When the referenced parent row is deleted, all child rows that refer to it are deleted automatically.

qa.q: What is entity integrity?
qa.a: It says that no attribute of a primary key can be NULL, so every row can be identified.

qa.q: Which constraint would you use to ensure age is between 15 and 60?
qa.a: A CHECK constraint, for example CHECK (age BETWEEN 15 AND 60).

qa.q: Difference between UNIQUE and PRIMARY KEY?
qa.a: Both enforce uniqueness, but a table can have only one primary key and it cannot be NULL, while it can have many UNIQUE constraints and they usually allow NULL.

quiz.q: Which constraint ensures that a foreign key value exists in the parent table?
quiz.why: Referential integrity links child rows to existing parent rows.

quiz.q: A primary key containing NULL violates
quiz.why: Entity integrity forbids NULL in primary key attributes.

quiz.q: ON DELETE CASCADE means
o: the foreign key is set to NULL
child rows are deleted with the parent
quiz.why: CASCADE propagates the delete to referencing rows.

quiz.q: CHECK (age >= 18) is a
quiz.why: It restricts the allowed values of a column, which is a domain-type constraint.

quiz.q: Which action is performed by ON DELETE SET NULL?
o: Sets the foreign key in child rows to NULL
quiz.why: The child rows stay but lose the reference.

lessons.title: Relational algebra
yt: relational algebra DBMS select project join division
relational algebra operators with examples

blocks.x: **Relational algebra** is a procedural query language: operators take one or two relations and return a relation. It is the theoretical base of SQL and of query optimisation.
Fundamental operators

x: **Selection σ**: picks rows that satisfy a condition. `σ_{cgpa>8}(Student)`.
**Projection π**: picks columns and removes duplicates. `π_{name, cgpa}(Student)`.
**Union ∪**, **Set difference −**, **Intersection ∩**: need **union-compatible** relations (same number of attributes with compatible domains). Intersection can be written as `R − (R − S)`.
**Cartesian product ×**: every tuple of R paired with every tuple of S; degree adds, cardinality multiplies.
**Rename ρ**: renames a relation or its attributes.

blocks.x: Derived operators

x: **Natural join ⋈**: product followed by selection on equal common attributes and removal of the duplicate columns.
**Theta join ⋈_θ** (**equijoin** when θ is equality): `R ⋈_{R.a = S.b} S`.
**Outer joins** (left, right, full): keep unmatched tuples from one or both sides, filling NULLs.
**Division ÷**: finds tuples in R related to **all** tuples in S.

blocks.x: Example data
`Student(roll, name, dept)`, `Enroll(roll, cid)`, `Course(cid, title)`.

x: Names of students in CSE: `π_{name}(σ_{dept='CSE'}(Student))`.
Titles of courses taken by student 5: `π_{title}(σ_{roll=5}(Enroll) ⋈ Course)`.
Students who took **every** course: `π_{roll,cid}(Enroll) ÷ π_{cid}(Course)`.

blocks.x: Useful identities

x: Selections can be cascaded: `σ_{A∧B}(R) = σ_A(σ_B(R))` and are commutative.
Push selection below join to shrink data early.
Projection reduces columns; do it before joins when possible.

blocks.x: Size rules

x: If |R| = m and |S| = n: |R × S| = m·n; |R ∪ S| ≤ m+n; |R ∩ S| ≤ min(m,n); |R − S| ≤ m.
Natural join of relations with no common attribute equals the Cartesian product.

blocks.x: Extended operators
Aggregation `G` with functions SUM, AVG, COUNT, MIN, MAX and grouping, e.g. `dept G_{avg(cgpa)}(Student)`.
Relational algebra on sets removes duplicates; SQL works on bags (multisets) unless DISTINCT is used.

qa.q: What is the difference between selection and projection?
qa.a: Selection (σ) chooses rows that satisfy a condition. Projection (π) chooses columns and removes duplicate rows.

qa.q: What are union-compatible relations?
qa.a: Two relations with the same number of attributes where corresponding attributes have compatible domains. Union, intersection and difference require this.

qa.q: What does the division operator find?
qa.a: The values in R that are paired with all values in S, for example students who enrolled in every course.

qa.q: If R has 4 tuples and S has 5 tuples, how many tuples does R × S have?
qa.a: 20, because every tuple of R is paired with every tuple of S.

qa.q: How is a natural join different from a Cartesian product?
qa.a: A natural join keeps only pairs that agree on all common attributes and shows each common attribute once; the Cartesian product keeps all pairs.

quiz.q: Which operator removes duplicate rows after choosing columns?
quiz.why: Projection in relational algebra returns a set, so duplicates vanish.

quiz.q: R has 6 tuples and S has 7. The cardinality of R × S is
quiz.why: Cartesian product multiplies cardinalities: 6 x 7 = 42.

quiz.q: Which operator finds "students who took all courses"?
quiz.why: Division answers "for all" queries.

quiz.q: Intersection can be expressed using
quiz.why: Removing from R everything not in S leaves R ∩ S.

quiz.q: For union, relations must be
quiz.why: Union needs the same number of attributes with compatible domains.

lessons.title: Relational calculus (tuple and domain)
yt: tuple relational calculus DBMS
relational calculus vs relational algebra safe expressions

blocks.x: **Relational calculus** is a **declarative** (non-procedural) query language. Instead of saying *how* to compute a result (as algebra does), you describe *what* the result should look like using predicate logic.
Tuple relational calculus (TRC)
A query has the form `{ t | P(t) }`: the set of all tuples `t` for which predicate `P` is true.

x: `t ∈ Student` binds the tuple variable to a relation.
`t[name]` or `t.name` selects an attribute.
Connectives: ∧ (and), ∨ (or), ¬ (not), ⇒ (implies).
Quantifiers: **∃** (there exists) and **∀** (for all).

blocks.x: Examples:

x: Students of CSE: `{ t | t ∈ Student ∧ t.dept = 'CSE' }`
Names of students with cgpa above 8: `{ t.name | t ∈ Student ∧ t.cgpa > 8 }`
Students who took course 'DB1': `{ s | s ∈ Student ∧ ∃e (e ∈ Enroll ∧ e.roll = s.roll ∧ e.cid = 'DB1') }`
Students who took **all** courses: `{ s | s ∈ Student ∧ ∀c (c ∈ Course ⇒ ∃e (e ∈ Enroll ∧ e.roll = s.roll ∧ e.cid = c.cid)) }`

blocks.x: Safe expressions

An expression is **safe** if it produces a finite result using only values that appear in the database. `{ t | ¬(t ∈ Student) }` is unsafe because infinitely many tuples are not in Student. Safe TRC has the same expressive power as relational algebra, which is why SQL (based on TRC) can be translated to algebra.
Domain relational calculus (DRC)

Variables range over **attribute values (domains)** rather than whole tuples. Form: `{ <x1, x2, ..., xn> | P(x1, ..., xn) }`. Example: `{ <n> | ∃r, d, g (<r, n, d, g> ∈ Student ∧ g > 8) }`. QBE (Query By Example) is based on DRC.
Algebra vs calculus
SQL is mostly declarative like TRC, but the optimiser turns it into relational algebra to execute it.

qa.q: What does the tuple relational calculus expression { t | t ∈ Student ∧ t.cgpa > 8 } return?
qa.a: All tuples of Student whose cgpa is greater than 8.

qa.q: What is a safe expression?
qa.a: One that always yields a finite result containing only values from the database. Unsafe example: { t | ¬(t ∈ R) }.

qa.q: What is the difference between TRC and DRC?
qa.a: In TRC variables stand for whole tuples; in DRC variables stand for individual attribute values (domain elements).

qa.q: Is relational algebra or calculus procedural?
qa.a: Algebra is procedural (you give a sequence of operations). Calculus is declarative (you describe the result).

qa.q: Which quantifier is used for "for all"?
qa.a: The universal quantifier ∀. The existential quantifier ∃ means "there exists".

quiz.why: Query By Example uses domain variables. SQL is closer to tuple calculus.

quiz.q: The quantifier ∀ means
quiz.why: ∀ is the universal quantifier.

quiz.why: Unsafe expressions such as { t | ¬(t ∈ R) } are not allowed.

quiz.q: Safe tuple calculus and relational algebra are
quiz.why: Codd's theorem shows they can express exactly the same queries.

{ s.Name | Student(s) AND FORALL c (Course(c) IMPLIES EXISTS e (Enrolled(e) AND e.SID = s.SID AND e.CID = c.CID)) }.
{ t | NOT Student(t) } is unsafe because it describes every possible tuple that is not in Student, which is an infinite set. Safe expressions only return values that come from the database.

lessons.title: SQL DDL: creating tables, data types and constraints
yt: SQL DDL create alter drop table constraints
SQL data types and constraints primary key foreign key check default

blocks.x: **SQL (Structured Query Language)** is the standard language of relational databases. Its commands fall into groups:

x: **DDL** (Data Definition): `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`, `TRUNCATE`, `RENAME`.
**DML** (Data Manipulation): `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `SELECT` (often counted as DQL, the query part).
**DCL** (Data Control): `GRANT`, `REVOKE`.
**TCL** (Transaction Control): `COMMIT`, `ROLLBACK`, `SAVEPOINT`.

blocks.x: Common data types

head: Type
Meaning
rows: Exact numbers with p digits, s after the point (use for money)
Variable length text up to n
True or false (in some systems stored as a small integer)

blocks.x: CREATE TABLE with constraints
Result of the last query: `1 | Asha | 1 | 0.0 | NULL`. The `cgpa` took its DEFAULT and `city` is NULL because no value was given.
Constraint recap

x: `PRIMARY KEY`: unique and not null, one per table.
`UNIQUE`: no repeated values.
`NOT NULL`: a value is required.
`CHECK`: a condition each row must satisfy.
`DEFAULT`: value used when none supplied.
`FOREIGN KEY ... REFERENCES`: referential integrity with `ON DELETE` / `ON UPDATE` actions.

blocks.x: You can also name constraints and write them at table level, which is needed for composite keys:

CREATE TABLE Enroll (
  roll  INT,
  cid   VARCHAR(5),
  marks INT,
  CONSTRAINT pk_enroll PRIMARY KEY (roll, cid),
  CONSTRAINT fk_stu FOREIGN KEY (roll) REFERENCES Student(roll)
);
ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE

ALTER TABLE Student ADD email VARCHAR(60);      -- add a column
ALTER TABLE Student MODIFY name VARCHAR(80);    -- change type (MySQL; Oracle also uses MODIFY)
ALTER TABLE Student DROP COLUMN city;           -- remove a column
TRUNCATE TABLE Enroll;                          -- delete all rows quickly, keep the table
DROP TABLE Enroll;                              -- delete table and its data
Differences: `DELETE` removes selected rows and can be rolled back in most systems; `TRUNCATE` removes all rows quickly (DDL, usually not rollbackable); `DROP` removes the whole table definition.
Always create parent tables before child tables, and drop in the opposite order, or the foreign keys will complain.

qa.q: What is the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP?
qa.a: DELETE removes chosen rows (with WHERE) and can be rolled back. TRUNCATE removes all rows quickly and keeps the structure. DROP removes the table itself, structure and data.

qa.q: Which type should be used for money, FLOAT or DECIMAL?
qa.a: DECIMAL (NUMERIC), because it is exact. FLOAT is approximate and can give rounding errors.

qa.q: What is the difference between CHAR and VARCHAR?
qa.a: CHAR(n) always stores n characters, padding with spaces. VARCHAR(n) stores only the characters given, up to n.

qa.q: Why must a composite primary key be declared at table level?
qa.a: A column-level PRIMARY KEY applies to one column. A key made of several columns must be written as PRIMARY KEY (col1, col2) after the column list.

qa.q: Which commands belong to DCL?
qa.a: GRANT and REVOKE, which give and take away privileges.

quiz.q: Which statement removes the table structure as well as its data?
quiz.why: DROP removes the table definition completely.

quiz.q: A column that must always have a value uses the constraint
quiz.why: NOT NULL rejects missing values.

quiz.q: Which data type is best for storing prices exactly?
quiz.why: DECIMAL stores exact numbers.

quiz.q: GRANT and REVOKE are
quiz.why: They control privileges, so they are data control language.

quiz.q: Which constraint supplies a value when the INSERT does not give one?
quiz.why: DEFAULT fills in the specified value.

blocks.x: We use a small sample database in this and the next lessons. Departments, students, courses and enrolments:
INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
`UPDATE` and `DELETE` without a `WHERE` clause affect **every** row. Always check the condition first with a `SELECT`.
SELECT anatomy

SELECT [DISTINCT] columns
FROM tables
WHERE row condition
GROUP BY columns
HAVING group condition
ORDER BY columns [ASC|DESC]
LIMIT n
The **logical order of execution** is FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, LIMIT. That is why an alias defined in SELECT cannot be used in WHERE.
Filtering and sorting
SELECT name, cgpa FROM Student WHERE cgpa >= 8 ORDER BY cgpa DESC;
Output:
SELECT DISTINCT city FROM Student ORDER BY city;
Output: Dehradun, Delhi, Lucknow, Patna.
Operators

x: Logical: `AND`, `OR`, `NOT`.
`BETWEEN a AND b` is inclusive. `IN (list)`.
`LIKE` pattern matching: `%` is any string, `_` is one character. `name LIKE '%a'` finds names ending in a (case rules depend on the system).
**NULL** needs `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL`. `dept_id = NULL` is never true, because any comparison with NULL gives UNKNOWN.

blocks.x: SELECT name FROM Student WHERE name LIKE '%a' AND dept_id IS NOT NULL;
Output: Asha, Chitra, Esha (Farhan has no department, and Dev and Bilal do not end in a).
SELECT name, cgpa FROM Student ORDER BY cgpa DESC LIMIT 3;
This returns the top three by cgpa (called `TOP 3` in SQL Server, `FETCH FIRST 3 ROWS ONLY` in Oracle and standard SQL).
Expressions and CASE

SELECT name, CASE WHEN cgpa >= 9 THEN 'A' WHEN cgpa >= 8 THEN 'B' ELSE 'C' END AS grade
FROM Student ORDER BY roll;
Output grades: Asha B, Bilal C, Chitra A, Dev C, Esha B, Farhan C.
Three-valued logic: comparisons with NULL return UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is TRUE.

qa.q: Why does WHERE dept_id = NULL return no rows?
qa.a: Any comparison with NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, not TRUE. Use IS NULL instead.

qa.q: In what order does the DBMS logically evaluate the clauses of SELECT?
qa.a: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, LIMIT. That is why SELECT aliases cannot be used in WHERE.

qa.q: What does the % wildcard mean in LIKE?
qa.a: It matches any sequence of zero or more characters. The underscore matches exactly one character.

qa.q: What happens if you run UPDATE without WHERE?
qa.a: Every row of the table is updated. Always test the WHERE condition with SELECT first.

qa.q: Is BETWEEN 5 AND 10 inclusive?
qa.a: Yes, it includes both 5 and 10.

quiz.why: WHERE works on rows. HAVING works on groups after GROUP BY.

quiz.why: DESC means descending order.

quiz.why: DISTINCT removes duplicate result rows.

lessons.title: SQL joins: inner, outer, cross and self
yt: SQL joins inner left right full outer cross self join explained
SQL join examples with output

blocks.x: A **join** combines rows from two or more tables based on a relationship between columns, usually primary key to foreign key. We use the sample database from the previous lesson.
Remember: Farhan has no department (NULL) and department ME has no students.
INNER JOIN
Keeps only matching pairs.

SELECT s.name, d.dname
FROM Student s INNER JOIN Dept d ON s.dept_id = d.dept_id;
Output: Asha CSE, Bilal CSE, Chitra ECE, Dev ECE, Esha CSE. Farhan disappears because his dept_id is NULL and never equals anything.
LEFT (OUTER) JOIN
Keeps **all rows of the left table**, filling NULL where there is no match.

SELECT s.name, d.dname
FROM Student s LEFT JOIN Dept d ON s.dept_id = d.dept_id;
The same five rows plus `Farhan | NULL`.
Reverse the tables to keep every department, including ME with no students:

SELECT d.dname, s.name
FROM Dept d LEFT JOIN Student s ON s.dept_id = d.dept_id;
Output ends with `ME | NULL`.
RIGHT and FULL OUTER JOIN
`RIGHT JOIN` keeps all rows of the right table. `FULL OUTER JOIN` keeps all rows of both. (MySQL has no FULL JOIN; it is simulated with `LEFT JOIN UNION RIGHT JOIN`.)

SELECT s.name, d.dname
FROM Student s FULL OUTER JOIN Dept d ON s.dept_id = d.dept_id;
This returns the five matches, `Farhan | NULL` and `NULL | ME`.
CROSS JOIN
Every row with every row (Cartesian product). 6 students x 3 courses = 18 rows.
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Student CROSS JOIN Course;
Output: 18.
Joining three tables

SELECT s.name, e.cid, e.marks
FROM Student s JOIN Enroll e ON s.roll = e.roll
               JOIN Course c ON c.cid = e.cid
WHERE c.credits = 4;
Six rows: Asha DB1 88, Asha OS1 79, Bilal DB1 65, Chitra DB1 92, Esha OS1 74, Esha DB1 81.
SELF JOIN
A table joined to itself using aliases. Pairs of students who live in the same city:

SELECT a.name AS s1, b.name AS s2
FROM Student a JOIN Student b ON a.city = b.city AND a.roll < b.roll;
Output: `Asha | Chitra` (Delhi) and `Bilal | Farhan` (Lucknow). The condition `a.roll < b.roll` avoids pairing a student with themself and listing each pair twice.
NATURAL JOIN and USING

`NATURAL JOIN` joins on all columns with the same name. `JOIN ... USING (col)` joins on a named common column. They are shorter but risky when a new same-named column appears, so most teams prefer explicit `ON`.
ON versus WHERE: for outer joins a filter placed in WHERE on the optional side can silently turn the outer join into an inner join.

qa.a: INNER JOIN returns only rows with a match in both tables. LEFT JOIN also returns every row of the left table, with NULLs for the right columns when there is no match.

qa.a: 18, the product of the two row counts.

qa.q: What is a self join and when do you use it?
qa.a: Joining a table with itself using two aliases. It is used for hierarchical or pair-wise data, such as employees and their managers or students from the same city.

qa.q: Why does Farhan not appear in the INNER JOIN of Student and Dept?
qa.a: His dept_id is NULL and NULL never equals any value, so there is no matching department row.

qa.q: How is FULL OUTER JOIN done in MySQL?
qa.a: MySQL has no FULL OUTER JOIN, so you combine a LEFT JOIN and a RIGHT JOIN with UNION.

lessons.title: Aggregate functions, GROUP BY and HAVING
yt: SQL aggregate functions group by having
SQL group by vs having difference with examples

blocks.x: An **aggregate function** reduces many rows to one value: `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`. Same sample database as before:
How aggregates treat NULL

x: `COUNT(*)` counts rows. `COUNT(col)` counts non-NULL values. `COUNT(DISTINCT col)` counts distinct non-NULL values.
`SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX` ignore NULLs.

blocks.x: SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(dept_id), AVG(cgpa) FROM Student;
Output: `6 | 5 | 8.05`. Farhan's NULL dept_id is not counted by `COUNT(dept_id)`.
GROUP BY
Splits rows into groups with equal values of the grouping columns, then applies aggregates per group.

SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS n, ROUND(AVG(cgpa), 2) AS avg_cgpa, MAX(cgpa) AS best
FROM Student GROUP BY dept_id;
Note that NULLs form their own group. **Rule:** every column in SELECT that is not inside an aggregate must appear in GROUP BY.
HAVING versus WHERE

x: `WHERE` filters **rows before** grouping and cannot use aggregates.
`HAVING` filters **groups after** aggregation and can use aggregates.

blocks.x:
SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM Student GROUP BY dept_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2;
Output: department 1 with 3 students and department 2 with 2. The NULL group has only 1, so it is removed.
You can combine both: `WHERE cgpa > 7 GROUP BY dept_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2` first discards students with low cgpa, then groups, then drops small groups.
Average marks per course

SELECT cid, AVG(marks) AS avgm, COUNT(*) AS takers
FROM Enroll GROUP BY cid ORDER BY avgm DESC;
Typical mistakes

x: Selecting a non-grouped column: `SELECT name, COUNT(*) ... GROUP BY dept_id` is invalid (or returns arbitrary values in lenient systems).
Using an aggregate in WHERE: write `HAVING` instead.
Expecting `AVG` over an empty set to be 0: it is NULL.

blocks.x: Order of clauses: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE ... GROUP BY ... HAVING ... ORDER BY.

qa.q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
qa.a: WHERE filters rows before grouping and cannot use aggregate functions. HAVING filters groups after aggregation and normally uses aggregates.

qa.q: What is the difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(column)?
qa.a: COUNT(*) counts all rows. COUNT(column) counts only rows where that column is not NULL.

qa.q: Do aggregate functions count NULL values in AVG?
qa.a: No. AVG, SUM, MIN and MAX ignore NULLs, so a row with NULL does not affect the average.

qa.q: Can we use a column in SELECT that is not in GROUP BY?
qa.a: Only if it is inside an aggregate function. Otherwise the query is invalid in standard SQL.

qa.q: How do NULL values behave in GROUP BY?
qa.a: All NULLs in the grouping column are placed in one group.

lessons.title: Subqueries and set operations
yt: SQL subquery correlated exists in not in

blocks.x: A **subquery** (nested query) is a SELECT inside another SQL statement, written in parentheses.
Scalar subquery (returns one value)
Students above the average cgpa (average is 8.05):
SELECT name FROM Student WHERE cgpa > (SELECT AVG(cgpa) FROM Student);
Output: Asha, Chitra, Esha.
Multi-row subquery: IN, ANY, ALL

SELECT name FROM Student
WHERE roll IN (SELECT roll FROM Enroll WHERE cid = 'DB1');
Output: Asha, Bilal, Chitra, Esha. `> ALL (subquery)` means greater than every value returned; `> ANY` means greater than at least one.
Correlated subquery
The inner query refers to a column of the outer query, so it is re-evaluated for each outer row.

SELECT name FROM Student s
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Enroll e WHERE e.roll = s.roll AND e.cid = 'OS1');
Output: Asha, Esha. `EXISTS` is true if the subquery returns at least one row and stops at the first match.
NOT IN and the NULL trap
SELECT name FROM Student WHERE roll NOT IN (SELECT roll FROM Enroll);

Output: Dev, Farhan (students with no enrolment). If the subquery returns even one NULL, `NOT IN` returns no rows at all, because the comparison becomes UNKNOWN. `NOT EXISTS` does not have this problem, so it is the safer form.
Subquery in SELECT and FROM

SELECT name, cgpa, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Enroll e WHERE e.roll = s.roll) AS courses
FROM Student s ORDER BY courses DESC, name LIMIT 3;
Output: Asha 2, Chitra 2, Esha 2. A subquery in FROM is called a **derived table** and must have an alias.
Set operations
Both queries must return the same number of compatible columns. They remove duplicates by default; `UNION ALL` keeps them.
Output: 1 and 5 (took both DB1 and OS1).

x: `UNION`: rows in either result.
`INTERSECT`: rows in both.
`EXCEPT` (`MINUS` in Oracle): rows in the first and not in the second. `DB1 EXCEPT OS1` gives 2 and 3.

blocks.x: Division-like query "students who took every course" is done with a double `NOT EXISTS`.
Joins are often faster and easier to read than nested subqueries, but subqueries express "for all" and "does not exist" logic well.

qa.q: What is a correlated subquery?
qa.a: A subquery that uses a column from the outer query, so it runs once for every row of the outer query.

qa.q: What is the difference between IN and EXISTS?
qa.a: IN compares a value to the list a subquery returns. EXISTS only checks whether the subquery returns any row at all and stops at the first.

qa.q: Why can NOT IN return no rows unexpectedly?
qa.a: If the subquery list contains a NULL, comparisons give UNKNOWN for every row, so none passes. NOT EXISTS avoids this.

qa.q: What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL?
qa.a: UNION removes duplicate rows from the combined result; UNION ALL keeps all rows and is faster.

qa.q: Which operator returns rows in the first query but not in the second?
qa.a: EXCEPT (MINUS in Oracle).

quiz.why: Comparing with NULL gives UNKNOWN, so no row qualifies.

quiz.why: UNION ALL skips the duplicate-elimination step.

problems.q: What does SELECT 1 WHERE 5 NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) return and why? How does NOT EXISTS avoid this problem?
problems.a: It returns no rows. 5 NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) means 5 <> 1 AND 5 <> 2 AND 5 <> NULL. The last comparison is unknown, so the whole condition is never true. NOT EXISTS tests whether a matching row exists and is not affected by NULL values in the same way, so it is the safer choice when the subquery column may contain NULL.

lessons.title: Views and indexes
yt: SQL views and indexes explained
database index clustered non clustered

blocks.x: Views
A **view** is a stored query that behaves like a virtual table. It stores no data of its own (except **materialised views**, which cache the result).
Result: Chitra 9.1, Asha 8.9, Esha 8.2.
Why use views?

x: **Security:** show only some columns or rows to a user group.
**Simplicity:** hide complex joins behind a name.
**Logical data independence:** applications keep working if the base tables change.

blocks.x: A view is **updatable** only when it maps clearly to rows of one base table (no DISTINCT, GROUP BY, aggregates or joins in most systems). `WITH CHECK OPTION` stops an update that would make a row vanish from the view. Drop with `DROP VIEW Toppers;`.
Indexes
An **index** is an extra data structure (usually a **B+ tree**, sometimes a hash) that lets the DBMS find rows without scanning the whole table, like the index at the back of a book.

CREATE INDEX idx_student_city ON Student(city);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_student_name ON Student(name);
Primary keys and unique constraints automatically get an index.
Types

x: **Clustered index:** decides the physical order of rows; only one per table. In many systems the primary key is clustered.
**Non-clustered (secondary) index:** separate structure holding key values and pointers to rows; many allowed.
**Dense** index has an entry for every record; **sparse** index has one entry per block.
**Composite index** on several columns: `(dept_id, cgpa)` helps queries that filter on `dept_id` or on `dept_id` and `cgpa`, but not on `cgpa` alone (left-most prefix rule).

blocks.x: Trade-offs

Indexes make `SELECT` with `WHERE`, `JOIN` and `ORDER BY` much faster, but they take space and slow `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` because every index must be updated. Index columns that are searched often and have many different values (high selectivity). Avoid indexing tiny tables or columns with few distinct values.
Seeing the effect
Most systems have `EXPLAIN` to show the query plan: a full table scan without the index and an index search with it.
A view saves a query; an index speeds up a query. They solve different problems.

qa.q: What is a view?
qa.a: A virtual table defined by a stored SELECT query. It does not hold its own data; it is computed from base tables when used.

qa.q: Give two reasons to use views.
qa.a: To restrict access to certain rows or columns (security) and to hide complex queries behind a simple name (simplicity, logical data independence).

qa.q: What is the difference between clustered and non-clustered index?
qa.a: A clustered index determines the physical order of the rows, so a table can have only one. A non-clustered index is a separate structure with pointers to the rows; a table can have many.

qa.q: Why not index every column?
qa.a: Indexes use storage and slow down INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE because they must be maintained, so only columns used for searching, joining or sorting are worth indexing.

qa.q: What data structure do most database indexes use?
qa.a: The B+ tree, which stays balanced and supports both exact and range searches.

quiz.why: A normal view saves the SELECT, not the data.

quiz.q: How many clustered indexes can a table have?
quiz.why: Rows can be physically ordered in only one way.

quiz.q: Which structure is most commonly used for database indexes?
quiz.why: B+ trees are balanced and efficient for disk access.

quiz.q: An index mainly improves the speed of
quiz.why: It speeds up lookups; writes become slightly slower.

quiz.q: WITH CHECK OPTION on a view
o: prevents updates that would make rows disappear from the view
quiz.why: It enforces that modified rows still satisfy the view condition.

lessons.title: Stored procedures, functions, triggers and cursors (PL/SQL)
yt: PL/SQL stored procedure function trigger cursor
MySQL trigger stored procedure tutorial

blocks.x: SQL is declarative. **PL/SQL** (Oracle) and similar extensions (T-SQL, MySQL stored programs) add variables, conditions, loops and error handling so logic can live **inside the database**.
PL/SQL block structure
Parts: `DECLARE` (optional), `BEGIN ... END` (required), `EXCEPTION` (optional). `%TYPE` copies a column's data type.
Stored procedure
A named, saved block that can take `IN`, `OUT` and `IN OUT` parameters and is called with `CALL` or `EXEC`. It does not have to return a value.
Function
Like a procedure but it **must return a value** and can be used inside SQL expressions.
Usage: `SELECT name, grade_of(cgpa) FROM Student;`
Cursor
A **cursor** lets you process a multi-row result one row at a time. **Implicit** cursors are created automatically for DML. **Explicit** cursors are declared:
Cursor attributes: `%FOUND`, `%NOTFOUND`, `%ISOPEN`, `%ROWCOUNT`. The life cycle is DECLARE, OPEN, FETCH, CLOSE.
Trigger

A **trigger** runs automatically when an event (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) happens on a table. It can run `BEFORE` or `AFTER`, and for each statement or **for each row**. In a row trigger, `:OLD` and `:NEW` (Oracle) or `OLD`/`NEW` (MySQL) hold the old and new values.
Uses: audit logs, enforcing complex rules, maintaining derived data. Misuse makes behaviour hard to follow and debug.
Procedure vs function vs trigger
The code on this page is Oracle PL/SQL. MySQL and SQL Server use similar ideas with different syntax (for example `DELIMITER`, `NEW`/`OLD`, or T-SQL `inserted`/`deleted`).

qa.q: What is the difference between a procedure and a function in PL/SQL?
qa.a: A function must return a value and can be called inside SQL statements. A procedure may return values only through OUT parameters and is called as a statement.

qa.q: What is a cursor and why is it needed?
qa.a: A cursor is a pointer to a query result that lets a program process the rows one at a time. It is needed because procedural code works on one record at a time while SELECT returns a set.

qa.q: What are the four steps of using an explicit cursor?
qa.a: Declare, open, fetch (usually in a loop) and close.

qa.q: What are :OLD and :NEW in a trigger?
qa.a: Row-level references to the row values before and after the change that fired the trigger.

qa.q: Give two uses of triggers.
qa.a: Maintaining an audit trail of changes and enforcing business rules that a simple constraint cannot express.

quiz.q: A trigger is executed
o: automatically when a specified event occurs

lessons.title: Anomalies and functional dependencies
yt: functional dependency DBMS Armstrong axioms attribute closure
insertion deletion update anomaly normalization

blocks.x: **Normalization** is the process of organising tables to reduce redundancy and avoid anomalies. It is guided by **functional dependencies**.
Why redundancy hurts: anomalies
Consider one table `StudentCourse(roll, name, course, instructor, room)` where each row repeats student and instructor details.

x: **Insertion anomaly:** you cannot record a new course until a student enrols in it.
**Deletion anomaly:** deleting the only student of a course also deletes the fact that the course and its instructor exist.
**Update anomaly:** changing an instructor's room needs many rows to be updated; missing one makes the data inconsistent.

blocks.x: Functional dependency (FD)

`X → Y` (X determines Y) means: whenever two tuples have the same X value, they must have the same Y value. Example: `roll → name`, because one roll number belongs to one student. An FD is a property of the **meaning** of the data, not of one particular instance.

x: **Trivial FD:** `Y ⊆ X`, such as `{roll, name} → name`.
**Non-trivial:** `Y` is not a subset of `X`.
**Full dependency:** Y depends on all of X, not on any proper subset.
**Partial dependency:** Y depends on part of a composite key.
**Transitive dependency:** `X → Y` and `Y → Z` give `X → Z` through a non-key Y.

blocks.x: Armstrong's axioms

x: **Reflexivity:** if Y ⊆ X then X → Y.
**Augmentation:** if X → Y then XZ → YZ.
**Transitivity:** if X → Y and Y → Z then X → Z.

blocks.x: Derived rules: **Union** (X → Y, X → Z ⇒ X → YZ), **Decomposition** (X → YZ ⇒ X → Y and X → Z), **Pseudotransitivity** (X → Y, WY → Z ⇒ WX → Z). The axioms are **sound** (they derive only valid FDs) and **complete** (they derive every implied FD).
Closure of an attribute set
`X+` is the set of all attributes determined by X. Algorithm: start with X+ = X; repeat: if some FD `A → B` has A ⊆ X+, add B; stop when nothing changes.
Example: R(A, B, C, D, E) with F = {A → B, B → C, CD → E}.

x: {A}+ : A → B gives B; B → C gives C. So {A}+ = {A, B, C}. D is missing, so CD → E cannot fire.
{A, D}+ : start {A, D}; add B, then C; now C and D are present so add E. {A, D}+ = {A, B, C, D, E}, so **AD is a super key**.

blocks.x: Uses of closure

x: Test whether `X → Y` follows from F: check Y ⊆ X+.
Find keys: X is a super key if X+ is all attributes.
Compare two FD sets: F and G are **equivalent** if each FD of one is implied by the other.

blocks.x: Normalization removes anomalies by splitting tables, using FDs as the guide.

lessons.title: Finding candidate keys, and the canonical (minimal) cover
yt: how to find candidate keys DBMS shortcut method
canonical cover minimal cover functional dependencies

blocks.x: Finding candidate keys

x: List all attributes of R and the set of FDs F.
Attributes that **never appear on the right side** of any FD must be in **every** key.
Attributes that appear **only on the right** side are in **no** key.

Compute the closure of the must-have set. If it covers all attributes, that set is the only key. If not, add other attributes one at a time (or in combinations) until the closure is complete, keeping the sets **minimal**.

blocks.x: Worked example
R(A, B, C, D, E), F = { AB → C, C → D, D → E, E → A }.

x: B never appears on the right, so B is in every key.
Try {A, B}: AB → C, C → D, D → E, so {A,B}+ = {A, B, C, D, E}. AB is a key.
Because E → A, D → E, C → D: replacing A by E, D or C also works. {B,C}+, {B,D}+, {B,E}+ each give everything.
**Candidate keys: AB, BC, BD, BE.** Prime attributes (in some key): A, B, C, D, E (all).

blocks.x: Prime and non-prime attributes
A **prime** attribute belongs to at least one candidate key. A **non-prime** attribute belongs to none. These terms define 2NF and 3NF in the next lesson.
Canonical cover (minimal cover)
A canonical cover Fc is an equivalent FD set that is as small as possible:

x: Every right side is a **single attribute**.
No left side contains an **extraneous attribute**.
No FD is **redundant** (implied by the others).

blocks.x: Procedure

x: **Split** right sides: `A → BC` becomes `A → B` and `A → C`.
**Remove extraneous left attributes:** in `XA → B`, A is extraneous if B is in the closure of `X` under F.
**Remove redundant FDs:** remove `X → A` if A is still in `X+` computed without that FD.

blocks.x: Worked example
F = { A → BC, B → C, A → B, AB → C }.

x: Split: A → B, A → C, B → C, A → B (duplicate), AB → C.
In `AB → C`: is B extraneous? Check A+ : A → B, A → C, so C is in A+. Yes, so replace by `A → C` (a duplicate).
Remove redundant: `A → C` follows from `A → B` and `B → C`, so delete it.

blocks.x: **Canonical cover: { A → B, B → C }.** A+ = {A, B, C}, so the key is A.
Why we care
The canonical cover is the starting point for the **3NF synthesis algorithm**, and it makes checking dependency preservation simpler.
Shortcut for keys: the attributes that appear nowhere on the right side must be in the key.

qa.q: Which attributes must belong to every candidate key?
qa.a: Those that never appear on the right-hand side of any functional dependency.

qa.q: What is a prime attribute?
qa.a: An attribute that is a member of at least one candidate key.

qa.q: When is a left-side attribute extraneous in an FD?
qa.a: In XA → B, attribute A is extraneous if B is already in the closure of X computed with all the FDs. Then A can be dropped without changing the meaning.

qa.q: List the three properties of a canonical cover.
qa.a: Single-attribute right sides, no extraneous attributes on the left, and no redundant FDs.

qa.q: In R(A,B,C) with A → B, B → C, what is the candidate key?
qa.a: A. It never appears on the right side, and A+ = {A, B, C}.

lessons.title: 1NF, 2NF and 3NF
yt: normalization 1NF 2NF 3NF with examples
partial dependency transitive dependency normal forms

blocks.x: A **normal form** is a rule about table design. Higher normal forms remove more redundancy.
First normal form (1NF)

Every attribute holds a single **atomic** value, and there are no repeating groups. A table with a cell `phones = "98xx, 97xx"` violates 1NF. Fix: one row per phone number, or a separate `Phone` table.
Second normal form (2NF)
The relation is in 1NF and **no non-prime attribute is partially dependent on a candidate key**. This matters only when a key is composite.

Example: `Enroll(roll, cid, name, grade)` with key `(roll, cid)` and FDs `(roll, cid) → grade`, `roll → name`. `name` depends only on `roll`, part of the key: a **partial dependency**, so it is not in 2NF. Decompose:

x: `Student(roll, name)` key roll
`Enroll(roll, cid, grade)` key (roll, cid)

blocks.x: Third normal form (3NF)
The relation is in 2NF and has **no transitive dependency** of a non-prime attribute on a key. Formally, for every non-trivial FD `X → A`, at least one of these holds:

x: X is a super key, or
A is a prime attribute.

blocks.x: Example: `Student(roll, name, dept, hod)` with `roll → dept` and `dept → hod`. Then `roll → hod` is transitive through `dept`, a non-key. Decompose:

x: `Student(roll, name, dept)`
`Dept(dept, hod)`

blocks.x: Putting them together

head: Normal form
Removes
Test
rows: No non-prime attribute depends on part of a key
Every FD X → A: X super key or A prime

blocks.x: Each normal form includes the one before it: 3NF implies 2NF implies 1NF.
How to find the highest normal form of a relation

x: Find all candidate keys, and the prime and non-prime attributes.
Check every FD for partial dependency of non-prime attributes on part of a key (2NF violation).
Check every FD: if the left side is not a super key and the right side is not prime, 3NF is violated.
If 3NF holds, check BCNF (next lesson).

blocks.x: Quick example
R(A, B, C, D) with keys AB and F = {AB → CD, B → C}. `B → C`: C is non-prime and B is only part of the key AB. That is a partial dependency, so the relation is in **1NF only**.
3NF synthesis

A dependency-preserving, lossless decomposition into 3NF always exists: take a canonical cover, make a table for each FD `X → Y` with attributes `XY`, merge tables with the same key, and add a table containing a candidate key if none of the tables contains one.
Memorise: "The key, the whole key, and nothing but the key."

qa.q: When is a relation in 2NF?
qa.a: When it is in 1NF and no non-prime attribute depends on a proper part of a candidate key (no partial dependency).

qa.q: What condition makes an FD X → A acceptable in 3NF?
qa.a: Either X is a super key or A is a prime attribute.

qa.q: Can a relation with a single-attribute primary key violate 2NF?
qa.a: No, partial dependency needs a composite key. A relation in 1NF with all keys simple is automatically in 2NF.

qa.q: What is a transitive dependency?
qa.a: A non-key attribute that depends on the key only through another non-key attribute, like roll → dept and dept → hod giving roll → hod.

qa.q: Does 3NF always preserve dependencies?
qa.a: Yes. A lossless and dependency-preserving 3NF decomposition always exists (the synthesis algorithm).

lessons.title: BCNF, lossless join and dependency preservation
yt: BCNF Boyce Codd normal form decomposition
lossless join decomposition dependency preserving

blocks.x: Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF)
A relation is in BCNF if for **every** non-trivial FD `X → Y`, X is a **super key**. It is stricter than 3NF because 3NF also allows the case "Y is prime".
Example where 3NF is not BCNF
R(Student, Course, Instructor) with

x: {Student, Course} → Instructor (a student gets one instructor per course)
Instructor → Course (each instructor teaches only one course)

blocks.x: Keys: {Student, Course} and {Student, Instructor}. All attributes are prime, so R is in 3NF. But in `Instructor → Course`, Instructor is not a super key, so it is **not in BCNF** and the course for an instructor is stored repeatedly.
BCNF decomposition algorithm
While some relation R has an FD `X → Y` violating BCNF: replace R by `R1 = X ∪ Y` and `R2 = R − (Y − X)`. For the example: R1(Instructor, Course) and R2(Student, Instructor). Both are in BCNF.
Properties of a good decomposition
Decomposing R into R1 and R2 should be:

x: **Lossless join:** joining R1 and R2 gives back exactly R (no spurious tuples).
**Dependency preserving:** every FD of R can be checked within the smaller tables without joining them.

blocks.x: Test for lossless binary decomposition
R1 and R2 give a lossless join if the common attributes form a key of at least one of them: `(R1 ∩ R2) → R1` or `(R1 ∩ R2) → R2` follows from F.
Example: R(A,B,C), F = {A → B}.

x: Decompose into R1(A,B), R2(A,C): R1 ∩ R2 = A, and A → B so A is a key of R1. **Lossless.**
Decompose into R1(A,B), R2(B,C): R1 ∩ R2 = B, and B is a key of neither. **Lossy**: joining can create false rows.

blocks.x: Dependency preservation

Example: R(A,B,C), F = {A → B, B → C}, decomposition R1(A,B), R2(A,C). The projection gives A → B in R1 and A → C in R2. B → C cannot be derived from these, so the decomposition is **lossless but not dependency preserving**.
Where BCNF and 3NF differ

x: A lossless, dependency-preserving decomposition into **3NF** always exists.
A lossless decomposition into **BCNF** always exists, but it may **not preserve all dependencies** (as in the Student/Course/Instructor example, where {Student, Course} → Instructor is lost).

blocks.x: Practical design usually aims for 3NF or BCNF, and sometimes **denormalises** on purpose to make reads faster.
BCNF: every determinant is a candidate key.

qa.a: When, for every non-trivial functional dependency X → Y, X is a super key.

qa.q: How is BCNF stricter than 3NF?
qa.a: 3NF allows an FD X → A where A is prime even if X is not a super key. BCNF does not allow that exception.

qa.q: What does lossless join decomposition mean?
qa.a: The natural join of the decomposed relations reproduces exactly the original relation with no extra or missing tuples.

qa.q: What is the lossless test for decomposing R into R1 and R2?
qa.a: The common attributes R1 ∩ R2 must be a key of R1 or of R2.

qa.q: Why might we stop at 3NF instead of BCNF?
qa.a: BCNF decomposition can lose dependency preservation, and 3NF can always keep it.

blocks.x: Multivalued dependency (MVD)

Suppose an employee has several skills and several languages, and these two sets are **independent**. Storing them together in `EmpInfo(emp, skill, language)` forces every skill to be paired with every language:
This is redundant, even though the relation has no non-trivial FD and is therefore already in BCNF. The cause is the **multivalued dependency** `emp ↠ skill` (and `emp ↠ language`).

`X ↠ Y` means: for a given X value, the set of Y values is independent of the other attributes. If two tuples have the same X, then swapping their Y parts gives two more tuples that must also be present.
Every FD is also an MVD, but not conversely. An MVD is **trivial** if Y ⊆ X or X ∪ Y is all attributes.
Fourth normal form (4NF)
A relation is in **4NF** if it is in BCNF and for every non-trivial MVD `X ↠ Y`, X is a super key.
Decomposition for the example:

x: `EmpSkill(emp, skill)`
`EmpLanguage(emp, language)`

blocks.x: Each has only trivial dependencies and no repeated cross products. Joining them reproduces the original table, so the decomposition is lossless.
Fifth normal form (5NF, project-join normal form)

A relation is in 5NF if every **join dependency** is implied by its candidate keys. Join dependencies appear when a relation can be rebuilt only from three or more projections, not from two. Such cases (for example the supplier-part-project example) are rare in practice.
Summary of the ladder

head: Form
Eliminates
rows: Join dependencies not implied by keys

blocks.x: Denormalisation

Sometimes designers combine tables again on purpose, accepting some redundancy to avoid expensive joins in reporting systems and data warehouses. This is a deliberate trade-off after normalising, not an excuse to skip it.
Independent multi-valued facts about the same entity belong in separate tables.

qa.q: What is a multivalued dependency?
qa.a: X ↠ Y means that for each X value the set of Y values is independent of the remaining attributes. It happens when one entity has several independent sets of values.

qa.q: When is a relation in 4NF?
qa.a: When it is in BCNF and every non-trivial multivalued dependency has a super key as its left side.

qa.q: Why is EmpInfo(emp, skill, language) in BCNF but still bad?
qa.a: It has no non-trivial FDs, so BCNF holds, but it stores every skill-language combination, which is redundancy caused by the MVDs emp ↠ skill and emp ↠ language.

qa.q: How is the EmpInfo table fixed?
qa.a: Split it into EmpSkill(emp, skill) and EmpLanguage(emp, language).

qa.q: What is 5NF about?
qa.a: Join dependencies: a relation is in 5NF if every join dependency in it is implied by its candidate keys.

problems.q: Define a multivalued dependency with the example Course ->> Teacher and Course ->> Book.
problems.a: A multivalued dependency X ->> Y means that for each value of X there is a set of values of Y, independent of the other attributes. A course can have several teachers and several books, and the choice of teacher is independent of the choice of book.

problems.q: R(Course, Teacher, Book) has Course ->> Teacher and Course ->> Book. DB has 2 teachers and 3 books for the Database course. How many rows does the Database course need in R and how many after the 4NF decomposition?
problems.a: In R every combination must appear: 2 x 3 = 6 rows. After the 4NF decomposition into CourseTeacher and CourseBook: 2 + 3 = 5 rows, and adding a book needs one row instead of one per teacher.

problems.q: Why is the relation in the previous problem already in BCNF yet still has redundancy? State when a relation is in 4NF and decompose it.
problems.a:
There is no non-trivial functional dependency, and the only key is all attributes (Course, Teacher, Book), so BCNF holds, yet the combinations repeat data.
A relation is in 4NF if for every non-trivial multivalued dependency X ->> Y, X is a superkey. Course is not a superkey, so decompose into CourseTeacher(Course, Teacher) and CourseBook(Course, Book).

rubric.t: BCNF holds because the key is all attributes

lessons.title: Transactions and the ACID properties
yt: transaction ACID properties DBMS
transaction states DBMS commit rollback

blocks.x: A **transaction** is a logical unit of work made of one or more database operations that must be treated as a whole. Example: transferring 500 from account A to account B.

read(A); A = A - 500; write(A);
read(B); B = B + 500; write(B);
If the system fails after `write(A)` but before `write(B)`, money disappears. Transactions prevent that.
ACID properties

x: **Atomicity:** all operations happen or none do. Ensured by the **recovery manager** using a log to undo partial work.
**Consistency:** a transaction takes the database from one consistent state to another (all integrity constraints hold). This is mainly the programmer's responsibility, helped by constraints.
**Isolation:** concurrent transactions behave as if they ran one after another. Ensured by the **concurrency-control manager** (locks, timestamps, MVCC).
**Durability:** once committed, changes survive crashes. Ensured by logging and forcing log records to stable storage.

blocks.x: For the transfer, the sum A + B must be the same before and after (consistency).
Transaction states

x: **Active:** executing operations.
**Partially committed:** the last statement has run, but the changes may still only be in memory.
**Committed:** changes safely recorded; they can no longer be undone by the system.
**Failed:** normal execution cannot continue.

**Aborted:** the transaction was rolled back and the database restored to its state before it began. The system may then **restart** it (if the failure was a hardware or software error) or **kill** it (logical error).

blocks.x: SQL control: `COMMIT` makes work permanent, `ROLLBACK` cancels it, `SAVEPOINT` marks a point to roll back to.
Result: account 1 holds 500, account 2 holds 700. Total unchanged at 1200.
Why concurrency?
Running transactions together improves throughput and reduces waiting. The cost is possible anomalies if isolation is not enforced:

x: **Lost update:** two transactions read the same value and both write, so one update vanishes.
**Dirty read:** reading data written by an uncommitted transaction that later rolls back.
**Non-repeatable read:** reading the same row twice and getting different values because another transaction committed in between.
**Phantom read:** a repeated range query returns new rows inserted by another committed transaction.

blocks.x: A in ACID needs undo, D needs redo, I needs concurrency control, and C needs correct programs and constraints.

qa.q: What does atomicity mean?
qa.a: A transaction is all-or-nothing. If any step fails, the effects of the already executed steps are undone.

qa.q: Which component ensures durability?
qa.a: The recovery manager, by writing log records to stable storage before commit so that committed changes can be redone after a crash.

qa.q: What is a dirty read?
qa.a: Reading a value written by a transaction that has not committed yet and may later roll back.

qa.q: What is the difference between ROLLBACK and COMMIT?
qa.a: COMMIT makes the transaction's changes permanent. ROLLBACK discards them and returns the database to the state before the transaction began.

qa.q: What is a lost update?
qa.a: Two transactions read the same data and update it based on the old value, so the later write overwrites the first update.

quiz.q: Which ACID property guarantees that committed data survives a crash?
quiz.why: Durability is implemented with logging and recovery.

quiz.why: Atomicity means all or nothing.

quiz.why: Dirty data may be rolled back later.

quiz.q: The state in which a transaction has executed its last statement but is not yet permanent is
quiz.why: After the last statement the transaction is partially committed until the commit is safely recorded.

quiz.q: Concurrency control mainly ensures
quiz.why: The concurrency-control manager provides isolation.

visuals.title: ACID properties
visuals.data: ACID; Atomicity: all or nothing; Consistency: rules stay true; Isolation: transactions do not disturb each other; Durability: committed data survives a crash

problems.q: Expand ACID and explain each property in one line.
problems.a: Atomicity: all operations of a transaction happen or none do. Consistency: a transaction takes the database from one valid state to another. Isolation: concurrent transactions behave as if they ran one after another. Durability: once committed, changes survive failures.

problems.q: A transfer of 500 from account A to B fails after the debit but before the credit. Which property is at risk and how does the DBMS protect it?
problems.a: Atomicity. The DBMS records every change in a log. After the failure the recovery manager sees that the transaction did not commit and uses the log to undo the debit (rollback), so either both steps occur or none do.

problems.q: Match each situation with an ACID property: (1) a bank restarts after a power cut and the committed deposit is still there; (2) two users try to book the last seat at the same time; (3) total money in two accounts is unchanged by a transfer; (4) half a transaction is undone. Then list the five states of a transaction.
problems.a:
(1) Durability. (2) Isolation. (3) Consistency. (4) Atomicity.
States: Active, Partially committed, Committed, Failed, Aborted (terminated).

lessons.title: Schedules and serializability
yt: serializability conflict serializable precedence graph
view serializability schedules DBMS

blocks.x: A **schedule** is the time order in which operations of several transactions are executed. Operations of each transaction keep their own order. A **serial** schedule runs one transaction completely before the next. Serial schedules are always correct but slow. We want schedules that are not serial but have the **same effect** as some serial one: they are **serializable**.
Conflicting operations
Two operations conflict if they:

x: belong to **different** transactions,
access the **same** data item, and
at least one is a **write**.

blocks.x: So the conflicting pairs are Read-Write, Write-Read and Write-Write. Two reads never conflict.
Conflict serializability
A schedule is **conflict serializable** if it can be converted to a serial schedule by swapping adjacent **non-conflicting** operations.
Precedence graph (serialization graph) test

x: Make a node for each transaction.
Add an edge `Ti → Tj` if an operation of Ti conflicts with a **later** operation of Tj.
The schedule is conflict serializable **if and only if the graph has no cycle**. A topological order of the graph gives an equivalent serial order.

blocks.x: Example 1 (serializable)
S1: R1(A) W1(A) R2(A) W2(A) R1(B) W1(B) R2(B) W2(B). All conflicts on A and B go from T1 to T2, so the graph has the single edge T1 → T2. No cycle: equivalent to T1 then T2.
Example 2 (not serializable)

x: R1(A) before W2(A): edge T1 → T2.
W2(A) before W1(A): edge T2 → T1.

blocks.x: The graph has a cycle T1 ⇄ T2, so S2 is not conflict serializable. (This is a lost-update pattern: T1's write ignores T2's.)
View serializability

Two schedules are **view equivalent** if: (1) each transaction reads the same initial values, (2) each read reads from the same writing transaction, and (3) the final write on each item is by the same transaction. A schedule is view serializable if it is view equivalent to a serial schedule.

x: Every conflict-serializable schedule is view serializable.
Some view-serializable schedules are not conflict serializable; they contain **blind writes** (writes without a preceding read).
Testing view serializability is NP-complete, so systems enforce conflict serializability.

blocks.x: Number of schedules
For n transactions the number of serial schedules is n!. For two transactions with m and k operations the total number of interleavings is (m+k)! / (m! k!).
Cycle in the precedence graph means not conflict serializable.

qa.q: When do two operations conflict?
qa.a: When they are from different transactions, access the same data item, and at least one of them is a write.

qa.q: How do we test conflict serializability?
qa.a: Build a precedence graph with an edge Ti → Tj for each conflict where Ti's operation comes first. The schedule is conflict serializable exactly when the graph has no cycle.

qa.q: Is a view-serializable schedule always conflict serializable?
qa.a: No. Every conflict serializable schedule is view serializable, but not the other way round; blind writes can make a schedule view serializable only.

qa.q: What is a serial schedule?
qa.a: One in which all operations of a transaction run together without interleaving with other transactions.

qa.q: How many serial schedules exist for 3 transactions?

quiz.why: R1(A) before W2(A) gives T1 to T2, and W2(A) before W1(A) gives T2 to T1.

o: Every view serializable schedule is conflict serializable
Every conflict serializable schedule is view serializable
quiz.why: Conflict serializability is the stricter, more practical test.

problems.q: Which pairs of operations from different transactions on the same data item conflict? Which do not?
problems.a: Conflicting pairs: read-write, write-read and write-write on the same item by different transactions. Read-read does not conflict.

problems.q: Schedule S: R1(A) W1(A) R2(A) W2(A) R1(B) W1(B). Draw the precedence graph and say whether S is conflict serializable.
problems.a: Conflicts on A: W1(A) before R2(A) gives T1 to T2; W1(A) before W2(A) gives T1 to T2. T2 does not touch B, so B adds nothing. Graph: T1 to T2 only, no cycle. So S is conflict serializable, equivalent to the serial order T1 then T2.

problems.q: Schedule R1(A) R2(A) W2(A) W1(A). Is it conflict serializable? How many serial schedules exist for 3 transactions?
problems.a:
Conflicts: R1(A) before W2(A) gives T1 to T2; R2(A) before W1(A) gives T2 to T1. The graph has a cycle T1 to T2 to T1, so the schedule is not conflict serializable (it also loses T2's update).
For 3 transactions there are 3! = 6 serial schedules.

lessons.title: Recoverable schedules and isolation levels
yt: recoverable cascadeless strict schedule DBMS
SQL isolation levels read committed repeatable read serializable

blocks.x: Serializability is about correct results. **Recoverability** is about what happens when a transaction aborts.
Recoverable schedule

A schedule is **recoverable** if whenever Tj reads data written by Ti, Ti **commits before** Tj commits. Bad example: T1 writes A, T2 reads A, T2 commits, then T1 aborts. T2 has committed a value based on data that never existed, and a committed transaction cannot be undone. This schedule is **not recoverable**.
Cascading rollback and cascadeless schedules

Even in a recoverable schedule, if T1 aborts after T2 read its uncommitted data, T2 must also abort, and so on for others: a **cascading rollback**, which wastes work. A **cascadeless (ACA, avoids cascading aborts)** schedule allows reads only of **committed** data: Tj reads an item written by Ti only after Ti commits.
Strict schedules

In a **strict** schedule, a transaction can neither read nor **overwrite** an item written by another transaction until that transaction commits or aborts. Strict schedules make recovery with simple before-image undo possible.
Hierarchy: **strict ⊂ cascadeless ⊂ recoverable ⊂ all schedules.**
Isolation levels in SQL
Full serializability costs concurrency, so SQL defines weaker levels. Each allows some anomalies:
(The table is the standard SQL definition. Real systems differ: for example PostgreSQL treats READ UNCOMMITTED as READ COMMITTED, and MySQL InnoDB's REPEATABLE READ also blocks most phantoms.)
Setting the level:
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;
Defaults: PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server use READ COMMITTED; MySQL InnoDB uses REPEATABLE READ.
Choosing a level

Use READ COMMITTED for most web applications, REPEATABLE READ for consistent reports within a transaction, and SERIALIZABLE for critical operations like financial rules that cannot tolerate any anomaly, accepting lower throughput.
Recoverable: commit order follows read-from order. Cascadeless: read only committed data. Strict: also write only over committed data.

qa.q: What is a recoverable schedule?
qa.a: One in which a transaction that reads data written by another transaction commits only after that other transaction has committed.

qa.q: What is a cascading rollback?
qa.a: When one transaction aborts, every transaction that read its uncommitted data must also abort, and so on, causing a chain of rollbacks.

qa.q: Which isolation level allows dirty reads?
qa.a: READ UNCOMMITTED.

qa.q: What is a phantom read?
qa.a: A transaction re-runs a range query and sees new rows inserted and committed by another transaction in the meantime.

qa.q: State the relationship between strict, cascadeless and recoverable schedules.
qa.a: Every strict schedule is cascadeless and every cascadeless schedule is recoverable, but not the reverse.

quiz.why: Cascadeless (ACA) schedules avoid reading uncommitted data.

quiz.q: Which isolation level prevents dirty reads but allows non-repeatable reads?
quiz.why: READ COMMITTED reads only committed values but they may change between reads.

quiz.q: Which anomaly is prevented only by SERIALIZABLE in the standard?
quiz.why: Phantoms are prevented at the SERIALIZABLE level in the standard definition.

T2 reads A after T1 aborts

problems.q: Differentiate between recoverable, cascadeless and strict schedules.
problems.a: Recoverable: a transaction commits only after every transaction whose data it read has committed. Cascadeless (avoids cascading aborts): a transaction reads only data written by committed transactions. Strict: it neither reads nor overwrites data written by an uncommitted transaction. Strict implies cascadeless implies recoverable.

problems.q: Is this schedule recoverable? W1(A) R2(A) C2 C1. Explain.
problems.a: Not recoverable. T2 read A written by T1 and committed before T1 committed. If T1 then aborts, T2 has already committed using a value that never existed, and it cannot be undone. A recoverable order would be C1 before C2.

problems.q: State which anomalies (dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom read) each SQL isolation level allows.
problems.a: Read Uncommitted: dirty reads, non-repeatable reads and phantoms possible. Read Committed: prevents dirty reads; non-repeatable reads and phantoms possible. Repeatable Read: prevents dirty and non-repeatable reads; phantoms possible in the standard (some databases such as MySQL InnoDB also prevent most phantoms). Serializable: prevents all three.

lessons.title: Lock-based concurrency control, 2PL and deadlocks
yt: two phase locking 2PL strict rigorous DBMS
deadlock wait for graph wait die wound wait

blocks.x: Locks
A **lock** controls concurrent access to a data item.

x: **Shared lock (S):** for reading; many transactions may hold S on the same item.
**Exclusive lock (X):** for writing; only one holder, no S locks at the same time.

blocks.x: Compatibility: S with S is allowed; S with X, X with S and X with X are not. A transaction asks the lock manager for a lock and waits if it is not granted.
Two-phase locking (2PL)
Each transaction has two phases:

x: **Growing phase:** it may acquire locks but not release any.
**Shrinking phase:** it may release locks but not acquire any.

blocks.x: The point where it holds all its locks is the **lock point**. **2PL guarantees conflict serializability**, and the order of lock points gives an equivalent serial order.
Problems of basic 2PL: it can still cause **cascading rollbacks** and does **not prevent deadlock**.
Variants

x: **Strict 2PL:** hold all **exclusive** locks until commit or abort. Gives strict (cascadeless) schedules. Widely used.
**Rigorous 2PL:** hold **all** locks until commit or abort. Transactions serialise in commit order.
**Conservative 2PL:** acquire all locks before starting. Prevents deadlock but is hard to know in advance and reduces concurrency.
**Lock conversion:** upgrade S to X in the growing phase, downgrade X to S in the shrinking phase.

blocks.x: Deadlock
A **deadlock** is when each transaction in a set waits for a lock held by another in the set, so none can proceed. Example: T1 holds X(A) and wants X(B); T2 holds X(B) and wants X(A).
Four conditions: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no pre-emption, circular wait.
Detection: wait-for graph

Nodes are transactions; an edge `Ti → Tj` means Ti waits for a lock held by Tj. A **cycle** means deadlock. The DBMS checks periodically and picks a **victim** to abort (usually the one with least work done, with care to avoid **starvation** of the same victim).
Prevention with timestamps
Each transaction has a timestamp (older = smaller). When Ti requests an item held by Tj:

x: **Wait-Die** (non-pre-emptive): if Ti is **older** it waits; if younger it **dies** (aborts and restarts with the same timestamp).
**Wound-Wait** (pre-emptive): if Ti is **older** it **wounds** Tj (forces it to abort); if younger it waits.

blocks.x: Both prevent cycles, and an aborted transaction keeps its original timestamp so it will eventually become the oldest.
Timeout
A simple approach: abort a transaction that has waited longer than a limit.
Multiple granularity locking
Locks can be at database, table, page or row level. **Intention locks** (IS, IX, SIX) on higher levels signal that lower-level locks are held, so conflicts are detected without examining every row.
2PL gives serializability; strict 2PL also gives cascadeless schedules; neither prevents deadlocks.

qa.q: State the two phases of two-phase locking.
qa.a: A growing phase in which locks are only acquired, followed by a shrinking phase in which locks are only released.

qa.q: What does 2PL guarantee, and what does it not?
qa.a: It guarantees conflict serializability. It does not guarantee freedom from deadlock or from cascading rollbacks.

qa.q: How does strict 2PL differ from basic 2PL?
qa.a: In strict 2PL, exclusive locks are kept until the transaction commits or aborts, which avoids cascading rollbacks.

qa.q: How is a deadlock detected?
qa.a: By building a wait-for graph and checking for a cycle.

qa.q: What is the difference between wait-die and wound-wait?
qa.a: In wait-die an older transaction waits for a younger one and a younger requester dies. In wound-wait an older requester aborts (wounds) the younger holder and a younger requester waits.

quiz.why: Strict 2PL holds X locks until the end, giving cascadeless schedules.
