problems.q: Context switching costs 1 ms. For a quantum of 1 ms versus 100 ms, discuss the effect on CPU efficiency and response time, and state a rule of thumb for choosing the quantum.
problems.a:
With quantum 1 ms and switch cost 1 ms, half of the CPU time is overhead (efficiency about 50%) but response time is excellent. With quantum 100 ms the overhead is about 1% (efficiency about 99%) but interactive processes may wait for a long time behind other processes, so response time is poor and RR approaches FCFS.
Rule of thumb: choose the quantum large compared with the switch cost, and so that about 80% of CPU bursts finish within one quantum.

rubric.t: Computes overhead for both quanta (about 50% and about 1%)
Links small quantum to good response time and large quantum to poor response time
States the 80 percent of bursts rule of thumb

lessons.title: Race conditions and the critical section problem
yt: critical section problem race condition Peterson solution
mutual exclusion progress bounded waiting

blocks.x: When several processes or threads access **shared data** at the same time, the final result can depend on the exact order of execution. This is a **race condition**.
A race in practice
Two threads each add 1,000,000 to a shared counter. `counter++` is really three steps: load, add, store. If both threads load the same value before either stores, one update is lost.
With the mutex the output is always `counter = 2000000`. Remove the lock/unlock lines and you will usually see a smaller number that changes on every run: that is the race.
The critical section problem
Each process has a **critical section** (CS), a segment of code that accesses shared data. The structure is:
A solution must satisfy three requirements:

x: **Mutual exclusion:** if one process is in its CS, no other may be.
**Progress:** if no process is in its CS and some want to enter, only those not in the remainder section decide who enters next, and the decision cannot be postponed forever.
**Bounded waiting:** there is a limit on how many times others can enter before a waiting process gets its turn (no starvation).

blocks.x: Peterson's solution (two processes)
Shared: `int turn; boolean flag[2];`. For process i (j is the other):
It meets all three requirements, but on modern CPUs with instruction reordering it needs memory barriers, so it is mostly of teaching value.
Hardware support

x: **Test-and-Set:** atomically reads a boolean and sets it to true. `while (TestAndSet(&lock)) ;` forms a **spinlock**.
**Compare-and-Swap (CAS):** atomically sets a variable only if it holds an expected value.
Disabling interrupts works on single-CPU systems only and is dangerous for user code.

blocks.x: A **spinlock** wastes CPU while waiting (busy waiting) but avoids a context switch, so it suits very short critical sections on multiprocessors.
Three requirements: mutual exclusion, progress, bounded waiting.

qa.q: What is a race condition?
qa.a: A situation in which the result of concurrent execution depends on the order in which the shared data is accessed, often giving wrong or unpredictable results.

qa.q: List the three requirements for a solution to the critical section problem.
qa.a: Mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting.

qa.q: How does Peterson's solution achieve mutual exclusion?
qa.a: Each process sets its flag to show interest and gives the turn to the other. A process enters only if the other is not interested or it is its turn, so both cannot be inside at once.

qa.q: What is a spinlock?
qa.a: A lock where a waiting process repeatedly checks the lock in a loop (busy waiting) instead of sleeping. It is efficient only for very short critical sections.

qa.q: Why is counter++ not safe in two threads?
qa.a: It is a non-atomic read-modify-write sequence, so two threads can read the same old value and one increment is lost.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a requirement of the critical section solution?
quiz.why: The three requirements concern correctness, not hardware speed.

quiz.why: There is a limit on how long a process can be bypassed.

quiz.why: It reads and sets a flag in one indivisible step.

quiz.why: The process loops while waiting.

quiz.why: It waits while the other is interested and it is the other's turn.

problems.q: What is the critical section problem? State the three requirements a correct solution must satisfy.
problems.a:
When several processes share data, the part of code that accesses the shared data is the critical section. The problem is to design a protocol so processes do not corrupt the data.
Requirements: 1) Mutual exclusion: only one process in its critical section at a time. 2) Progress: if no process is in the critical section, one of those wanting to enter must be chosen without indefinite postponement. 3) Bounded waiting: a limit on how many times others may enter before a waiting process gets its turn.

rubric.t: Correct definition of critical section problem

problems.q: Explain Peterson's solution for two processes. Show why it ensures mutual exclusion.
problems.a:
Shared variables: flag[2] (flag[i] = true means process i wants to enter) and turn (whose turn it is). Process i: flag[i] = true; turn = j; while (flag[j] && turn == j) wait; critical section; flag[i] = false.
If both want to enter, both set their flags, but turn can hold only one value; the process that wrote turn last is the one that waits, so only the other enters. Therefore both cannot be in the critical section together. Progress and bounded waiting also hold.

rubric.t: Correct algorithm with flag and turn
Explains that turn decides who waits when both want to enter
Mentions progress and bounded waiting are satisfied

problems.q: This lock is proposed: while (lock == 1) ; lock = 1; /* critical section */ lock = 0; Show an interleaving where two processes enter the critical section together, and explain how an atomic test-and-set fixes it.
problems.a:
P1 reads lock == 0 and leaves the while loop, but a context switch occurs before it executes lock = 1. P2 now also reads lock == 0, leaves the loop and sets lock = 1. When P1 resumes it sets lock = 1 and enters too. Both are inside the critical section.
The problem is that checking and setting the lock are two separate steps. Test-and-set reads the old value and writes 1 in one indivisible hardware instruction, so only one process can see 0 and acquire the lock.

rubric.t: Valid interleaving between the check and the assignment
Identifies the non-atomic check-then-set as the cause

lessons.title: Semaphores and the classic synchronisation problems
yt: semaphore in operating system wait signal binary counting
producer consumer readers writers dining philosophers semaphore solution

blocks.x: A **semaphore** S is an integer variable accessed only through two **atomic** operations:

x: `wait(S)` (also `P`, `down`): `while (S <= 0) block; S--;`
`signal(S)` (also `V`, `up`): `S++;` and wake one waiting process.

blocks.x: To avoid busy waiting the OS implements a semaphore with a **queue**: `wait` blocks the process in the queue, `signal` moves one back to ready.
Types

x: **Counting semaphore:** any non-negative value, counts available resource units (like 5 identical printers).
**Binary semaphore (mutex lock):** value 0 or 1, used for mutual exclusion.

blocks.x: Mutual exclusion
Initialise `mutex = 1`. Then `wait(mutex); critical section; signal(mutex);`.
Ordering (signalling)
To make S2 run only after S1: initialise `sync = 0`; the first process does `S1; signal(sync);`, the second does `wait(sync); S2;`.
Producer-consumer (bounded buffer)
A producer puts items into a buffer of size N, a consumer takes them out. Semaphores: `mutex = 1` (protect the buffer), `empty = N` (free slots), `full = 0` (filled slots).
Swapping `wait(empty)` and `wait(mutex)` in the producer can cause **deadlock**: if the buffer is full the producer holds the mutex and waits for `empty`, while the consumer can never get the mutex.
A runnable C version:
Output: `sum of consumed items = 55` (1+2+...+10), whatever the interleaving.
Readers-writers problem

Many readers may read together, but a writer needs exclusive access. In the **first** version readers get priority (writers may starve). Shared: `readcount = 0`, `mutex = 1` (protects readcount), `wrt = 1`. The first reader locks `wrt`, the last reader releases it.
Dining philosophers

Five philosophers share five chopsticks; each needs two to eat. If all pick up the left chopstick at once, there is a **deadlock**. Solutions: allow at most four to sit; pick up both chopsticks only if both are free (inside a critical section); use an asymmetric rule (odd philosophers pick left first, even pick right first).
Problems with semaphores

Incorrect use (wait/signal swapped or forgotten) causes deadlock or violates mutual exclusion. **Priority inversion** can occur when a low-priority process holds a lock needed by a high-priority one; it is solved by **priority inheritance**.
Monitors

A **monitor** is a high-level construct that allows only one process to be active inside at a time, with **condition variables** (`wait`, `signal`). Java's `synchronized` and `wait/notify` are monitor-style tools.
Mutex = 1 for exclusion; empty = N and full = 0 for the bounded buffer; always `wait(empty)` before `wait(mutex)`.

qa.q: What is the difference between a binary and a counting semaphore?
qa.a: A binary semaphore takes only 0 or 1 and is used for mutual exclusion. A counting semaphore can take any non-negative integer and counts available units of a resource.

qa.q: In the producer-consumer solution, what do empty, full and mutex represent?
qa.a: empty counts free buffer slots (initial N), full counts filled slots (initial 0) and mutex gives mutual exclusion on the buffer (initial 1).

qa.q: Why can swapping wait(empty) and wait(mutex) in the producer cause deadlock?
qa.a: If the buffer is full, the producer would hold the mutex while waiting on empty, and the consumer then cannot enter to free a slot.

qa.q: How can the dining philosophers deadlock be avoided?
qa.a: By allowing at most four philosophers at the table, picking up both chopsticks atomically, or making the pick-up order asymmetric for odd and even philosophers.

qa.q: What is priority inversion?
qa.a: A high-priority process is stuck waiting for a lock held by a low-priority process that is itself pre-empted by medium-priority work. Priority inheritance fixes it.

problems.q: Write the producer and consumer for a bounded buffer of size N using semaphores empty, full and mutex. Explain why swapping wait(empty) and wait(mutex) in the producer can cause deadlock.
problems.a:
Initial: empty = N, full = 0, mutex = 1.
Producer: wait(empty); wait(mutex); add item; signal(mutex); signal(full).
Consumer: wait(full); wait(mutex); remove item; signal(mutex); signal(empty).
If the producer does wait(mutex) first and then wait(empty) when the buffer is full, it sleeps while holding mutex. The consumer cannot get mutex to remove an item and free a slot, so both wait forever: deadlock.

rubric.t: Correct producer and consumer using three semaphores
Explains the deadlock from holding mutex while waiting

problems.q: (a) A counting semaphore starts at 10. After 6 wait operations and 4 signal operations complete, what is its value? (b) In the dining philosophers problem with 5 philosophers and 5 chopsticks, show how deadlock can happen and give two ways to avoid it.
problems.a:
(a) 10 - 6 + 4 = 8.
(b) If every philosopher picks up the left chopstick at the same moment, each waits for the right one held by a neighbour: circular wait, deadlock.
Fixes: allow at most 4 philosophers to sit at the table; pick up both chopsticks only if both are free (inside a critical section); or make odd philosophers pick left first and even philosophers pick right first.

rubric.t: Deadlock scenario with everyone holding the left chopstick

lessons.title: Deadlocks: conditions, prevention, avoidance (Banker's), detection and recovery
yt: deadlock in operating system four conditions bankers algorithm
resource allocation graph deadlock detection recovery

blocks.x: A **deadlock** is a set of processes each waiting for a resource held by another in the set, so none can continue.
Four necessary conditions (Coffman)
All four must hold together:

x: **Mutual exclusion:** a resource can be used by only one process at a time.
**Hold and wait:** a process holds some resources while waiting for others.
**No preemption:** resources cannot be forcibly taken away.
**Circular wait:** a cycle of processes, each waiting for a resource held by the next.

blocks.x: Resource-Allocation Graph (RAG)

Vertices are processes (circles) and resource types (rectangles with dots for instances). A **request edge** P → R and an **assignment edge** R → P. If there is **no cycle**, there is no deadlock. If there is a cycle: with **single-instance** resources it means deadlock; with multi-instance resources it may or may not.
Handling deadlocks

x: **Prevention:** make at least one condition impossible.

blocks.x: - Break hold-and-wait: request all resources at once or release before requesting more (low utilisation, starvation). - Break no-preemption: take resources from waiting processes. - Break circular wait: give every resource type a number and require requests in increasing order. - Mutual exclusion cannot usually be broken (printers).

x: **Avoidance:** the OS knows the maximum needs in advance and grants a request only if the system stays in a **safe state**.
**Detection and recovery:** allow deadlocks, detect them, and recover.
**Ignore (ostrich algorithm):** used by Unix and Windows for general resources, because deadlocks are rare.

blocks.x: Safe state and Banker's algorithm

A state is **safe** if there is a **safe sequence** of all processes such that each can finish with the resources currently free plus those released by earlier ones. An unsafe state is not necessarily a deadlock, but may lead to one.

Data structures (n processes, m resource types): `Available[m]`, `Max[n][m]`, `Allocation[n][m]`, `Need = Max − Allocation`. **Safety algorithm:** Work = Available; repeatedly find an unfinished process with Need ≤ Work, add its Allocation to Work and mark it finished. If all finish, the state is safe.
Worked example
Five processes, three resource types (A, B, C). Available = (3, 3, 2).
Find a safe sequence:
Safe sequence **<P1, P3, P0, P2, P4>** (others are also possible), so the state is safe.

**Resource-request algorithm:** if P1 requests (1,0,2): it is ≤ Need (1,2,2) and ≤ Available (3,3,2). Pretend to grant it (Available = (2,3,0), P1 Allocation = (3,0,2), Need = (0,2,0)) and run the safety check. It succeeds with the same style of sequence, so the request is **granted**.
Detection
For single instances, build a **wait-for graph** and look for cycles. For multiple instances, use a Banker-like algorithm with current requests instead of needs.
Recovery

x: **Process termination:** abort all deadlocked processes, or abort one at a time until the cycle breaks (choose by priority, work done, resources held).
**Resource preemption:** take a resource from a victim, roll the victim back to a safe state, and avoid starving the same victim.

blocks.x: Deadlock needs all four conditions; breaking any one prevents it. Banker's algorithm avoids it by staying in safe states.

qa.q: What are the four necessary conditions for deadlock?
qa.a: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait.

qa.q: What is a safe state?
qa.a: A state in which there exists a sequence of all processes (a safe sequence) such that each can complete using the available resources plus those released by earlier processes in the sequence.

qa.q: Is an unsafe state the same as a deadlock?
qa.a: No. An unsafe state means a deadlock is possible, but not certain. A deadlock state is always unsafe.

qa.q: How does resource ordering prevent deadlock?
qa.a: By numbering resource types and forcing every process to request them in increasing order, it makes circular wait impossible.

qa.q: How is Need computed in the Banker's algorithm?
qa.a: Need = Max − Allocation for each process and resource type.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a necessary condition for deadlock?
quiz.why: The four conditions are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait.

quiz.q: A cycle in a RAG with single-instance resources means
quiz.why: With single instances a cycle is both necessary and sufficient for deadlock.

quiz.q: In the Banker's example, a safe sequence is
quiz.why: P1 first because Need (1,2,2) fits in Available (3,3,2); the rest follow.

quiz.q: Deadlock avoidance requires the OS to know in advance
o: the maximum resource needs of processes
quiz.why: The Banker's algorithm uses Max claims.

quiz.q: Which prevention method breaks circular wait?
o: Impose an ordering on resource types
quiz.why: Increasing-order requests make cycles impossible.

problems.a: 1) Mutual exclusion: a resource can be used by only one process at a time (a printer). 2) Hold and wait: a process holds one resource while waiting for another. 3) No preemption: a resource cannot be forcibly taken away. 4) Circular wait: a closed chain of processes each waiting for a resource held by the next. All four must hold together.

problems.q: Five processes and three resource types (A, B, C). Allocation: P0 010, P1 200, P2 302, P3 211, P4 002. Max: P0 753, P1 322, P2 902, P3 222, P4 433. Available: 332. Compute the Need matrix and find a safe sequence using the Banker's algorithm.

problems.q: In the same system P1 now requests (1,0,2). Should the request be granted? Show the checks. Also explain how breaking the circular wait condition prevents deadlock.
problems.a:
Check 1: Request (1,0,2) <= Need of P1 (1,2,2): yes. Check 2: Request <= Available (3,3,2): yes.
Pretend to grant: Available = 332 - 102 = 230; P1 Allocation = 302; P1 Need = 020.
Safety check: P1 (020 <= 230) finishes, Work = 532; P3 finishes, Work = 743; P0 finishes, Work = 753; P2 finishes; P4 finishes. A safe sequence exists, so the request can be granted.
Preventing circular wait: give every resource type a number and require processes to request resources in increasing order, so a cycle can never form.

lessons.title: Memory management basics and contiguous allocation
yt: memory management contiguous allocation first fit best fit worst fit fragmentation
logical vs physical address MMU relocation register

blocks.x: Programs must be in main memory to run. The OS decides where each process goes and protects it from others.
Address binding

x: **Logical (virtual) address:** generated by the CPU, seen by the program.
**Physical address:** the real location in memory.
Binding can happen at **compile time** (absolute code), **load time** (relocatable code), or **execution time** (needs hardware support; used by modern OSs).

blocks.x: The **Memory Management Unit (MMU)** translates logical to physical addresses. In the simplest scheme a **relocation (base) register** is added to every logical address, and a **limit register** checks that the address is within the process's size. Protection: if `logical ≥ limit`, trap to the OS.
Swapping
A process can be temporarily **swapped out** to a backing store (disk) and later brought back, so total memory used can exceed physical memory. Swapping is slow, so systems limit it.
Contiguous allocation
Each process occupies **one contiguous block**.

x: **Fixed (static) partitions:** memory is divided into fixed-size partitions. Simple, but suffers **internal fragmentation** (unused space inside an allocated partition).
**Variable (dynamic) partitions:** a partition is made exactly as large as the process. Leads to **external fragmentation**: enough total free space, but scattered in pieces too small to use.

blocks.x: Placement strategies for a hole

x: **First fit:** first hole big enough. Fast.
**Best fit:** smallest hole that is big enough. Leaves tiny leftovers; must search the whole list.
**Worst fit:** largest hole. Leaves large leftovers; usually worst in practice.

blocks.x: Example: holes of 100, 500, 200, 300, 600 KB and requests 212, 417, 112, 426 KB in order.
Best fit uses memory most efficiently here: all four processes are placed.
Fragmentation

x: **Internal:** wasted space inside an allocated block.
**External:** wasted space between blocks.

blocks.x: **Compaction** shifts processes together to make one large hole (needs execution-time binding and is costly). **Paging** removes external fragmentation altogether.
The 50-percent rule
With first fit, for every N allocated blocks about N/2 blocks are lost to fragmentation, so one third of memory may be unusable.
Fixed partitions waste inside (internal fragmentation); variable partitions waste between (external fragmentation).

qa.q: What is the difference between a logical and a physical address?
qa.a: A logical address is generated by the CPU and used by the program. A physical address is the actual location in main memory. The MMU maps logical to physical.

qa.q: What is the role of the limit register?
qa.a: It holds the size of the process's address space, and any logical address beyond it causes a trap, which protects other processes.

qa.q: Differentiate internal and external fragmentation.
qa.a: Internal fragmentation is unused space inside an allocated partition. External fragmentation is free memory split into small non-contiguous holes that cannot satisfy a request.

qa.q: Which placement strategy is usually best?
qa.a: First fit and best fit are generally better than worst fit; first fit is faster, best fit wastes the least in many cases.

qa.q: What is compaction?
qa.a: Moving processes in memory to combine all free holes into one large block. It needs dynamic (execution-time) relocation and takes time.

quiz.why: The partition is larger than the process needs.

quiz.q: Which strategy picks the smallest hole that fits?
quiz.why: Best fit searches for the tightest hole.

quiz.q: Compaction can solve
quiz.why: Moving processes closes the gaps between them.

quiz.q: The relocation register value is added to
o: every logical address to get the physical address
the physical address to get the logical address
quiz.why: The MMU adds the base to each logical address.

quiz.why: 300 is the smallest hole of at least 212.

First fit: 212 goes to 500 (leaves 288), 417 goes to 600 (leaves 183), 112 goes to 288 (the remainder of the 500K partition), 426 does not fit anywhere and must wait.

problems.q: Explain internal and external fragmentation. How does compaction help and what is its cost?
problems.a:
Internal fragmentation is wasted space inside an allocated block (a process gets a 4K block but needs 3K). External fragmentation is free memory split into many small holes that are not contiguous, so a large request fails even though the total free space is enough.
Compaction moves processes together so free holes merge into one large block. It is costly because it needs CPU time to copy memory and requires dynamic relocation.

problems.q: The same partitions (100K, 500K, 200K, 300K, 600K) and processes (212K, 417K, 112K, 426K) are used with worst fit. Show the allocation and the remaining holes. Which of first, best and worst fit gave the best result here and why?

Holes left: 100, 83, 200, 300, 276.
Best fit was the best: it placed all four processes because it saved the large 600K partition for the large 426K process, while first and worst fit used up the large partitions early.

lessons.title: Paging, page tables and the TLB
yt: paging in operating system page table TLB effective access time
multilevel paging inverted page table

blocks.x: **Paging** removes external fragmentation by allowing a process's physical memory to be **non-contiguous**.
Basic method

x: Physical memory is divided into fixed-size blocks called **frames**.
Logical memory is divided into blocks of the same size called **pages**.
A **page table** per process maps each page number to a frame number.

blocks.x: A logical address has two parts: **page number p** (index into the page table) and **page offset d** (position within the page). If the page size is 2^n, the low n bits are the offset.
Example
Page size 1 KB (1024 bytes). Logical address 5000.

x: Page number = 5000 / 1024 = 4 (integer division), offset = 5000 mod 1024 = 904.
Suppose the page table maps page 4 to frame 9.
Physical address = 9 × 1024 + 904 = **10120**.

blocks.x: Internal fragmentation
The last page of a process is usually partly empty. On average half a page per process is wasted, so smaller pages waste less but need larger page tables.
Page table size

A 32-bit logical address with 4 KB pages (12-bit offset) has 20 bits for the page number: 2^20 = 1,048,576 entries. At 4 bytes per entry the page table is **4 MB per process**, which is too large to keep contiguous. Solutions:

x: **Hierarchical (multilevel) paging:** page the page table; only the needed parts exist. A two-level scheme splits the page number into outer and inner indexes.
**Hashed page tables** for large address spaces.
**Inverted page table:** one entry per physical frame (not per page), searched by (process id, page number). Saves memory, but lookup is slower and needs hashing.

blocks.x: Page table entry contents
Frame number, **valid/invalid bit**, **protection bits** (read, write, execute), **reference bit**, **dirty (modified) bit**.
Translation Look-aside Buffer (TLB)
A page table in memory means **two memory accesses** per reference (one for the table, one for the data). The **TLB** is a small, fast associative cache of recent page-to-frame translations.

x: **TLB hit:** frame number found in the TLB, one memory access.
**TLB miss:** consult the page table, then update the TLB.

blocks.x: Effective Access Time (EAT)

With TLB access time 20 ns, memory access 100 ns, and hit ratio 80%: EAT = 0.8 × (20 + 100) + 0.2 × (20 + 100 + 100) = 96 + 44 = **140 ns**. With hit ratio 98%: EAT = 0.98 × 120 + 0.02 × 220 = 117.6 + 4.4 = **122 ns**. The higher the hit ratio, the closer EAT gets to the cost of a single access.
Shared pages
Read-only code (such as a text editor) can be shared: several page tables point to the same frames, saving memory.
Page = logical block, frame = physical block. Address = page number + offset.

qa.q: What is the difference between a page and a frame?
qa.a: A page is a fixed-size block of logical memory; a frame is a fixed-size block of physical memory of the same size. The page table maps pages to frames.

qa.q: Why does paging not suffer from external fragmentation?
qa.a: Any free frame can hold any page, so no contiguous space is needed. Only internal fragmentation in the last page remains.

qa.q: What is the TLB?
qa.a: A small, fast hardware cache holding recent page-to-frame translations, avoiding an extra memory access to the page table.

qa.q: How many page table entries are needed for a 32-bit address space with 4 KB pages?
What is an inverted page table?
qa.a: A single table with one entry per physical frame, storing which process and page occupies it. It saves memory but needs hashing to search quickly.

quiz.why: 5000 divided by 1024 is 4 (remainder 904).

quiz.q: The offset part of a logical address
o: gives the position inside the page
quiz.why: The offset is copied unchanged into the physical address.

quiz.why: Frames are interchangeable.

quiz.q: Multilevel paging mainly reduces
o: the memory needed for page tables
quiz.why: Only the parts of the page table in use need to exist.

problems.a:
(a) 1 KB = 2^10, so offset = 10 bits and page number = 16 - 10 = 6 bits (64 pages).
(b) Page number = 6716 / 1024 = 6 (integer division); offset = 6716 - 6 x 1024 = 6716 - 6144 = 572.

problems.a:
Physical address = frame x page size + offset = 9 x 1024 + 572 = 9216 + 572 = 9788.
A page table entry also stores a valid/invalid bit, protection bits (read/write/execute), a reference bit and a dirty (modified) bit.

rubric.t: Lists at least valid and protection bits plus reference or dirty

lessons.title: Segmentation and segmented paging
yt: segmentation in operating system segment table address translation
paging vs segmentation difference

blocks.x: Programmers think of a program as a set of **segments**: main code, functions, stack, heap, global data. **Segmentation** gives the OS the same view: memory is divided into variable-size logical units.
Logical address

A logical address is `<segment number s, offset d>`. The **segment table** has one entry per segment with a **base** (starting physical address) and a **limit** (segment length). The hardware checks `d < limit`; if not, it traps. Otherwise physical address = base + d.
Example

x: Address (0, 1222): 1222 ≥ 1000, so an **addressing error (trap)**.

blocks.x: Advantages

x: Matches the programmer's view; easy to share and protect segments (for example make code read-only).
No internal fragmentation.

blocks.x: Disadvantages

x: **External fragmentation**, since segments are of different sizes and must be placed contiguously.
Allocation is harder than with fixed-size pages.

blocks.x: Paging versus segmentation
Segmented paging

Combine both: the address space is divided into segments, and each segment is **paged**. The segment table entry points to a **page table** for that segment. This keeps logical protection and sharing while removing external fragmentation. Intel x86 used segmentation with paging in 32-bit mode; modern 64-bit systems use mostly flat paging.
Segmentation = logical units of different sizes; paging = physical units of the same size.

qa.q: What does a segment table entry contain?
qa.a: A base address (where the segment starts in physical memory) and a limit (its length).

qa.q: How is a logical address translated in segmentation?
qa.a: The segment number indexes the segment table; if the offset is less than the limit, the physical address is base plus offset, otherwise a trap occurs.

qa.q: Which fragmentation occurs in segmentation?
qa.a: External fragmentation, because segments have variable sizes and need contiguous memory.

qa.q: How does segmented paging help?
qa.a: It pages each segment, so the logical benefits of segments (sharing, protection) are kept while external fragmentation is removed.

qa.q: Name one difference between paging and segmentation.
qa.a: Pages are fixed in size and invisible to the programmer, while segments vary in size and match logical units of the program.

quiz.why: Segments correspond to logical parts of the program.

lessons.title: Virtual memory and demand paging
yt: virtual memory demand paging page fault handling steps
copy on write virtual memory

blocks.x: **Virtual memory** lets a program run even if it is larger than physical memory. Only the parts needed are kept in memory; the rest stay on disk. It separates the programmer's large logical address space from the limited physical memory.
Benefits
Programs can be larger than RAM, more programs fit at once (higher multiprogramming), less I/O is needed to load a program, and processes can share pages easily.
Demand paging
A page is loaded **only when it is needed** (lazy swapper). The page table has a **valid/invalid bit**: valid means the page is in memory; invalid means it is not (or the address is illegal).
Page-fault handling steps

x: The CPU references a page marked invalid, causing a **trap**.
The OS checks an internal table: if the reference is illegal, terminate the process; if just not in memory, continue.
Find a **free frame** (or choose a victim using page replacement).
Schedule a **disk read** of the page into the frame.
When the read completes, update the page table (frame number, valid bit = 1).
**Restart the instruction** that caused the fault.

blocks.x: **Pure demand paging** starts a process with no pages in memory.
Performance of demand paging

Let p be the **page-fault rate** (0 ≤ p ≤ 1). EAT = (1 − p) × memory access time + p × page-fault service time. With memory access 200 ns and page-fault service time 8 ms (8,000,000 ns), and p = 1/1000: EAT = 0.999 × 200 + 0.001 × 8,000,000 = 199.8 + 8000 = **8199.8 ns ≈ 8.2 µs**, about **41 times slower** than a memory access. To keep slowdown below 10%, p must be below about 1 in 399,990. So page-fault rates must be extremely low.
Copy-on-write (COW)
After `fork()`, parent and child **share** the same pages marked read-only. Only when one writes is the page **copied**. This makes process creation fast and saves memory.
Memory-mapped files
A file is mapped to virtual addresses (`mmap`), so file I/O becomes ordinary memory access handled by paging.
Frame allocation

x: **Equal** and **proportional** allocation (proportional to process size).
**Global replacement:** a process can take frames from others (better throughput, less predictable).
**Local replacement:** a process replaces only its own frames.

blocks.x: Locality of reference
Programs tend to use the same pages and nearby pages repeatedly (**temporal and spatial locality**). Demand paging works well only because of locality.
A page fault is not an error: it is a request for the OS to bring a page in.

qa.q: What is demand paging?
qa.a: A scheme in which pages are loaded into memory only when they are referenced, instead of loading the whole program in advance.

qa.q: List the steps in handling a page fault.
qa.a: Trap to the OS, verify the reference is legal, find a free frame, read the page from disk into the frame, update the page table, and restart the instruction.

qa.q: What does the valid/invalid bit show?
qa.a: Valid means the page is legal and currently in memory; invalid means it is either outside the address space or not currently in memory.

qa.q: How does copy-on-write speed up fork()?
qa.a: The child shares the parent's pages read-only, and a page is copied only if either process writes to it, avoiding copying unused pages.

qa.q: Why must the page-fault rate be very low?
qa.a: Servicing a fault takes milliseconds while a memory access takes nanoseconds, so even a small fault rate greatly increases the effective access time.

lessons.title: Page replacement: FIFO, Optimal, LRU and Belady's anomaly
yt: page replacement algorithms FIFO LRU optimal numerical
belady's anomaly explained

blocks.x: When a page fault occurs and **no free frame** exists, the OS must pick a **victim** page to replace. Goal: **minimise page faults**. We judge algorithms on a **reference string**.
If the victim page is **dirty** (modified) it must be written back; a **modify bit** avoids writing clean pages.
Standard example
FIFO
Replace the page that has been in memory **longest**. Easy, but may remove a heavily used page. **Page faults = 15.**
Optimal (OPT or MIN)
Replace the page that will **not be used for the longest time in the future**. Gives the lowest possible faults but needs future knowledge, so it is only a yardstick. **Page faults = 9.**
LRU (Least Recently Used)

Replace the page **not used for the longest time in the past**; uses the past as a guide to the future. Implementation by counters (time-of-use stamps) or a stack of page numbers. **Page faults = 12.** LRU is a good approximation of OPT and never suffers from Belady's anomaly.
Approximations of LRU

x: **Reference bit:** the hardware sets a bit when a page is used; the OS periodically clears it.
**Second-chance (clock):** pages are in a circular list. If the reference bit is 0, replace; if 1, clear it and give a second chance, moving on.
**Enhanced second chance** uses (reference, modify) pairs.
**LFU/MFU:** replace the least/most frequently used page.

blocks.x: Belady's anomaly
For FIFO, **adding frames can increase faults**. Reference string 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5:

x: 3 frames: **9 faults**.
4 frames: **10 faults**.

blocks.x: Algorithms called **stack algorithms** (OPT, LRU) never show this anomaly.
Simulation in code
Output:
Hit ratio
Hit ratio = hits / references = (references − faults) / references. For OPT here: (20 − 9) / 20 = 55%.
OPT is the best but impossible; LRU is the best practical idea; FIFO can show Belady's anomaly.

qa.q: What is a reference string?
qa.a: The sequence of page numbers a process accesses, used to evaluate page replacement algorithms.

qa.q: Why is the optimal algorithm not used in practice?
qa.a: It needs to know the future page references, which the OS cannot know. It serves as a benchmark.

qa.q: What is Belady's anomaly?
qa.a: In some algorithms such as FIFO, increasing the number of frames can increase the number of page faults.

qa.q: How does the second-chance algorithm work?
qa.a: Pages are checked in circular order. A page with reference bit 0 is replaced; one with bit 1 has its bit cleared and is skipped, getting a second chance.

qa.q: Which algorithms are free from Belady's anomaly?
qa.a: Stack algorithms such as LRU and Optimal.

quiz.why: OPT looks forward in time.

problems.a:
LRU: 12 page faults. Optimal: 9 page faults.
Optimal replaces the page that will not be used for the longest time in the future. This needs knowledge of future references, which the OS does not have, so it is used only as a benchmark for other algorithms.

problems.q: Use the string 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5 with FIFO. Count the faults with 3 frames and with 4 frames. What is this phenomenon called and why does it not happen with LRU?
problems.a:
With 3 frames FIFO gives 9 page faults; with 4 frames it gives 10 page faults. More frames caused more faults: this is Belady's anomaly.
LRU is a stack algorithm: the set of pages in memory with n frames is always a subset of the set with n+1 frames, so adding frames can never increase faults.

lessons.title: Thrashing and the working-set model
yt: thrashing in operating system working set model page fault frequency
what is thrashing and how to prevent it

blocks.x: **Thrashing** happens when a process (or the whole system) spends more time **paging** than executing, because it does not have enough frames for its active pages.
How it develops

x: The OS sees low CPU utilisation and admits more processes.
Each process gets fewer frames, so page faults rise.
Processes wait for the paging disk, so the ready queue empties and CPU utilisation falls further.
The OS admits even more processes. Utilisation collapses.

blocks.x: A graph of CPU utilisation against the degree of multiprogramming rises, then **drops sharply** at the thrashing point.
Cause: locality

At any time a process uses a **locality** (a set of pages used together, such as a function and its data). If the allocated frames are fewer than the size of the current locality, the process keeps faulting.
Preventing thrashing

x: **Working-set model:** the **working set** WS(t, Δ) is the set of pages referenced in the most recent Δ page references (the **working-set window**). The OS gives each process enough frames for its working set. If the total demand D = Σ|WSi| exceeds the number of available frames, suspend a process (swap it out).
**Page-fault frequency (PFF):** monitor each process's fault rate. If it is above an upper limit, give it more frames; if below a lower limit, take frames away. If no free frames, suspend a process.
**Use local replacement:** one thrashing process cannot steal frames from others.
**Limit the degree of multiprogramming.**

blocks.x: Example

Reference string with Δ = 5: ...2 6 1 5 7 7 7 7 5 1... At a moment where the last five references are 7 7 7 7 5, the working set is {7, 5}, which needs 2 frames. Later, with last five 6 1 5 7 7 the set is {6, 1, 5, 7}, needing 4 frames.
Practical advice
Add RAM, reduce the number of running programs, and keep working sets small (good algorithms and data layout).
Thrashing is a vicious circle: low utilisation leads to more processes, which leads to more faults and lower utilisation.

qa.q: What is thrashing?
qa.a: A state in which a system spends most of its time swapping pages in and out instead of executing, because processes do not have enough frames.

qa.q: What is the working set of a process?
qa.a: The set of pages referenced in the most recent Δ references, which approximates the pages it is currently using (its locality).

qa.q: How does page-fault frequency control prevent thrashing?
qa.a: It sets upper and lower fault-rate limits. A process above the limit gets more frames, a process below it gives frames up, and a process is suspended if no frames are free.

qa.q: Why does adding more processes when CPU utilisation is low make thrashing worse?
qa.a: More processes share the same frames, so each gets fewer, page faults increase and CPU utilisation falls even more.

qa.q: Does local replacement help?
qa.a: Yes, it stops one thrashing process from taking frames from others, so the trouble stays contained.

quiz.why: WS(t, Δ) approximates the current locality.

quiz.why: Fewer processes means more frames per process.

quiz.q: If total working-set demand exceeds available frames the OS should
quiz.why: Frames must cover the working sets of running processes.

quiz.q: PFF stands for
quiz.why: It monitors how often a process faults.

problems.q: What is thrashing? State its main cause and one way to prevent it.
problems.a: Thrashing is a state in which the system spends more time swapping pages in and out than executing useful instructions, so CPU utilisation falls sharply. The main cause is too high a degree of multiprogramming: processes do not have enough frames for their working sets. Prevention: reduce the degree of multiprogramming (suspend a process), use the working set model, or the page fault frequency scheme.

problems.q: Using a working set window of 4 references on the string 1,2,1,3,2,4,4,5,6,5,6,7, find the working set after the 6th reference and after the 12th reference.
problems.a:
After the 6th reference the last 4 references are 1,3,2,4, so WS = {1,2,3,4} with size 4.
After the 12th reference the last 4 references are 6,5,6,7, so WS = {5,6,7} with size 3.

problems.q: Three processes have working set sizes 20, 30 and 25 frames and the system has 60 frames. Compute the total demand D and decide what the OS should do. Which process suspension would fix it?
problems.a: D = 20 + 30 + 25 = 75 frames, which is greater than the 60 available, so thrashing will occur. The OS should suspend a process and free its frames. Suspending the 20-frame process leaves D = 55 <= 60, which fits; suspending the 25-frame process leaves 50, also fits; suspending the 30-frame process leaves 45 and also fits. Suspending the smallest enough process loses the least progress, so the 20-frame one is the minimal sufficient choice.

lessons.title: File concepts, access methods and directory structure
yt: file system concepts access methods directory structure operating system
file attributes operations types OS

blocks.x: A **file** is a named collection of related information stored on secondary storage. The OS gives it a logical view independent of the physical device.
File attributes
Name, identifier, type, location, size, protection (permissions), time stamps (created, modified, accessed), and owner.
File operations

Create, write, read, **seek** (reposition), delete, truncate, open and close. `open()` loads file metadata into the system-wide **open-file table** and the per-process open-file table, and returns a **file descriptor**.
File types and extensions
Regular files (text, binary), directories, and in Unix special files (device files, pipes, sockets). Extensions like `.c` or `.pdf` hint at the type; Unix may also use **magic numbers**.
Access methods

x: **Sequential access:** records are read in order; a **current position pointer** moves forward. Typical for text files and tapes.
**Direct (random) access:** read any block by number: `read(n)`. Needed by databases.
**Indexed access:** an index file points to records; search the index, then go directly to the record.

blocks.x: Directory structure
A **directory** maps names to file control blocks (or inodes).

x: **Single-level:** one directory for all files. Name clashes, no grouping.
**Two-level:** a directory for each user. Isolates users but no sharing of subdirectories.
**Tree-structured:** directories contain files and subdirectories. Uses **absolute paths** (`/home/anil/notes.txt`) and **relative paths** (`../notes.txt`). Most common.

**Acyclic graph:** allows sharing through **links**. A **hard link** is another name for the same inode (the file lives until the last link is removed). A **symbolic (soft) link** is a small file containing a path; it can dangle if the target is deleted.
**General graph:** may have cycles; needs garbage collection or cycle checking.

blocks.x: File protection

Unix uses **owner, group, other** with read, write, execute bits (rwx). Example `rwxr-x---`: owner can do everything, group can read and execute, others have nothing. Access-control lists (ACLs) give finer control.
File system mounting
A file system on a device is **mounted** at a mount point in the directory tree to make it accessible.
Consistency semantics
When several users share a file: **Unix semantics** (writes immediately visible), **session semantics** (changes visible only after close, used in AFS), **immutable shared files**.
A directory is itself a file that maps names to metadata.

qa.q: What is a file descriptor?
qa.a: A small integer returned by open() that identifies an open file in a process's open-file table.

qa.q: What is the difference between sequential and direct access?
qa.a: Sequential access reads records in order from the current position. Direct access can read or write any block by its number without reading the earlier ones.

qa.q: What is the difference between hard and soft links?
qa.a: A hard link is an additional directory entry for the same inode, and the data survives until all hard links are removed. A soft link is a separate file containing the target path and breaks if the target is removed.

qa.q: What does the mode rwxr-x--- mean?
qa.a: The owner has read, write and execute permission, the group has read and execute, and everyone else has no permission.

qa.q: Why is a tree-structured directory preferred over a single-level directory?
qa.a: It allows grouping, avoids filename clashes between users and projects, and supports path names.

problems.q: List five common file attributes and five basic file operations.
problems.a: Attributes: name, type, location, size, protection (permissions), timestamps (created, modified), owner. Operations: create, open, read, write, seek (reposition), delete, truncate, close.

problems.q: Explain sequential, direct and indexed access methods with one use case each.
problems.a: Sequential access reads records one after another in order (log files, tape). Direct (random) access jumps to any block number directly without reading earlier ones (databases, fixed-size records). Indexed access keeps an index of keys that points to records, so a search finds the position quickly and then uses direct access (a book index, database index).

problems.q: Compare single-level, two-level, tree-structured and acyclic-graph directories. For an acyclic graph with sharing, what happens to a hard link and to a soft link when the original file is deleted?
problems.a:
Single-level: one directory for all files, name clashes, no grouping. Two-level: one directory per user, no sharing of files between users easily. Tree: hierarchy with sub-directories and path names, natural grouping. Acyclic graph: allows shared files and directories using links.
Hard link: another name for the same inode, the data stays until the last link is removed. Soft (symbolic) link: stores the path to the file; if the original is deleted it becomes a dangling link and access fails.

lessons.title: File allocation methods, inodes and free-space management
yt: file allocation methods contiguous linked indexed FAT inode
free space management bit vector linked list

blocks.x: Disks are divided into **blocks** (typically 4 KB). The OS decides which blocks hold each file.
Contiguous allocation
A file occupies consecutive blocks; the directory stores the **start block and length**.

x: Pros: fast sequential and direct access (very few seeks); simple.
Cons: **external fragmentation**, files cannot easily grow, must know size in advance.

blocks.x: Linked allocation
Each block contains a **pointer to the next block**; the directory stores the first (and last) block.

x: Pros: no external fragmentation; files grow easily.
Cons: no efficient direct access (to reach block n you follow n pointers); pointers use space; one corrupt pointer loses the rest.

blocks.x: **FAT (File Allocation Table)** keeps all the pointers in a table at the start of the disk, which can be cached in memory, making direct access practical (used in FAT16/FAT32).
Indexed allocation
Each file has an **index block** listing the addresses of its data blocks.

x: Pros: direct access without external fragmentation.
Cons: the index block is overhead, even for tiny files. For large files use **linked index blocks**, **multilevel index** or **combined** schemes.

blocks.x: The Unix inode

An **inode** stores a file's metadata (owner, permissions, size, timestamps, link count) and block pointers. A classic inode has **12 direct pointers**, one **single indirect**, one **double indirect** and one **triple indirect** pointer. The file name is not in the inode; it is in the directory entry.
Maximum file size example
Block size 4 KB, pointer size 4 bytes, so a block holds 1024 pointers.

x: Direct: 12 × 4 KB = 48 KB.
Single indirect: 1024 × 4 KB = 4 MB.
Double indirect: 1024² × 4 KB = 4 GB.
Triple indirect: 1024³ × 4 KB = 4 TB.

blocks.x: Total about **4 TB**, mostly from the triple indirect block. Small files use only direct pointers, so access is fast.
Free-space management

x: **Bit vector (bitmap):** one bit per block (1 = free). Simple and quick to find contiguous free blocks; large for big disks.
**Linked list** of free blocks: no waste, but traversal is slow.
**Grouping** (first free block stores the addresses of many free blocks) and **counting** (store address plus count of contiguous free blocks).

blocks.x: Comparison
Journaling
Modern file systems (ext4, NTFS) write metadata changes to a **journal (log)** first, so after a crash they can replay or discard them and avoid inconsistency (compare WAL in databases).
Contiguous = fast but rigid; linked = flexible but slow random access; indexed = best of both with an index overhead.

qa.q: What are the disadvantages of contiguous allocation?
qa.a: External fragmentation, difficulty growing a file, and the need to know its size when it is created.

qa.q: Why is linked allocation poor for direct access?
qa.a: To reach the nth block you must follow n pointers through earlier blocks, one disk read each.

qa.q: What does FAT improve over simple linked allocation?
qa.a: It stores all next-block pointers in a table that can be cached in memory, so following the chain is fast and direct access becomes practical.

qa.q: What does a Unix inode contain and not contain?
qa.a: It contains metadata (owner, permissions, size, timestamps, link count) and block pointers. It does not contain the file name, which is kept in the directory entry.

qa.q: How big can a file be with 12 direct pointers and one single indirect pointer at 4 KB blocks and 4-byte pointers?

quiz.why: Files need consecutive free blocks.

quiz.q: Which scheme stores next-block pointers in a table at the start of the disk?
quiz.why: FAT collects all chain pointers in one table.

quiz.q: In a Unix inode with 4 KB blocks and 4-byte pointers, a single indirect block covers
quiz.why: 1024 pointers x 4 KB = 4 MB.

quiz.q: The file name is stored in
quiz.why: The inode holds metadata and pointers, not the name.

quiz.why: It records which blocks are free.

problems.q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of contiguous, linked and indexed allocation.
problems.a: Contiguous: advantage is fast sequential and direct access; disadvantage is external fragmentation and difficulty growing files. Linked: advantage is no external fragmentation and easy growth; disadvantage is slow direct access and a lost pointer breaks the file. Indexed: advantage is direct access without external fragmentation; disadvantage is the extra space and access for the index block.

problems.q: A Unix inode has 12 direct pointers, one single, one double and one triple indirect pointer. Block size is 4 KB and a pointer is 4 bytes. Find the maximum file size.
problems.a: Pointers per block = 4096 / 4 = 1024. Direct: 12 x 4 KB = 48 KB. Single: 1024 x 4 KB = 4 MB. Double: 1024^2 x 4 KB = 4 GB. Triple: 1024^3 x 4 KB = 4 TB. Total is about 4 TB + 4 GB + 4 MB + 48 KB, i.e. just over 4 TB.

rubric.t: Direct, single, double and triple sizes

problems.q: With the same inode, in which part of the inode does data block number 5000 (counting from 0) lie, and how many block reads are needed to get it if the inode is already in memory?
problems.a:
Blocks 0 to 11 are direct. The single indirect covers blocks 12 to 1035 (1024 blocks). The double indirect starts at block 1036. Since 5000 is greater than 1035, it lies in the double indirect region.
Offset = 5000 - 1036 = 3964. First-level index = 3964 / 1024 = 3, second-level index = 3964 mod 1024 = 892.
Block reads: double-indirect block, then the second-level index block, then the data block = 3 reads.

rubric.t: Identifies the double indirect region with ranges

lessons.title: Disk structure and disk scheduling
yt: disk scheduling algorithms FCFS SSTF SCAN C-SCAN LOOK numerical
seek time rotational latency disk access time

blocks.x: A hard disk has **platters** with **tracks** (circles), divided into **sectors**, with read/write heads on an arm. **Cylinder** = the tracks at the same arm position on all platters.
Disk access time

x: **Seek time:** moving the head to the correct cylinder (largest part).
**Rotational latency:** waiting for the sector to rotate under the head; average = half a rotation. At 7200 rpm one rotation takes 60/7200 s = 8.33 ms, so average latency = 4.17 ms.
**Transfer time:** reading the data.

blocks.x: Disk access time = seek + rotational latency + transfer time. The OS reduces seek time by scheduling requests. (SSDs have no seek, so scheduling matters less.)
Algorithms
Request queue (cylinders 0 to 199): **98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67**, with the head at **53**.
FCFS
Serve in arrival order: 53 → 98 → 183 → 37 → 122 → 14 → 124 → 65 → 67. Total head movement = **640 cylinders**. Fair but wild swings.
SSTF (Shortest Seek Time First)
Always the nearest request: 53 → 65 → 67 → 37 → 14 → 98 → 122 → 124 → 183. Total = **236**. Good throughput but may **starve** distant requests.
SCAN (elevator)
The head moves in one direction (here towards 199), serving requests, goes to the **end**, then reverses. Order: 65, 67, 98, 122, 124, 183, (199), 37, 14. Total = (199 − 53) + (199 − 14) = **331**.
C-SCAN (circular SCAN)

Moves in one direction only; at the end it **jumps back** to cylinder 0 and continues in the same direction, giving more uniform waiting times. Order: 65, 67, 98, 122, 124, 183, (199), (0), 14, 37. Total (counting the return jump) = **382**.
LOOK and C-LOOK

Like SCAN and C-SCAN, but the head goes only as far as the **last request** in each direction instead of the disk edge. LOOK order: 65, 67, 98, 122, 124, 183, 37, 14. Total = (183 − 53) + (183 − 14) = **299**.
Summary
Choosing
For heavily loaded disks SCAN/LOOK-type algorithms perform well and avoid starvation. Linux uses variants of **deadline**, **CFQ**/**BFQ** or simple **noop** (for SSDs).
Disk management
Low-level formatting, partitioning, boot blocks, bad-block management, and **RAID** (redundant arrays: RAID 0 striping, 1 mirroring, 5 striped with parity) for speed and reliability.
Seek time dominates, so schedule requests to reduce head movement.

qa.q: What are the components of disk access time?
qa.a: Seek time (moving the head), rotational latency (waiting for the sector to arrive) and transfer time (reading or writing the data).

qa.q: Why can SSTF cause starvation?
qa.a: Requests far from the head can be postponed indefinitely if new requests keep arriving near the head.

qa.q: How is SCAN different from LOOK?
qa.a: SCAN goes all the way to the disk edge before reversing. LOOK reverses at the last pending request in that direction.

qa.q: What is the average rotational latency of a 7200 rpm disk?
qa.a: Half of one rotation: one rotation is 8.33 ms, so the average is about 4.17 ms.

qa.q: What is the advantage of C-SCAN over SCAN?
qa.a: It treats the cylinders as a circular list, giving more uniform waiting times for requests at both ends of the disk.

quiz.q: For queue 98,183,37,122,14,124,65,67 with the head at 53, FCFS total head movement is
Which algorithm always picks the nearest request?
quiz.why: SSTF = Shortest Seek Time First.

quiz.q: SSTF suffers from
quiz.why: Far requests may never be chosen.

quiz.q: The elevator algorithm is
quiz.why: SCAN moves like an elevator in one direction, then back.

quiz.q: Which component of disk access time is usually the largest?
quiz.why: Mechanical arm movement dominates.

visuals.title: Total head movement for requests 98,183,37,122,14,124,65,67 with head at 53 (disk 0-199)
visuals.data: FCFS=640;SSTF=236;SCAN=236;LOOK=208;C-SCAN=382

problems.q: Request queue 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67 with the head at cylinder 53. Find the total head movement for FCFS and SSTF.
Same queue and the head moving towards 0 first on a disk of cylinders 0 to 199. Find the total head movement for SCAN and LOOK.
problems.a:
SCAN: 53 down to 0 is 53, then up to 183 is 183. Total = 236 cylinders.
LOOK: 53 down to 14 is 39, then up to 183 is 169. Total = 208 cylinders. LOOK turns around at the last request instead of the disk edge.

rubric.t: LOOK reverses at the last request

problems.q: Same queue, head moving upward. Find the head movement for C-SCAN (counting the return jump) and explain why C-SCAN gives more uniform waiting time than SCAN.
problems.a:
C-SCAN: 53 up to 199 is 146, jump back to 0 is 199, then 0 up to 37 (last request below 53 is 37) is 37. Total = 146 + 199 + 37 = 382 cylinders. (If the return jump is not counted: 183.)
In SCAN, cylinders in the middle get serviced twice as often as the edges, so edge requests wait longer. C-SCAN always sweeps in one direction and treats the disk like a circular list, giving more uniform waiting.

rubric.t: Mentions the return sweep without servicing

lessons.title: I/O systems: polling, interrupts, DMA and buffering
yt: IO systems polling interrupt DMA operating system
buffering caching spooling operating system

blocks.x: The OS controls a huge variety of devices (disks, keyboards, network cards, printers) through a common framework.
I/O hardware

x: A **device controller** is the electronics that operates a device. The CPU talks to it through **registers** (status, command, data).
**Port-mapped I/O** uses special I/O instructions and a separate address space; **memory-mapped I/O** maps device registers into normal memory addresses.

blocks.x: Three ways to do I/O

x: **Programmed I/O with polling (busy waiting):** the CPU repeatedly reads the device status register until it is ready. Simple, but wastes CPU time.

**Interrupt-driven I/O:** the CPU starts the operation and continues with other work; the device sends an **interrupt** when done, and the **interrupt handler** responds. Good for slow devices, but each byte can cost an interrupt.

**Direct Memory Access (DMA):** a **DMA controller** moves a whole block between the device and memory **without CPU involvement**. The CPU only sets up the transfer (address, count, direction) and gets **one interrupt** at the end. Best for bulk transfer such as disks.

blocks.x: **Cycle stealing:** DMA occasionally takes bus cycles from the CPU.
Kernel I/O subsystem

x: **Scheduling:** order I/O requests (as in disk scheduling).

**Buffering:** a memory area holding data in transit. Reasons: speed mismatch between device and CPU, differing transfer sizes, and **copy semantics**. **Double buffering** lets one buffer fill while the other is used.
**Caching:** a fast copy of data that is also stored elsewhere (disk cache).
**Spooling:** holding output for a device that cannot interleave requests, such as a printer.
**Error handling and protection:** I/O instructions are privileged.

blocks.x: Device drivers
A **device driver** is device-specific kernel code giving the kernel a uniform interface. Because drivers run in kernel mode, buggy drivers are a major cause of crashes.
Blocking and non-blocking I/O

x: **Blocking:** the process waits until the I/O finishes.
**Non-blocking:** returns immediately with whatever is available.
**Asynchronous:** starts the I/O and the process continues; it is notified when complete.

blocks.x: Interrupt handling in brief

On an interrupt the CPU saves the current state, finds the handler in the **interrupt vector**, runs the **interrupt service routine**, then restores state and resumes. **Interrupt priorities** let important devices pre-empt less important ones, and **maskable** interrupts can be disabled.
Polling wastes CPU, interrupts free it, DMA also frees it from the data copying.

qa.q: What is the difference between polling and interrupt-driven I/O?
qa.a: In polling the CPU repeatedly checks the device status, wasting time. In interrupt-driven I/O the device signals the CPU when it needs attention, so the CPU can do other work meanwhile.

qa.q: How does DMA improve I/O performance?
qa.a: A DMA controller transfers a block directly between memory and the device, so the CPU is involved only at the start and end, and gets one interrupt per block instead of one per byte.

qa.q: What is buffering and why is it used?
qa.a: Storing data temporarily in memory while it is being transferred. It smooths speed differences between devices and the CPU and lets sizes of transfers differ.

qa.q: What is spooling?
qa.a: Queuing output (or input) for a device that serves one job at a time, such as a printer, so that programs do not have to wait.

qa.q: What is a device driver?
qa.a: Kernel software that knows the details of one device type and gives the rest of the OS a standard interface to it.

quiz.q: Busy waiting on a device status register is called
quiz.why: The CPU keeps asking whether the device is ready.

quiz.q: Which method transfers a block without CPU involvement in the data copy?
quiz.why: A DMA controller moves the data itself.

quiz.q: Double buffering allows
o: filling one buffer while the other is processed
two devices to share a port
quiz.why: The CPU and device work in parallel.

quiz.q: Memory-mapped I/O means
o: device registers appear as memory addresses
devices have a separate address space
quiz.why: Normal load and store instructions access the device.

quiz.q: On an interrupt, the CPU locates the handler through the
quiz.why: The vector holds handler addresses.

visuals.title: One DMA read
visuals.data: CPU > DMA controller : set address and byte count; DMA controller > Disk : request block; Disk > Memory : data moves directly; DMA controller ~> CPU : one interrupt when finished

problems.q: Differentiate between polling and interrupt-driven I/O.
problems.a: Polling: the CPU repeatedly checks the device status register in a loop, wasting CPU time but simple and fast for very quick devices. Interrupt-driven: the device signals the CPU with an interrupt when it is ready, so the CPU can do other work meanwhile, but each interrupt has overhead.

problems.q: Compare programmed I/O, interrupt-driven I/O and DMA for transferring a large block of data.
problems.a: Programmed I/O: the CPU moves every byte itself and waits on the device; CPU is fully busy. Interrupt-driven: the CPU is interrupted for each byte or word, so it can work in between but pays interrupt overhead per unit. DMA: the CPU programs a DMA controller with the memory address and byte count, and the controller moves the whole block directly between device and memory; the CPU gets one interrupt at the end. DMA is best for large transfers.

problems.q: Explain cycle stealing in DMA and describe the steps of one DMA read from disk to memory.
problems.a:
Cycle stealing: the DMA controller takes control of the memory bus for a few cycles at a time, briefly delaying the CPU, so both share memory.
Steps: 1) the driver gives the DMA controller the destination address and count; 2) the controller requests data from the disk; 3) the disk sends data and the controller writes it to memory, incrementing the address and decrementing the count; 4) when the count reaches zero the controller sends an interrupt to the CPU; 5) the OS handles the interrupt and marks the I/O complete.

rubric.t: Only one interrupt at the end

lessons.title: Protection and security in operating systems
yt: operating system protection security access matrix authentication
domain of protection access control list capability

blocks.x: **Protection** controls access of programs, processes and users to the resources defined by the OS (internal). **Security** defends the system against external and internal attacks (viruses, intruders, denial of service).
Principle of least privilege
Programs and users should get only the privileges needed for their task, nothing more. It limits the damage of bugs and attacks.
Domain of protection

A **domain** is a set of (object, access-rights) pairs. A process executes in a domain. In Unix, a domain is the user ID, plus a special bit: the **setuid** bit makes a program run with the owner's privileges (used by `passwd`, risky if misused).
Access matrix
Rows are domains, columns are objects, entries are rights.
Storing the whole matrix wastes space, so it is implemented as:

x: **Access-control list (ACL):** per object, a list of (domain, rights). Easy to revoke; used by file systems.
**Capability list:** per domain, a list of objects with rights (unforgeable tokens). Efficient access checks, harder revocation.

blocks.x: Authentication

x: **Passwords:** stored as **salted hashes**, never plain text. Salt defeats precomputed rainbow tables. Attacks: brute force, dictionary, phishing, guessing.
**Multi-factor authentication:** something you know (password), have (phone, token), are (fingerprint).
**One-time passwords** and **biometrics**.

blocks.x: Common threats

x: **Malware:** virus (attaches to programs), worm (spreads by itself over a network), trojan horse (disguised as useful software), ransomware, spyware.
**Buffer overflow:** writing past the end of a buffer to overwrite the return address. Defences: bounds checks, stack canaries, **ASLR** (randomised addresses), **NX** (non-executable stack).
**Denial of Service (DoS/DDoS):** flooding to exhaust resources.
**Privilege escalation, social engineering, man-in-the-middle.**

blocks.x: Defence mechanisms
Firewalls, intrusion detection, patching, antivirus, encryption, logging and auditing, sandboxing (containers, virtual machines), and secure boot.
Security levels
Physical, network, operating system and application level: a chain is only as strong as its weakest link.
Least privilege + strong authentication + patching prevent most incidents.

qa.q: What is the principle of least privilege?
qa.a: Give each user or program only the minimum access rights it needs to do its job, which limits the harm from mistakes or attacks.

qa.q: What is the difference between an ACL and a capability list?
qa.a: An ACL is stored with each object and lists the domains that may access it. A capability list is stored with each domain and lists the objects it may access.

qa.q: Why are passwords stored as salted hashes?
qa.a: A hash hides the actual password, and a random salt makes identical passwords hash differently and stops rainbow-table attacks.

qa.q: What is a buffer overflow attack and one defence?
qa.a: Writing more data than a buffer holds to overwrite neighbouring memory, such as the return address. Defences include bounds checking, stack canaries, ASLR and non-executable stacks.

qa.q: What is the difference between a virus and a worm?
qa.a: A virus needs a host program and user action to spread; a worm spreads by itself across networks.

problems.q: Differentiate between protection and security in an operating system. Give one threat and one defence.
problems.a: Protection is the internal mechanism that controls access of programs, processes and users to resources defined by the system (permissions, modes). Security is the wider defence of the system against external and internal attacks, including authentication, encryption and network defence. Threat example: a virus or password guessing. Defence example: strong passwords with hashing, antivirus, firewalls.

rubric.t: Correct difference between protection and security

problems.q: Access matrix: domain D1 has F1: read; domain D2 has F1: read and F2: read, write; domain D3 has F1: read, write, execute. Write the access control list for F1 and the capability list for D2.
problems.a:
ACL for F1: D1 {read}; D2 {read}; D3 {read, write, execute}.
Capability list for D2: (F1, read) and (F2, read, write).

rubric.t: ACL for F1 with all three domains

problems.q: Explain how a buffer overflow attack works and list three defences used by modern operating systems and compilers.
problems.a:
A program copies input into a fixed-size buffer without checking its length. Extra data overwrites neighbouring memory on the stack, including the return address. The attacker sets the return address to injected code, so when the function returns, the attacker's code runs with the program's privileges.
Defences: bounds checking and safe functions; stack canaries that detect overwrites; non-executable stack (NX/DEP); address space layout randomisation (ASLR).

lessons.title: Linux practice: shell commands, permissions and processes
yt: linux commands for beginners chmod ps kill grep pipe
fork exec wait C program Linux

blocks.x: Linux is the most widely studied Unix-like OS. This lesson turns the theory into commands.
Navigating and files

x: `pwd` print working directory, `ls -l` long listing, `cd dir` change directory.
`mkdir`, `rmdir`, `touch file`, `cp a b`, `mv a b`, `rm file`, `rm -r dir`.
`cat`, `less`, `head -n 5 file`, `tail -f log` (follow a log).
`find . -name "*.c"`, `grep -n "main" file.c`, `wc -l file`.

blocks.x: Pipes and redirection

x: `>` overwrite, `>>` append, `<` input.
`ls | wc -l` sends the output of `ls` into `wc` and counts the files: a **pipe** is an IPC mechanism.
`2>&1` merges errors with output.

blocks.x: Permissions
`ls -l` shows `-rwxr-xr-- 1 anil dev 120 Oct 10 notes.sh`: type, owner, group, other. Each permission is a number: **r = 4, w = 2, x = 1**. So `rwx` = 7, `r-x` = 5, `r--` = 4.

x: `chmod 754 notes.sh` sets owner = rwx (7), group = r-x (5), others = r-- (4).
`chmod u+x file` adds execute for the owner; `chmod go-w file` removes write for group and others.
`chown user:group file` changes ownership.

blocks.x: Directories need **x** to enter them and **r** to list them.
Processes

x: `ps aux` list processes; `top` live view; `pstree` tree.
`kill PID` sends SIGTERM (polite stop), `kill -9 PID` sends SIGKILL (forced).
`command &` runs in the background; `jobs`, `fg`, `bg` manage jobs; `nice -n 10 cmd` lowers priority.
A process has a **PID** and a **PPID** (parent). The first process is `init`/`systemd` with PID 1.

blocks.x: fork and exec together
A shell starts a command by `fork()` (copy itself) then `exec()` (replace the child with the program), and `wait()` for it.
Output:

hello from the child via exec
child exit status: 0
After a successful `exec` the child's old code is gone; the new program runs in the same process (same PID).
Signals and inter-process communication
Signals (`SIGINT` from Ctrl+C, `SIGTERM`, `SIGKILL`, `SIGSEGV`) notify a process asynchronously. Other IPC: pipes, named pipes (FIFOs), message queues, shared memory and sockets.
Memory and disk tools
`free -h` memory use, `df -h` disk free, `du -sh dir` directory size, `mount` shows mounted file systems, `vmstat` for paging and swapping statistics.
chmod digits: r=4, w=2, x=1; add them for each of owner, group, other.

qa.q: What does chmod 754 do?
qa.a: It gives the owner read, write and execute (7), the group read and execute (5), and others read only (4).

qa.q: What is the difference between kill and kill -9?
qa.a: kill sends SIGTERM, which lets the process clean up and exit. kill -9 sends SIGKILL, which the process cannot catch or ignore.

qa.q: How does a shell run a program?
qa.a: It forks a child process, the child calls exec to replace itself with the program, and the shell waits for the child to finish.

qa.q: What does the pipe in ls | wc -l do?
qa.a: It connects the standard output of ls to the standard input of wc, which counts lines, so you get the number of entries.

qa.q: What does a directory's x permission mean?
qa.a: Permission to enter (traverse) the directory; r allows listing its names.

chmod 644 file gives the owner
quiz.why: 6 = 4 + 2 = read and write.

quiz.q: Which signal cannot be caught or ignored?
quiz.why: SIGKILL always terminates the process.

quiz.q: After exec succeeds, the process
o: runs a new program with the same PID
quiz.why: exec replaces the memory image, not the process identity.

quiz.q: The command to see running processes is
quiz.why: ps (or top) lists processes.

problems.a:
(a) find . -name "*.log" -size +1M
(b) grep -c "error" app.log
(c) ps aux | grep java | grep -v grep | wc -l

rubric.t: find command with name and size
Pipeline with ps, grep and wc

problems.q: Explain what the shell does when you type ls. Then explain the difference between >, >> and |, and what ls > out.txt 2>&1 does.
problems.a:
The shell reads the command, calls fork() to create a child process, the child calls exec() to replace itself with the ls program, and the parent calls wait() until the child ends.
> redirects output to a file, overwriting it; >> appends; | sends the output of one command as input to the next.
ls > out.txt 2>&1 sends standard output to out.txt and also sends standard error (stream 2) to the same place as stream 1.

social-internship-1.title: Social Internship 1
social-internship-1.tagline: Plan, run and report a community internship.

lessons.title: Understanding the social internship
yt: social internship community engagement students India
how to choose NGO internship project

blocks.x: A **social internship** is a structured period in which a student works with a community, NGO, school, government body or social enterprise to understand and help solve a real social problem. Your course lists Social Internship as a credit-bearing activity: the university sets the hours, mentor and format, so follow your official guidelines and notices first. This module is a **practical guide**, not a replacement for them.
Learning outcomes

x: Apply technical skills for social good (for example a digital literacy class, a simple website for an NGO, an IoT water-level sensor for a village tank).
Develop empathy, communication, teamwork and leadership.
Understand social problems and policy: education, health, environment, livelihoods, digital inclusion.
Practise professional skills: planning, documentation, reporting.
Connect to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

blocks.x: Typical steps

x: **Get guidelines** from your department: duration, credits, evaluation, report format, mentor.
**Choose a theme** and organisation.
**Get approval** from your internal mentor and an acceptance letter from the host.
**Plan** the work with objectives and a timeline.
**Do the work** and keep a daily/weekly diary.
**Prepare the report and presentation**; get a completion certificate from the host.
**Reflect** on learning.

blocks.x: Possible themes for engineering students

head: Theme
Example activities
rows: Teach UPI safety, smartphone basics, DigiLocker, cyber awareness
Free coding or maths classes for school students
Waste segregation drive, tree plantation, air-quality sensors
Simple soil-moisture or water-tank IoT prototype
Awareness camps with a hospital NGO, BMI/hygiene sessions
Help NGOs for the visually impaired use screen readers
Website or social-media page for local artisans

blocks.x: Choosing a good project
Is the need real (talk to the community)? Can you finish it in the time? Do you have the skills and permission? Can the NGO continue it after you leave? Does it avoid harm?
Ethics and safety

Respect dignity and consent; take photos only with permission; protect personal data; do not accept money from beneficiaries; for work with children follow child-safety rules; take a teammate on field visits; keep your family and mentor informed; avoid unsafe locations; follow the host's rules.
Roles
Student, internal mentor (faculty), external mentor (NGO/community), and beneficiaries. Communicate regularly with your mentor.
Social work starts with listening, not with solutions.

qa.q: What is a social internship?
qa.a: A structured, supervised period of working with a community or organisation to address a social need while learning practical and professional skills.

qa.q: How can engineering students contribute in a social internship?
qa.a: By using technical skills for digital literacy classes, websites for NGOs, simple IoT or software tools, environmental drives and awareness sessions.

qa.q: Why should you listen to the community before choosing a project?
qa.a: To make sure the project addresses a real need, builds trust and avoids imposing unwanted solutions.

qa.q: List ethical rules during a social internship.
qa.a: Respect dignity and consent, protect privacy and data, follow child-safety rules, avoid taking money from beneficiaries, and work safely under supervision.

qa.q: Who are the mentors in a social internship?
qa.a: An internal mentor from the university and an external mentor from the host organisation.

problems.q: What is a social internship and what are its three main objectives?
problems.a: A social internship is a structured experience in which a student works with a community, NGO or social organisation to understand and help address a real social issue. Objectives: develop empathy and social responsibility, apply classroom knowledge to real problems, and build skills such as communication, teamwork and reporting.

problems.q: Write a short proposal (5 to 6 lines) for a 4-week social internship on digital literacy for senior citizens: problem, goal, activities and expected outcome.
problems.a: Problem: many senior citizens in the neighbourhood cannot use UPI, video calls or government portals safely. Goal: help 20 senior citizens use these services confidently in 4 weeks. Activities: a survey of needs in week 1, weekly two-hour hands-on sessions in weeks 2 and 3, practice with a helper in week 4. Outcome: at least 15 of the 20 can complete a UPI payment and a video call on their own, shown by a short test.

rubric.t: Clear problem and goal with a number

problems.q: Of 120 households surveyed, 78 have no internet access and 30 of those say cost is the main reason. Find both percentages and suggest how to rank the need. Why is a sample chosen, and how can bias be reduced?
problems.a:
No access: 78 / 120 = 65%. Cost as the main reason: 30 / 78 = 38.5% of those without access (25% of all households). Since a majority lacks access, internet access and training are high-priority needs; combine with urgency and feasibility.
A sample saves time and cost when surveying everyone is not possible. Reduce bias by choosing households randomly, covering different areas, using neutral questions and asking everyone the same way.
