blocks.x: Theory of Computation (TOC) asks: **what can be computed, and how efficiently?** It studies abstract machines and the languages they accept.
Basic terms

x: **Alphabet (Σ):** a finite, non-empty set of symbols. Σ = {0, 1} is the binary alphabet.
**String:** a finite sequence of symbols from Σ. The **empty string** is ε (epsilon), with length 0.
**Length |w|:** number of symbols. |0110| = 4.
**Concatenation:** xy puts y after x. εw = wε = w.
**Substring, prefix, suffix:** for w = abc, prefixes are ε, a, ab, abc; suffixes are ε, c, bc, abc.
**Reversal w^R:** (abc)^R = cba.

blocks.x: Powers of an alphabet
Σ^k is the set of all strings of length k. For Σ = {0,1}: Σ^0 = {ε}, Σ^1 = {0,1}, Σ^2 = {00,01,10,11}. There are 2^k strings of length k.

x: **Σ\*** (Kleene closure) = Σ^0 ∪ Σ^1 ∪ Σ^2 ∪ … = all strings including ε.

blocks.x: Language
A **language** L is any subset of Σ\*. Examples over {0,1}:

x: L1 = strings that end in 01.
L2 = strings with equal number of 0s and 1s.
The empty language ∅ (no strings) is different from {ε} (one string, the empty string).

blocks.x: Operations on languages
Union L1 ∪ L2, intersection, complement (Σ\* − L), concatenation L1L2 = {xy | x ∈ L1, y ∈ L2}, Kleene star L\* (zero or more concatenations), reversal.
Chomsky hierarchy preview
Each class strictly contains the one above it in the table.
A language is just a set of strings; a machine "accepts" a language if it says yes exactly for the strings in it.

qa.a: A finite, non-empty set of symbols, such as {0,1} or {a,b}.

qa.q: Name the four classes of the Chomsky hierarchy with their machines.
qa.a: Regular (finite automata), context-free (pushdown automata), context-sensitive (linear bounded automata), and recursively enumerable (Turing machines).

lessons.title: Deterministic finite automata (DFA)
yt: DFA design examples theory of computation
DFA divisible by 3 construction

blocks.x: A **DFA** is a machine with a finite number of states that reads an input string one symbol at a time and, for each symbol, moves to exactly one next state.
Formal definition
A DFA is a 5-tuple **M = (Q, Σ, δ, q0, F)**:

x: Q: finite set of states
Σ: input alphabet
δ: Q × Σ → Q, the **transition function** (total: defined for every state and symbol)
q0 ∈ Q: start state
F ⊆ Q: set of accepting (final) states

blocks.x: A string w is **accepted** if starting from q0 and following δ on every symbol, we end in a state of F. The language of M is L(M) = {w | M accepts w}.
Representations
Transition diagram (circles for states, double circle for accepting, arrow for start) and transition table.
Example 1: strings ending in 01
States: q0 (start, nothing useful seen), q1 (last symbol was 0), q2 (last two were 01, accepting).
Trace of 1101: q0 →1→ q0 →1→ q0 →0→ q1 →1→ q2: accepted.
Example 2: binary numbers divisible by 3
Track the remainder of the number read so far. Reading bit b turns value v into 2v + b, so new remainder = (2r + b) mod 3. States 0, 1, 2 are the remainders; state 0 is start and accepting.
Check 110 (= 6): 0 →1→ 1 →1→ 0 →0→ 0: accepted. Check 101 (= 5): 0 →1→ 1 →0→ 2 →1→ 2: rejected. (This was verified by program for all numbers below 20.)
Design tips

x: Decide what the machine must **remember** (a remainder, last symbols, a count).
One state per distinct piece of memory.
Add a **dead (trap) state** for strings that can never be accepted.
Test with short accepted and rejected strings.

blocks.x: Counting-type languages

"Strings with an even number of 0s" needs 2 states (even, odd). "Exactly two 1s" needs 4 states (zero, one, two, more than two (dead)). A DFA cannot count without bound, so {0^n 1^n} is **not** regular.
Complement and product

x: Complement: swap accepting and non-accepting states of a (complete) DFA.
Intersection or union: build the **product automaton** with state pairs (p, q).

blocks.x: A DFA has exactly one move for every (state, symbol) pair; its states are its memory.

qa.q: Define a DFA formally.
qa.a: A 5-tuple (Q, Σ, δ, q0, F) where Q is the finite state set, Σ the alphabet, δ: Q×Σ→Q the transition function, q0 the start state and F the set of accepting states.

qa.q: What is a dead state?
qa.a: A non-accepting state from which the machine can never reach an accepting state; it absorbs unwanted strings.

qa.q: How do you complement a DFA's language?
qa.a: Make the DFA complete, then swap accepting and non-accepting states.

qa.q: How many states does a DFA for "binary numbers divisible by 3" need?
qa.a: Three states representing remainders 0, 1 and 2.

qa.q: Why can a DFA not recognise 0^n 1^n?
qa.a: It has only finitely many states and so cannot remember an unbounded count of 0s.

problems.a:
States are the remainder 0, 1, 2 (start and final = remainder 0). Reading bit b changes the value v to 2v + b, so the new remainder is (2r + b) mod 3: from 0: 0 goes to 0, 1 goes to 1; from 1: 0 goes to 2, 1 goes to 0; from 2: 0 goes to 1, 1 goes to 2.
110: 0 -1-> 1 -1-> 0 -0-> 0, accepted (6). 101: 0 -1-> 1 -0-> 2 -1-> 2, rejected (5).

lessons.title: NFA, epsilon-NFA and subset construction
yt: NFA to DFA conversion subset construction
epsilon NFA closure conversion

blocks.x: A **Nondeterministic Finite Automaton (NFA)** may have zero, one or several possible moves on a symbol. It accepts a string if **some** sequence of choices leads to an accepting state.
Definition
NFA = (Q, Σ, δ, q0, F) but **δ: Q × Σ → 2^Q** (a set of next states, possibly empty). An **ε-NFA** also allows δ(q, ε), moving without reading input.
Example: ends with 01
q0 loops on 0 and 1; on 0 it may also go to q1; q1 goes to q2 on 1 (q2 accepting).
This NFA has 3 states and a very simple design: it "guesses" when the final 01 begins.
Subset construction (NFA → DFA)
Each DFA state is a **set of NFA states**.

x: Start with {q0} (for ε-NFA, its ε-closure).
For each reachable set S and symbol a, the next set is the union of δ(q, a) over q ∈ S.
A set is accepting if it contains an NFA accepting state.

blocks.x: Applying this to the example (verified by program) gives only three reachable sets:
This is the same machine as the DFA of the previous lesson. In the worst case an n-state NFA needs **2^n** DFA states.
ε-closure
ε-closure(q) = all states reachable from q using only ε moves (including q). Used to remove ε-transitions: δ'(q, a) = ε-closure of δ(ε-closure(q), a).
Equivalence
NFAs, ε-NFAs and DFAs all accept exactly the **regular languages**; non-determinism gives convenience, not extra power.
Where NFAs help
Easy construction from regular expressions (Thompson's construction), union of languages (new start state with ε to both), concatenation and star.
NFA = parallel guessing; DFA = one deterministic path. Both recognise the same languages.

qa.q: How does an NFA differ from a DFA?
qa.a: An NFA can have several or no transitions for a state and symbol (and ε transitions), and accepts if any path reaches an accepting state. A DFA has exactly one transition per state and symbol.

qa.q: Does an NFA recognise more languages than a DFA?
qa.a: No. Both recognise exactly the regular languages, although the DFA may need exponentially more states.

qa.q: What is ε-closure?
qa.a: The set of states reachable from a state by following only ε-transitions, including the state itself.

qa.q: Outline the subset construction.
qa.a: Start from the ε-closure of the NFA start state, repeatedly compute the set of states reachable on each symbol for every new set, and mark a set accepting if it contains an NFA final state.

problems.q: Give three differences between a DFA and an NFA. Do they accept the same class of languages?
problems.a: A DFA has exactly one transition for each state and symbol; an NFA may have zero, one or many. An NFA may have epsilon moves (in epsilon-NFA). A DFA follows a single path; an NFA accepts if at least one path ends in a final state. They accept the same class: regular languages.

problems.a: epsilon-closure(q0) = {q0, q1, q2}: the states reachable using only epsilon moves, including q0 itself. A DFA built by subset construction has at most 2^n states: 2^4 = 16 (many are usually unreachable).

lessons.title: Regular expressions and conversion with automata

DFA to regular expression state elimination Arden's theorem

blocks.x: A **regular expression (RE)** describes a language using three operations.
Definition
Over alphabet Σ:

x: ∅, ε and each symbol a are REs.
If R and S are REs then **R + S** (union, written | in programs), **RS** (concatenation) and **R\*** (star) are REs.

blocks.x: Precedence: star highest, then concatenation, then union.
Examples over {0,1}

x: `(0+1)*01` — strings ending in 01.
`0*10*10*` — strings with exactly two 1s.
`(00)*` — even number of 0s only (no 1s).
`1(0+1)*0` — starts with 1 and ends with 0.

blocks.x: Algebraic laws
RE → ε-NFA (Thompson's construction)
Build small machines for ε, a; combine by union (new start with ε to both), concatenation (ε from the first's final to the second's start) and star (ε loops back and a bypass).
DFA → RE

x: **State elimination:** remove states one at a time, replacing paths through them with RE labels on edges.
**Arden's theorem:** if R = Q + RP and ε ∉ P then R = QP\*. Write one equation per state and solve.

blocks.x: Example: language of a DFA where state A (start, final) loops on 0 and goes to B on 1; B goes back to A on 1 and loops on 0 gives (0 + 10\*1)\*.
Regular expressions in practice
Used in `grep`, text editors, validators and lexical analysers (compiler design). Python example:

import re
pattern = re.compile(r'^[01]*01$')
for s in ["1101", "0110", "01", "1"]:
    print(s, bool(pattern.match(s)))
phone = re.compile(r'^[6-9]\d{9}$')
print(bool(phone.match("9876543210")), bool(phone.match("1234567890")))
Output:

1101 True
0110 False
01 True
1 False
True False
Closure properties of regular languages
Closed under union, intersection, complement, concatenation, star, reversal, difference. Decision problems (emptiness, membership, equivalence) are all decidable.
RE, DFA, NFA and ε-NFA describe exactly the same class: the regular languages.

qa.q: Write a regular expression for strings over {0,1} that end with 01.
State Arden's theorem.
qa.a: If P and Q are regular expressions and ε is not in P, then the equation R = Q + RP has the unique solution R = QP*.

qa.q: How is a RE converted to an NFA?
qa.a: By Thompson's construction: build base automata for symbols and combine them for union, concatenation and star using ε-transitions.

qa.q: Are regular languages closed under complement?
qa.a: Yes. Complete a DFA and swap accepting and non-accepting states.

qa.q: Give one practical use of regular expressions.
qa.a: Pattern searching with grep, input validation, and tokenising source code in the lexical analysis phase of a compiler.

problems.q: Show that (a + b)* and (a*b*)* describe the same language. State Arden's theorem.
problems.a:
(a + b)* generates every string over {a, b}. In (a*b*)* any string can be broken into letters, and each letter fits one chunk a*b* (a single a or a single b), so (a*b*)* also produces every string. Both include epsilon. They are equal.
Arden's theorem: if P does not contain epsilon, the equation R = Q + RP has the unique solution R = QP*. It is used to convert a finite automaton into a regular expression.

lessons.title: Pumping lemma, DFA minimisation and Moore/Mealy machines
yt: pumping lemma for regular languages proof examples
DFA minimization table filling method
Moore and Mealy machine

blocks.x: Pumping lemma for regular languages
**Statement:** if L is regular, there is a **pumping length p** such that every string w ∈ L with |w| ≥ p can be split w = xyz where

x: |xy| ≤ p,
x y^i z ∈ L for every i ≥ 0.

blocks.x: Idea: a long string forces a DFA to repeat a state (pigeonhole), so the loop can be repeated or removed. It is used only to **prove a language is not regular** (proof by contradiction), never to prove regularity.
Example: L = {0^n 1^n | n ≥ 0} is not regular

Assume regular with pumping length p. Take w = 0^p 1^p. Since |xy| ≤ p, y consists only of 0s. Then xy²z has more 0s than 1s, so it is not in L. Contradiction. Other non-regular languages: {ww^R}, {a^n b^m | n > m}, {a^(n²)}, balanced parentheses, primes.
DFA minimisation (table-filling / Myhill-Nerode)
Two states are **equivalent** if no string distinguishes them (they lead to the same accept/reject outcome).

x: Remove unreachable states.
Mark every pair (accepting, non-accepting) as distinguishable.
Repeat: mark (p, q) if for some symbol a the pair δ(p,a), δ(q,a) is already marked.
Unmarked pairs are equivalent; merge them.

blocks.x: The result is the **unique minimal DFA** (up to renaming). Example: states A (start), B, C, D, E with F = {E}; if transitions make B≡D and C≡E in function, they merge into fewer states.
Myhill-Nerode theorem

A language is regular iff it has finitely many equivalence classes of strings under the relation "x ~ y if for all z, xz ∈ L ⇔ yz ∈ L". The number of classes equals the number of states of the minimal DFA.
Machines with output

x: **Moore machine:** output depends only on the **state**. For n input symbols it produces n+1 outputs (output of the start state first).
**Mealy machine:** output depends on the **state and current input** (on transitions). It produces n outputs for n inputs.
Any Moore machine has an equivalent Mealy machine and vice versa (a Mealy may need extra states to convert to Moore).

blocks.x: Example Mealy: output 1 whenever the input has just completed "11". Used in sequential circuit design and protocol controllers.
Applications of finite automata
Lexical analysis, text search, vending machines, traffic lights, protocol state machines, game AI.
Pumping lemma proves non-regularity; table filling gives the smallest DFA.

qa.q: State the pumping lemma for regular languages.
qa.a: If L is regular there is a length p such that any string w in L with |w| ≥ p can be written xyz with |y| > 0, |xy| ≤ p and x y^i z in L for all i ≥ 0.

qa.q: Can the pumping lemma prove that a language is regular?
qa.a: No. It gives a necessary condition only, so it can only be used to show non-regularity.

qa.q: Prove briefly that 0^n 1^n is not regular.
qa.a: For w = 0^p 1^p, y lies inside the 0s, so pumping y up gives more 0s than 1s, a string outside the language, contradicting the lemma.

qa.q: What is the difference between Moore and Mealy machines?
qa.a: In a Moore machine the output depends only on the current state; in a Mealy machine it depends on the state and the current input.

qa.q: What does the Myhill-Nerode theorem say?
qa.a: A language is regular exactly when the number of Myhill-Nerode equivalence classes is finite, and that number equals the size of the minimal DFA.

problems.q: State the pumping lemma for regular languages. For what is it used?
problems.a: If L is regular there is a pumping length p such that every string s in L with |s| >= p can be split into xyz with |xy| <= p, |y| >= 1 and x y^i z in L for every i >= 0. It is used to prove that a language is not regular (it cannot prove regularity).

problems.q: Prove that L = { a^n b^n | n >= 0 } is not regular.
problems.a: Assume L is regular with pumping length p. Take s = a^p b^p. Since |xy| <= p, y consists only of a's, say y = a^k with k >= 1. Pumping with i = 2 gives a^(p+k) b^p, which has more a's than b's and is not in L. Contradiction, so L is not regular.

problems.q: A DFA has states A (start), B, C, D (final), E. Transitions: A on a or b goes to B or C respectively (a to B, b to C); B, C and E each go to D on a and to E on b; D goes to D on a and to E on b. Minimise it and describe the language. Then state the difference between Moore and Mealy machines.
problems.a:
B, C and E have identical behaviour (a to D, b to E, none final), so they merge into one state M. A on a or b goes to M; M on a goes to D, on b stays in M; D on a stays in D, on b goes to M. Three states: A, M, D. The language is strings of length at least 2 that end in a.
Moore machine: the output depends only on the current state. Mealy machine: the output depends on the current state and the input symbol (on the transition).

lessons.title: Grammars, derivations and the Chomsky hierarchy
yt: context free grammar derivation tree leftmost rightmost
ambiguity in context free grammar

blocks.x: A **grammar** G = (V, T, P, S) generates strings:

x: V: variables (non-terminals), T: terminals, P: production rules, S: start symbol.

blocks.x: Context-free grammars (CFG)
Every production has a single non-terminal on the left: A → α, where α is a string of terminals and non-terminals.
Example: balanced a^n b^n
S → aSb | ε Derivation of aabb: S ⇒ aSb ⇒ aaSbb ⇒ aabb.
Example: arithmetic expressions
E → E + T | T, T → T \* F | F, F → ( E ) | id This grammar encodes precedence (\* binds tighter than +) and left associativity.
Example: palindromes over {a,b}
S → aSa | bSb | a | b | ε
Derivations and parse trees

x: **Leftmost derivation:** always expand the leftmost non-terminal; **rightmost** expands the rightmost.
A **parse (derivation) tree** has the start symbol at the root, non-terminals at internal nodes and terminals at leaves; the leaves read left to right give the **yield**.

blocks.x: Ambiguity

A grammar is **ambiguous** if some string has two different parse trees (equivalently, two leftmost derivations). Example: E → E + E | E \* E | id gives two trees for id + id \* id. Fix by rewriting with precedence levels as above. Some languages are **inherently ambiguous** (every grammar is ambiguous), and ambiguity is undecidable in general.
Simplification of CFGs

x: Remove **ε-productions** (nullable variables).
Remove **unit productions** A → B.
Remove **useless symbols** (non-generating, unreachable).

blocks.x: Normal forms

x: **Chomsky Normal Form (CNF):** every rule is A → BC or A → a. Any derivation of a string of length n takes 2n − 1 steps.
**Greibach Normal Form (GNF):** A → aα where α is a string of variables. Every step produces one terminal.

blocks.x: Hierarchy of grammars
CFGs generate nested structures such as brackets and expressions; regular languages cannot.

qa.q: Define a context-free grammar.
qa.a: A 4-tuple (V, T, P, S) of variables, terminals, productions of the form A → α with a single variable on the left, and a start symbol.

qa.a: One in which some string has two or more distinct parse trees (leftmost derivations).

qa.a: It is unambiguous and builds in operator precedence and associativity, so every expression has one parse tree.

S => aSb => aaSbb => aabb (the last step uses S to epsilon).
Ambiguity: id + id * id has two different parse trees: one groups (id + id) * id and the other groups id + (id * id). A grammar with more than one parse tree for some string is ambiguous.

problems.q: Convert S to aSb | ab into Chomsky normal form.
problems.a: Introduce A to a and B to b. S to ab becomes S to AB. S to aSb becomes S to ASB, which has three symbols on the right, so introduce X to SB and write S to AX. CNF: S to AX | AB, X to SB, A to a, B to b. Every production is either two non-terminals or one terminal.

lessons.title: Pushdown automata (PDA)
yt: pushdown automata introduction design a^n b^n
PDA to CFG conversion

blocks.x: A **pushdown automaton** is a finite automaton plus a **stack** of unbounded size. The stack gives it memory that can count and match, so it recognises context-free languages.
Definition
PDA = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q0, Z0, F):

x: Γ: stack alphabet, Z0: initial stack symbol.
δ(q, a, X) = set of (p, γ): in state q, reading a (or ε) with X on top of the stack, move to p and replace X by the string γ.

blocks.x: Acceptance by **final state** or by **empty stack**; the two are equivalent in power.
Example: L = {a^n b^n | n ≥ 1}
Idea: push an A for each a; pop an A for each b; accept if the stack returns to Z0.

x: δ(q0, a, A) = (q0, AA)
δ(q1, ε, Z0) = (q2, Z0), q2 accepting.

blocks.x: Trace of aabb: stack Z0 → AZ0 → AAZ0 → AZ0 → Z0 → accept.
Example: palindromes w w^R

Needs **non-determinism**: the machine pushes the first half and *guesses* the middle, then pops while matching. A deterministic PDA cannot find the middle, so **DPDA is strictly weaker than NPDA** (unlike DFA and NFA).
Equivalence with CFG

x: CFG → PDA: the stack simulates leftmost derivations (push start symbol; replace a variable by a production right side; match terminals with input).
PDA → CFG: variables [p X q] meaning "going from p to q while popping X".

blocks.x: So context-free languages = languages accepted by PDAs.
Closure properties of CFLs
Closed under union, concatenation, star, reversal, and substitution. **Not closed** under intersection or complement. Intersection with a regular language is context-free.
Pumping lemma for CFLs

If L is context-free there is p such that any w ∈ L with |w| ≥ p can be written uvxyz with |vy| > 0, |vxy| ≤ p, and u v^i x y^i z ∈ L for all i ≥ 0. Proof that {a^n b^n c^n} is not context-free: any window of length ≤ p can touch at most two kinds of symbol, so pumping unbalances the counts.
Applications
Parsers in compilers use PDA-like stack machines (LL, LR parsers) for checking program syntax such as matching braces.
Stack = unbounded but last-in-first-out memory: ideal for nesting.

qa.q: What extra component does a PDA have over an FA?
qa.a: A stack, which lets it remember an unbounded amount of information in last-in-first-out order.

qa.q: Is every NPDA equivalent to a DPDA?
qa.a: No. Deterministic PDAs accept a strictly smaller class of languages; for example, the palindrome language w w^R needs non-determinism.

qa.q: Design idea of a PDA for a^n b^n.
qa.a: Push a symbol for every a, pop one for every b, and accept when the input ends and the stack holds only the bottom marker.

qa.q: Are context-free languages closed under intersection?
qa.a: No. For example {a^n b^n c^m} and {a^m b^n c^n} are context-free but their intersection {a^n b^n c^n} is not.

qa.q: What does the pumping lemma for CFLs say?
qa.a: Long strings split as uvxyz with |vy| > 0 and |vxy| ≤ p such that u v^i x y^i z stays in the language for all i ≥ 0.

problems.q: Why can a finite automaton not accept { a^n b^n } but a pushdown automaton can?
problems.a: A finite automaton has a fixed number of states, so it cannot count an unbounded number of a's. A pushdown automaton has a stack, which gives unbounded memory: it pushes a symbol for each a and pops one for each b, and accepts if the counts match.

problems.q: Trace the PDA for a^n b^n on the input aabb, showing the stack after each symbol (bottom marker Z).
problems.a: Start: stack Z. Read a: push A, stack AZ. Read a: push A, stack AAZ. Read b: pop A, stack AZ. Read b: pop A, stack Z. Input finished and only Z remains, so the string is accepted.

rubric.t: Correct stack contents at each step

problems.q: Describe a PDA and a grammar for even-length palindromes w w^R over {a, b}. Why is nondeterminism needed?
problems.a:
Grammar: S to aSa | bSb | epsilon. PDA: in the first phase push each symbol read; at some point guess nondeterministically that the middle has been reached and move to the second phase; in the second phase pop and compare with each input symbol; accept when input ends and the stack returns to Z.
Nondeterminism is needed because the PDA cannot know where the middle of the input is, so it must try every possible midpoint.

lessons.title: Turing machines
yt: turing machine introduction design examples
turing machine a^n b^n construction

blocks.x: A **Turing machine (TM)** has a finite control and an **infinite tape** divided into cells, with a head that can read, write and move left or right. It is the standard model of what is *computable*.
Formal definition
TM = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q0, B, F):

x: Γ ⊇ Σ is the tape alphabet; B ∈ Γ − Σ is the blank.
δ: Q × Γ → Q × Γ × {L, R} (deterministic): read a symbol, write a symbol, move, change state.
Accepts when it reaches a state in F. It may also **halt and reject**, or **loop forever**.

blocks.x: Example: the a^n b^n idea

To accept {a^n b^n}: repeatedly (1) mark the leftmost unmarked a with X, (2) move right to the first unmarked b and mark it Y, (3) return left. When no a's remain, check that no unmarked b's remain. Unlike a PDA the same idea extends to a^n b^n c^n, which a PDA cannot do.
Example: unary increment
Tape 111 (value 3), head on first 1: move right across 1s; on blank write 1; halt. Result 1111.
Languages

x: **Recursively enumerable (RE) / Turing-recognisable:** some TM accepts exactly the strings in L (may loop on others).
**Recursive / Turing-decidable:** some TM that **always halts** accepts L.

blocks.x: Every recursive language is RE; the reverse is false.
Variants (all equally powerful)

x: Multi-tape TM, multi-track tape, two-way infinite tape.
**Non-deterministic TM**: accepted languages same as deterministic TMs (simulation may be exponentially slower).
TM with stay option.

blocks.x: A multi-tape machine can be simulated by a single-tape machine with a quadratic slowdown.
Church-Turing thesis

Any effectively computable function can be computed by a Turing machine. It is a thesis (not a theorem) supported by every alternative model (lambda calculus, recursive functions, RAM machines) turning out equivalent.
Universal Turing machine
A TM that takes the description of any TM M and an input w and simulates M on w. It is the theoretical model of a stored-program computer.
Linear bounded automaton
A TM whose head cannot move beyond the input; it recognises context-sensitive languages.
TM power = any algorithm. Halting and looping are the two sides of "recognise" versus "decide".

qa.q: Write the components of a Turing machine.
qa.a: States, input alphabet, tape alphabet with a blank, transition function, start state, blank symbol and accepting states, working on an infinite tape.

qa.q: What is the difference between recursive and recursively enumerable languages?
qa.a: For a recursive language some TM halts on every input with the correct answer. For an RE language a TM accepts strings in the language but may loop forever on others.

qa.q: State the Church-Turing thesis.
qa.a: Anything that can be computed by an effective procedure can be computed by a Turing machine.

qa.q: Does adding more tapes make a TM more powerful?
qa.a: No. A multi-tape TM can be simulated by a single-tape TM, only with some slowdown.

qa.q: What is a universal Turing machine?
qa.a: A TM that can simulate any other TM given its encoding and an input, like a general-purpose stored-program computer.

The tape is an infinite memory on which the head reads and writes.

problems.a:
Replace + with 1, then go to the end and erase the last 1 (replace it with a blank). The tape holds 11111, which is 3 + 2 = 5.
Church-Turing thesis: anything that can be computed by an effective procedure can be computed by a Turing machine. Variants such as multi-tape and nondeterministic Turing machines have the same power as the basic machine.

lessons.title: Decidability, the halting problem and reductions
yt: halting problem proof undecidability
decidable undecidable problems reduction rice theorem

blocks.x: A problem is **decidable** if a Turing machine halts with the right yes/no answer for every input. Some problems are **undecidable**: no algorithm can exist.
Counting argument
There are only countably many Turing machines (programs are finite strings) but uncountably many languages, so most languages have no machine at all.
The halting problem
**HALT = {⟨M, w⟩ | M halts on input w}** is undecidable. Proof sketch by contradiction (diagonalisation):

x: Suppose a decider H(M, w) exists.
Build D(M): run H(M, M); if H says "halts", loop forever; if H says "loops", halt.
Run D on its own code D. If D halts, then H said D loops on D (so D loops), contradiction. If D loops, then H said it halts, contradiction.

blocks.x: Therefore H cannot exist. HALT is recursively enumerable (run M, wait) but not recursive.
Other undecidable problems

x: Acceptance A_TM = {⟨M, w⟩ | M accepts w}.
Emptiness E_TM: is L(M) = ∅?
Equivalence of two TMs.
Post Correspondence Problem (PCP).
Whether a CFG is ambiguous; whether two CFGs generate the same language.
**Rice's theorem:** every non-trivial property of the *language* a TM accepts is undecidable.

blocks.x: Decidable problems (examples)

x: For DFAs: acceptance, emptiness, equivalence.
For CFGs: membership (CYK algorithm), emptiness.
Whether a number is prime, whether a graph is connected.

blocks.x: Reductions

To show B undecidable, **reduce a known undecidable problem A to B**: a computable map turning instances of A into instances of B with the same answer. If B were decidable then A would be too, a contradiction.
Closure properties
Recursive languages are closed under complement; RE languages are not. A language L is recursive iff both L and its complement are RE.
Practical meaning
No program can perfectly decide, for all programs, whether they terminate, are bug-free, or equal each other. Static analysis tools therefore use approximations.
Undecidable does not mean hard; it means no algorithm solves every instance.

qa.q: What is the halting problem and is it decidable?
qa.a: Given a program and an input, decide whether the program eventually halts. It is undecidable: no algorithm solves it for all pairs.

qa.q: Why is HALT recursively enumerable?
qa.a: A TM can simulate M on w and accept if the simulation halts, so halting instances are recognised, though non-halting ones are never confirmed.

qa.q: What is a reduction?
qa.a: A computable transformation of instances of one problem into another so that answers are preserved. It transfers decidability or undecidability between problems.

qa.q: If a language and its complement are both RE, what follows?

problems.q: Differentiate between decidable and Turing-recognizable languages with an example of each.
problems.a: A decidable language has a Turing machine (a decider) that halts on every input with accept or reject; example: whether a number is prime. A Turing-recognizable language has a machine that accepts every string in the language but may loop forever on strings outside it; example: the halting problem language.

problems.q: Explain the halting problem and sketch why it is undecidable.
problems.a: The halting problem asks whether a given program halts on a given input. Suppose a decider H exists. Build a program D that, given a program P, runs H(P, P) and does the opposite: if H says halts, D loops forever; if H says loops, D halts. Running D on itself: if D(D) halts then H says halts so D loops: contradiction; if D(D) loops then H says loops so D halts: contradiction. So H cannot exist.

problems.q: If A reduces to B and B is decidable, what follows? Use the undecidability of halting to show that "does a program ever print hello" is undecidable.
problems.a:
If A reduces to B and B is decidable then A is decidable (contrapositive: if A is undecidable, B is undecidable).
Given (M, w), build M' that simulates M on w and prints hello only if M halts. M' prints hello exactly when M halts on w. A decider for the print-hello problem would therefore decide the halting problem, which is impossible. So it is undecidable.

blocks.x: Decidable does not mean practical. Complexity theory classifies decidable problems by the **time** (or space) needed as input size n grows.
Class P
Problems solvable by a **deterministic** TM in polynomial time O(n^k). Examples: sorting, shortest path, matching, primality (AKS), linear programming.
Class NP
Problems whose "yes" answers can be **verified** in polynomial time given a certificate; equivalently solvable by a **non-deterministic** TM in polynomial time. Examples:

x: **SAT:** is there an assignment satisfying a Boolean formula?
**Hamiltonian path / TSP (decision)**
**Subset sum, Clique, Vertex cover, Graph colouring (k ≥ 3)**

blocks.x: P ⊆ NP. Whether **P = NP** is the biggest open question (Clay Millennium Prize, 1,000,000 USD).
Reductions and completeness
A **polynomial-time reduction** A ≤p B converts instances of A into instances of B in polynomial time.

x: **NP-hard:** every problem in NP reduces to it (may be outside NP).
**NP-complete:** NP-hard **and** in NP.

blocks.x: **Cook-Levin theorem (1971):** SAT is NP-complete. Then other problems are shown NP-complete by reducing from SAT: SAT ≤p 3-SAT ≤p Clique ≤p Vertex Cover, etc. If any NP-complete problem is solved in polynomial time, then P = NP.
Quick comparison of growth
For n = 50: n² = 2,500 but 2^n ≈ 1.1 × 10^15 steps. Exponential algorithms become impossible quickly.

head: Class
Meaning
rows: At least as hard as NP-complete

blocks.x: Coping with NP-hard problems
Approximation algorithms, heuristics (genetic algorithms, simulated annealing), special cases, randomised algorithms, and exponential-time algorithms with pruning (branch and bound).
Space classes
L ⊆ NL ⊆ P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE = NPSPACE ⊆ EXPTIME (Savitch's theorem gives PSPACE = NPSPACE).
Verifying is easy for NP; finding may be hard. NP-complete problems are all equally hard to each other.

qa.q: Define the classes P and NP.
qa.a: P is the set of decision problems solvable in polynomial time by a deterministic machine. NP is the set solvable in polynomial time by a non-deterministic machine, i.e. whose solutions are verifiable in polynomial time.

qa.q: What is an NP-complete problem?
qa.a: A problem that is in NP and to which every problem in NP can be reduced in polynomial time.

qa.q: What does the Cook-Levin theorem state?
qa.a: The Boolean satisfiability problem SAT is NP-complete.

qa.q: Is every NP-hard problem in NP?
qa.a: No. NP-hard problems need not be decision problems or have verifiable certificates; the halting problem is NP-hard but not in NP.

qa.q: What happens if an NP-complete problem is shown to be in P?
qa.a: Then P = NP.

problems.q: Define the classes P and NP. Is P a subset of NP?
problems.a: P is the set of decision problems solvable by a deterministic machine in polynomial time. NP is the set of decision problems whose solutions can be verified in polynomial time (equivalently solved by a nondeterministic machine in polynomial time). Yes, P is a subset of NP, because anything solvable quickly can be verified quickly. Whether P = NP is open.

rubric.t: P is a subset of NP

problems.q: What does NP-complete mean? What follows if one NP-complete problem is solved in polynomial time? Name the first problem proved NP-complete and two others.
problems.a: A problem is NP-complete if it is in NP and every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time. If one NP-complete problem is in P then all of NP is in P, so P = NP. SAT was the first (Cook-Levin theorem). Others: 3-SAT, Clique, Vertex Cover, Hamiltonian Cycle, Subset Sum.

problems.q: State the relation between Vertex Cover and Independent Set. For the path a-b-c-d-e (edges ab, bc, cd, de) show a vertex cover of size 2 and the matching independent set.
problems.a:
A set S is an independent set if and only if its complement V minus S is a vertex cover, so one problem reduces to the other in polynomial time.
Vertex cover {b, d} covers ab, bc, cd and de. Its complement {a, c, e} is an independent set because no two of them are adjacent.
